Description: Sword linked to the last independent Nawab of Bengal, symbol of resistance against British East India Company. The blade is steel with a curved form typical of 18th-century Indo-Persian swords. Its association with Siraj-ud-Daulah makes it a powerful emblem of the Battle of Plassey and the beginning of colonial rule in the Indian subcontinent.

Used by Isa Khan against Mughal forces, emblem of Bengal’s independence. This bronze cannon is a massive piece of artillery, cast with decorative rings and possibly inscriptions. Isa Khan was a leader of the Baro-Bhuiyan confederacy who resisted Mughal expansion into Bengal. The cannon represents the fierce resistance and military capability of the region before it came under full Mughal control.

Finding_Place: Bengal (exact provenance unrecorded; acquired through historical Bengal collections)
Description: A steel combat helmet of the kulah khud type, representing the military material culture of the independent Bengal Sultanate. The skull is formed by hand-hammering a single piece of steel into a hemispherical dome with a pointed or slightly conical top, a form derived from Central Asian and Persian military traditions that entered Bengal through Turkic and Afghan rulers during the early Sultanate period. The exterior surface bears engraved or chiseled floral and geometric decoration, with a band of Quranic or Persian calligraphic inscriptions running along the lower rim in naskh or nasta'liq script — a standard feature of high-status Islamic military equipment of the period. A central spike socket (mighfer) surmounts the dome, flanked by one or two plume holders for ceremonial egret feathers. A riveted chainmail aventail (bargustawan) hangs from the lower edge, originally covering the neck, shoulders, and sides of the face. A sliding nasal bar is attached at the front. The interior retains visible hammer marks from its manufacture. The helmet reflects the synthesis of Central Asian, Persian, and local Bengali metalworking traditions that characterized Sultanate-era arms production in Bengal, and stands as one of the few surviving pieces of military headgear from this period held in a Bangladeshi public collection.

Coins inscribed with ruler’s name, Islamic phrases, mint city; ornate calligraphy. These gold dinars and tankas were struck by various sultans of the independent Bengal Sultanate, including rulers like Ghiyasuddin Iwaz Shah, Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah, and Alauddin Hussain Shah. The coins feature elegant Arabic script and sometimes the Bengali date. They reveal the economic prosperity and political sovereignty of medieval Bengal.

Handwritten letter by Nobel laureate poet Rabindranath Tagore. The letter is written in Bengali script on paper, likely addressed to a contemporary or discussing literary or social matters. Tagore's intimate correspondence provides insight into his thoughts, creative process, and relationships. Such manuscripts are invaluable for understanding the cultural renaissance of Bengal in the early 20th century.

Iconic sketches depicting human suffering during famine; cornerstone of modern Bangladeshi art. Zainul Abedin created a series of ink drawings in 1943 documenting the Bengal Famine. Using Chinese ink on paper, he portrayed skeletal figures, desperate crowds, and scenes of death on the streets of Calcutta. The raw, unflinching realism of these sketches shocked the world and established Abedin as a pioneering modernist artist in South Asia. These works also served as a powerful critique of British colonial policies and indifference.

Watercolor depicting Nabanna festival celebrating new rice harvest. In this vibrant work, Abedin moves away from tragedy to celebrate the resilience of rural life. The painting shows farmers gathering ripe paddy, women cooking the first rice of the season, and the community sharing in the abundance. The composition is filled with movement and earthy colors, reflecting the cyclical nature of agricultural life and the hope that follows hardship. The Nabanna festival remains an important cultural event in Bangladesh.

Depicts Santal men and women in traditional dress with dignity. Abedin was deeply interested in the indigenous Santal community of Bengal. This watercolor portrays a peaceful village scene: Santal women in red-bordered white saris carrying water pots, men in loincloths working or playing drums. Unlike ethnographic illustrations that otherize, Abedin’s treatment gives the Santals a sense of agency and humanity, celebrating their distinct culture as an integral part of Bengal’s heritage.

Artifact_Name: A descriptive catalogue of the Sanskrit and Bengali manuscripts
Description: Rare manuscripts in Sanskrit and Bengali covering philosophy, religion, literature. The collection includes palm-leaf manuscripts of Hindu religious texts like the Bhagavata Purana, Buddhist philosophical treatises, and medical works (Ayurveda). Some are illustrated with miniature paintings. These fragile artifacts are preserved in climate-controlled cases and are crucial for studying the intellectual history of pre-modern Bengal. They also demonstrate the long tradition of manuscript culture in the region before the printing press.

Four-armed Vishnu holding conch, discus, mace, lotus. Carved from fine-grained black basalt, this Pala-period sculpture stands approximately 1 meter tall. Vishnu is shown in a rigid frontal pose (samabhanga) wearing a tall cylindrical crown (kiritamukuta). The four attributes are held in his four hands: shankha (conch), chakra (discus), gada (mace), and padma (lotus). The figure is flanked by two small attendants or personifications of his consorts, Lakshmi and Saraswati. The carving is crisp and highly polished, typical of the Pala stone carving tradition.

Vishnu as boar rescuing earth goddess Bhudevi. This relief panel depicts the third avatar of Vishnu. The god has the body of a man and the head of a wild boar. He raises the earth goddess (personified as a small female figure) on his left tusk while trampling the serpent king Shesha. The composition is dynamic, with swirling lines suggesting the cosmic waters. Below, figures of sages and gods witness the event. The iconography follows the Vaishnava canon of the medieval period.

Durga slaying buffalo demon, lion vehicle below. This stele depicts the goddess in her most celebrated form. Durga has ten arms holding various weapons given by the gods: trident, discus, sword, bow, arrow, mace, shield, conch, noose, and a drinking cup. Her lion leaps onto the buffalo demon Mahishasura, who emerges from the slain animal’s neck. Durga’s trident pierces the demon’s chest. The relief is filled with energy and dramatic tension, symbolizing the triumph of good over evil.

Kali standing on Shiva, garland of heads, skirt of arms. This fearsome sculpture of the goddess Kali shows her in her cremation ground aspect. She stands on the prone body of her consort Shiva, who lies calmly on a lotus. Kali has four arms: one holds a sword, another a severed head, the lower two make gestures of blessing and reassurance. She wears a garland of fifty human heads and a skirt of severed arms. Her eyes are bulging, and her tongue protrudes. The sculpture is a profound expression of tantric philosophy, where destruction and creation are intertwined.

Ganesha seated with rat vehicle, potbelly, holding axe, noose. This well-preserved sculpture shows Ganesha in a lalitasana (relaxed seated pose) on a lotus pedestal. His vahana (vehicle), a bandicoot rat, is depicted nibbling on a sweet at the base. Ganesha’s four hands hold a broken tusk, a noose (pasha), an axe (parashu), and a bowl of sweets. His trunk curls to the left to reach the sweets. The elephant-headed god is beloved as the remover of obstacles and the lord of beginnings. The carving displays the characteristic softness and fleshiness of Pala art.

Parasurama (Sanskrit: "Rama with the Axe") is the sixth of the ten avatars (Dashavatara) of Vishnu, representing the warrior-brahmin who rid the earth of the kshatriya class twenty-one times. This blackstone sculpture, carved in approximately the 11th century CE and discovered at Tongibari, Dhaka, depicts the four-armed god standing in tribhanga — the classical three-bend contrapposto pose of Indian sculpture — on a visvapadma, a fully bloomed lotus pedestal.

The four-armed goddess is depicted seated in padmasana (lotus posture) or vajrasana on a lotus throne, her body frontal and perfectly composed in deep meditation. The two front hands rest joined in her lap in dhyana-mudra — the gesture of meditative absorption, both palms open and resting one upon the other, the universal hand gesture of concentrated inner stillness. This is the central visual statement of the entire sculpture: the supreme goddess, in all her cosmic power, choosing the posture of meditation — of inward withdrawal from the phenomenal world — before the Shiva-linga that rises massively before her.

The linga is depicted at a scale that makes it the dominant vertical element of the lower composition — deliberately monumental, establishing Shiva's presence as the object of the goddess's devotion even in his unanthropomorphic, purely symbolic form. The relationship between the meditating goddess and the linga encodes the entire theology of Shaiva-Shakta non-dualism: Shiva and Shakti are inseparable — she is the power by which he acts, he is the consciousness in which she subsists, and her meditation before his linga is simultaneously an act of devotion and a self-recognition.

In the upper right hand she holds an akshamala — a rosary of prayer beads — the attribute of continuous japa (silent recitation of the divine name), linking her meditation to the devotional practices of human worshippers below. In the upper left hand she holds a pustaka — a manuscript or book — identifying her simultaneously with divine knowledge (jnana), the preservation of sacred learning, and the goddess Sarasvati's domain of wisdom and speech. This combination of dhyana-mudra, akshamala, and pustaka in a Shaiva goddess image is iconographically unusual and accounts for much of the scholarly debate over identification.

The back-slab is elaborately carved in the dense, richly populated Southeast Bengal style, consistent with the Vikramapura school's characteristic treatment of the sculptural field as a complete cosmological assembly. The face — as described by Banglapedia — carries half-closed eyes, beautifully carved eyebrows, and lips invested with a serene and sublime grace hardly matched in any other sculpture of the period. The Sena period's characteristic tendency toward fuller, more sensuous facial modelling — departing from the restrained meditative composure of the earlier Pala school — is here elevated to a standard of refined perfection

Artifact_Name: Famine Sketch — Dead Bodies on Riverbank
Famine Sketch — Man Lying Face Down

Description: Garuda, the divine eagle-vehicle (vahana) of Vishnu, is depicted in Indian sculptural tradition as a powerful winged male figure with an eagle's beak and round eyes. His mythology is elaborated in the first book of the Mahabharata: he was the son of the sage Kashyapa by Vinata, daughter of Daksha. Vinata had lost her freedom to Kadru — Kashyapa's other wife and mother of the serpents — in a wager, and was serving as Kadru's slave at the time of Garuda's birth. The serpents promised to free Vinata if Garuda brought them the elixir of immortality (amrita) from heaven. In accomplishing this task Garuda carried an enormous burden through the sky — from which derives his name: guru (heavy) and ura (flying). After a fierce battle with the gods, while returning with the amrita, he encountered Vishnu. Vishnu was so pleased by Garuda's extraordinary self-restraint — that he had not tasted the amrita even when it was within his grasp — that a mutual exchange of boons followed: Garuda received immortality without drinking the amrita and was granted a place above Vishnu on the flagstaff, while Vishnu received him as his eternal mount. Garuda's two other well-known names, Garutmat and Suparna, are found in the Rigveda, and the story of his conquest of the amrita is itself of Vedic origin.

This sculpture represents Vishnu in a standing posture (samapadasana) upon a lotus pedestal, carved in the characteristic Pala school of art style. Vishnu is adorned with a tall crown and regal ornaments — earrings, necklaces, armlets, and waist-belt — reflecting divine kingship. His four hands hold the traditional attributes:

Shankha (conch) — symbol of primordial sound and creation.

Chakra (discus) — emblem of cosmic order and destruction of evil.

Gada (mace) — representing strength and mental power.

Padma (lotus) — signifying purity and spiritual liberation.

Flanking Vishnu are his two consorts: Lakshmi, goddess of wealth and beauty, seated on a lotus, and Saraswati, goddess of knowledge and music, also seated on a lotus. The back-slab (chaalchitra) is richly carved with a kirtimukha (lion face) at the top to ward off evil, flying celestial beings (gandharvas) offering praise, and a long garland (vanamala) cascading down Vishnu’s body.

This rare sculpture portrays Vishnu in his Vamana (Trivikrama) incarnation, the dwarf who expands to cosmic size to subdue King Bali. Vishnu is shown with one leg raised, symbolizing his cosmic stride across the universe. He holds the mace and discus, emphasizing divine power and cosmic order. The carving style is typical of the Pala dynasty, with elaborate detailing on ornaments, crown, and body posture. The myth behind this form narrates how Vishnu, as the dwarf Brahmin, asked Bali for three steps of land, then expanded to measure earth, heaven, and finally placed his foot on Bali’s head, sending him to the underworld. This sculpture embodies both mythological narrative and artistic mastery, representing Vishnu’s role as preserver of cosmic balance.

Credit_Donor: Sri Krishna Kanti, Chakrabarti, Sebait Kali Mandir, Munshiganj

Description:
Maheshvara is either two-or four-armed, Uma is two-armed. Maheshvara’s bull is shown below his right foot, Uma’s lion below her left foot.
The10th-11th century image from Joradeul (Dhaka), now in BNM, is an excellent two-armed Maheshvara holding a small flower in the right hand and pressing the left breast of Uma with the left hand. Both the deities are shown inside a cave, perhaps indicating Mount Kailasa, and on top in the middle a meditative Shiva is shown with his bull and other deities. An illustration of trixula intertwined with a snake is at the right side of Shiva.

Depicts Saraswati seated on lotus, holding vina and book. A variant of ID 15, this Saraswati has a slightly different arrangement of her arms. The vina is held higher, and her lower right hand is in the vitarka mudra (teaching gesture). The book (pustaka) is shown as a bound manuscript. The pedestal includes not only the swan but also two female attendants playing drums. The background arch is carved with flying celestial beings (vidyadharas) offering garlands. This sculpture is more elaborate than the previous one, suggesting it might have been the main icon of a larger Saraswati temple. The refinements of the carving—the folds of the sari, the curls of hair, the strings of the vina—are exceptionally fine.

Depicts Karttikeya with six heads, riding peacock, holding spear. Karttikeya, also known as Murugan or Skanda, is the son of Shiva and Parvati and the commander of the celestial army. This sculpture shows him with six heads (shadanan), though only three are visible in the relief. He rides a peacock, whose feathers are carved with great detail. His primary hand holds a spear (shakti), the weapon given by his mother Parvati. His other hands hold a cock (his banner) and a vajra-like club. The six heads represent his six aspects and are arranged in a honeycomb pattern. This icon is rare in Bengal because Karttikeya worship was more common in South India. Its presence indicates the spread of pan-Indian Hindu traditions.

Depicts Manasa seated on lotus with seven-hooded snake canopy. Manasa is the folk goddess of snakes, widely worshipped in Bengal to cure snakebites and ensure fertility. This stele shows Manasa in a rare sculptural form, as most images of her are clay or metal. She sits on a lotus, her two arms holding a snake in each hand. Above her, a seven-hooded cobra spreads its hoods like a canopy. Two female attendants stand on either side, each holding a pot of milk (an offering to snakes). The base includes worshippers offering eggs and milk. This sculpture blends high Hindu iconographic convention with local folk religion, illustrating how Bengal’s art accommodated diverse belief systems.

Depicts Chamunda, emaciated goddess dancing on corpse with skull garland. Chamunda is a form of the goddess Durga/Kali associated with cremation grounds and disease (specifically smallpox). This sculpture shows her as an emaciated old woman with sagging breasts, a sunken belly, and a skeletal face. She dances on a corpse, holding a skull-topped staff (khatvanga) and a noose. Her hair stands on end, and she wears a garland of skulls. Flames emanate from her body. This terrifying form was meant to scare away evil spirits and disease. Worshippers would offer blood sacrifices to appease her. The sculpture is carved with extreme realism, particularly in the depiction of emaciation, making it one of the most unsettling yet artistically powerful pieces in the collection.

Panel depicting seven mother goddesses flanked by Shiva and Ganesha. The Saptamatrikas are seven mother goddesses who are the shaktis (energies) of major male gods: Brahmi (Brahma), Maheshvari (Shiva), Kaumari (Karttikeya), Vaishnavi (Vishnu), Varahi (Varaha), Indrani (Indra), and Chamunda (Durga). This long frieze shows all seven seated in a row, each with their distinctive attributes and vehicles. On the far left is Ganesha, and on the far right is a fierce form of Shiva called Virabhadra. The panel likely came from the lintel of a temple dedicated to the mother goddesses. Such panels were used for fertility rituals and to protect the community from harm. The carving is in low relief but each figure is distinct.

Depicts divine couple Lakshmi and Vishnu seated together. This is the Vaishnava counterpart to the Umamaheshvara panel. Vishnu (Narayana) and his consort Lakshmi sit on a lotus throne. Vishnu has four arms holding his attributes, while Lakshmi has two arms, one holding a lotus and the other resting on Vishnu’s arm. Below them are their respective vehicles: Garuda (the eagle) for Vishnu, and two elephants (representing abundance) for Lakshmi. The composition symbolizes prosperity and preservation. The carving is more rounded and fleshy compared to the Shaiva panel, reflecting the different aesthetic ideals of Vaishnava iconography. The elephants are shown pouring water from pots, a classic motif from the Abhisheka Lakshmi imagery.

Depicts sacred bull vehicle of Shiva, seated or reclining. This life-size or near-life-size sculpture of Nandi is one of the largest stone animal sculptures in the museum. The bull is shown in a relaxed, seated posture with legs tucked under, head held high, and a hump on the neck. A bell hangs from the neck. The carving emphasizes the animal’s strength and tranquility. Nandi sculptures were placed facing the sanctum in every Shiva temple, serving as the gatekeeper and the devoted listener (it is believed that if you whisper your prayers in Nandi’s ear, he will convey them to Shiva). This particular example has a smooth polish and shows minimal wear, indicating it was housed indoors for centuries.

Depicts armed warrior figure placed at temple entrances. Dvarapalas are fearsome guardian figures placed on either side of temple doors to ward off evil. This sculpture shows a stout, muscular figure wielding a large club (gada). His face is fierce with bulging eyes, flared nostrils, and a mustache. He wears a short dhoti, heavy jewelry, and a crown. One hand is on his hip, the other holds the club. The posture is one of alert readiness. This dvarapala likely formed a pair with a mirror-image counterpart now lost. The carving emphasizes bulging muscles and a sense of raw power. Such guardians were carved from the same black basalt as the main deity and were an integral part of the temple’s iconographic program.

Depicts river goddesses Ganga and Yamuna on mounts crocodile and tortoise. These bracket figures were used as architectural supports under the eaves of temples. The goddess Ganga stands on a crocodile (makara), and the goddess Yamuna stands on a tortoise (kurma). Both hold pots of water and lotus flowers. Their bodies are sensuously carved, with curved hips and elaborate jewelry. The figures are not freestanding but are carved in high relief against a slab that would have been attached to the temple wall. These goddesses are placed at the entrance of temples to purify the worshipper, symbolizing the sacred rivers of North India. Their presence in Bengal temples shows the spread of Ganges-Yamuna imagery from the heartland.

Depicts female figure grasping tree branch, symbol of fertility. A salabhanjika is a female figure standing under a tree, holding a branch. The pose is highly stylized: the figure bends at the waist, one leg crossed over the other, arms reaching up to a flowering tree. This iconography originated from the ancient belief that women touching tree branches could cause the tree to flower (fertility magic). In temples, such figures were placed on pillars or walls as auspicious symbols. This particular salabhanjika has a playful expression, and the tree is rendered with dense foliage. Her jewelry and textiles are intricately carved. The figure’s nudity above the waist is typical for such auspicious female figures in medieval Indian art.

Finding_Place: Jora Deul site, Rajshahi District, North Bengal
Description:
Gaja-Lakshmi — gaja meaning elephant and Lakshmi the goddess of prosperity, fortune, and auspiciousness — is one of the oldest and most continuously reproduced sacred images in the entire Indian artistic tradition, appearing first on the railings of the Buddhist stupa at Sanchi (c. 1st century BCE) and persisting unbroken through the Pala period and beyond. The image encodes a precise theological idea: Lakshmi standing or seated at the cosmic centre, flanked symmetrically by two royal elephants who pour water or amrita (immortal nectar) over her head from raised vessels (kalasha) or from their trunks — an act of divine consecration (abhisheka) that simultaneously identifies her as the supreme goddess worthy of royal anointing and as the source of all abundance that flows from that anointing into the world.

In this sculpture, the goddess stands gracefully at the centre in a gentle tribhanga pose — the characteristic three-bend stance of classical Indian sculpture — her weight distributed with elegant composure. She holds lotus flowers (padma) in her raised hands, the lotus being her primary attribute and the symbol of purity, divine origin, and inexhaustible fertility. Her face carries the serene, inward-looking expression characteristic of the early Pala school — a subtle smile, half-closed eyes conveying meditative contentment rather than outward engagement, a face of composed divine authority. The ornamentation is carefully executed: a beaded necklace, armlets, a girdle with pendant ornaments, and ankle bangles are rendered with the minute attention to jewellery detail that defines North Bengal Pala carving, though the early Pala style retains a softness and restraint in these ornamental elements compared to the more lavish later 11th–12th century pieces.

The two flanking elephants are shown rearing or standing on either side, their trunks raised and curved toward the goddess, each pouring water from a vessel — the abhisheka stream falling over her head in the ancient consecration gesture that confers sovereignty and divine legitimacy. This bilateral symmetry creates the perfectly balanced, stable composition that makes the Gaja-Lakshmi image one of the most visually satisfying in all of Bengal's sculptural tradition. The elephants also carry their own iconographic weight: as symbols of the cardinal directions (dik-gaja), their presence implies that Lakshmi's sovereignty extends to all four corners of the universe.

Depicts Shiva and Parvati seated together on bull Nandi. This unusual sculpture shows the divine couple not on a lotus throne but riding their vahana, the bull Nandi. Shiva sits in front, holding a trident and a drum. Parvati sits behind him, her arms around his waist. Nandi is shown walking, with all four legs visible. The composition is more dynamic than the static seated panels, suggesting movement and travel. This might represent the couple’s procession during festivals when temple icons were taken out on chariots. The carving is less formal than other pieces, with a folk-art quality that suggests it might have been made for a smaller, rural temple. The faces are round and cheerful.

Head of Buddha with serene expression, refined Pala style. This fragment is only the head of a Buddha statue, but it is one of the finest examples of Pala Buddhist sculpture. The Buddha’s face is oval with a calm, downcast gaze (half-closed eyes in meditation). The lips are full and slightly curved in a faint smile. The ears are elongated with empty earlobes (from princely earrings he renounced). The hair is arranged in tight spiral curls ending in a pointed ushnisha (cranial bump). The forehead bears the urna (a dot signifying wisdom). The polish is so fine that the stone feels like soap. This head, though detached from its body, conveys an extraordinary sense of peace and transcendence, reflecting the Buddhist ideal of nirvana.

A black stone 10th-century image of the Buddha seated in bhumisparsha-mudra (earth-touching gesture — the gesture of Shakyamuni at the moment of his enlightenment) on a double-petalled lotus throne. Three branches of the Bodhi tree (Ficus religiosa) are shown rising above the figure, situating the scene at Bodh Gaya, the site of the Buddha's awakening. Two Vidyadharas (divine knowledge-bearers) each carrying a garland hover symmetrically against stylised clouds on either side of the composition — celestial witnesses to the enlightenment. The image draws particular scholarly notice for the exceptional iconographic programme of its pedestal: in front of the pedestal, alongside the double vajra (vishva-vajra — the crossed thunderbolt symbol of indestructible reality), the Seven Jewels (sapta-ratna) of a World-Conquering King (Rajachakravartin) are depicted together with offerings and the figure of the donor. The inclusion of the royal sapta-ratna — the seven precious possessions of a universal monarch: the wheel, elephant, horse, jewel, woman, general, and treasurer — alongside the Bodhi-tree enlightenment scene creates a theologically complex image equating the Buddha's spiritual sovereignty with the temporal sovereignty of the ideal world-ruler.

Artifact_Name: Buddha in Samadhi-mudra under Mahabodhi Shikhara
Description: A large (102 cm high) black basalt image of the Buddha seated in samadhi-mudra — the meditation gesture, hands damaged — under a trefoil arch, above which rises the shikhara (tower) of a temple modelled on the Mahabodhi temple at Bodh Gaya. The Mahabodhi temple shikhara is flanked by standing Vidyadharas and devotees carved in relief, situating the meditating Buddha within the sacred architectural context of the site of his enlightenment. The trefoil arch framing the figure is a compositional device characteristic of the mature Pala period, creating a sanctuary-within-a-sanctuary effect in which the sculpture itself becomes a miniature sacred building. The size of the image — approximately life-scale from the waist upward — indicates it was a major devotional focal point of its original temple context.

Depicts Vajrapani holding thunderbolt, protector of Buddha. Vajrapani is the bodhisattva who wields the vajra (thunderbolt) and acts as the guardian of the Buddha. In this sculpture, he is shown in a fierce, athletic pose, standing with legs apart and holding a raised vajra in his right hand. His left hand makes the tarjani mudra (threatening gesture). He wears a garland of snakes, and his hair is on fire (symbolizing his wrathful energy). Unlike the gentle Avalokiteshvara, Vajrapani is muscular and aggressive, representing the power needed to overcome obstacles on the path to enlightenment. Despite his fearsome appearance, he is a bodhisattva, meaning he uses his power not for destruction but for protection of the dharma.

Artifact_Name: Astamahabhaya-Tara — Tara Rescuing from Eight Great Perils (Inscribed)
Description:
The most celebrated Tara sculpture in the BNM collection and one of the most iconographically complex Tara images known from Bengal. The seated goddess is shown in lalitasana or lalitaksepa — the graceful asymmetric seated posture — two-armed in the standard Tara mode. She is attended by Mahamayuri ("Great Peacock Goddess") to her right and Ekajata ("She of the Single Topknot") to her left — a specific attendant pairing distinct from the Khadiravani Tara triad, reflecting the iconographic flexibility and liturgical richness of the Tara cult in late Pala Bengal.

What makes this image exceptional is the programme of eight smaller seated Tara figures arranged around the central goddess, each one representing Tara's intervention to rescue a devotee from one of the eight great perils (astamahabhaya): lion, elephant, fire, serpent, robber/enemy, water/flood, imprisonment, and the peril of evil spirits or demons. This iconographic programme — visualising Tara as simultaneously the single central goddess and the eight-fold active rescuer from all of life's great dangers — transforms the sculpture from a single devotional image into a complete miniature cosmological system, making it one of the most theologically sophisticated pieces in the BNM collection.

The type is accordingly named Astamahabhaya-Tara — "Tara of the Eight Great Perils" — and is documented in the Sadhanamala as a distinct form of the goddess with its own meditation text and ritual. The Sompara, Vajrayogini provenance connects this image to the site that has yielded some of the most important Buddhist sculptures in Southeast Bengal — confirming the Vajrayogini area of Munshiganj as a major centre of advanced Vajrayana practice and its attendant high-quality sculptural production.

The presence of an inscription recording the donor's name gives this piece exceptional historical value, as named donor inscriptions on Bengal Buddhist sculptures of this period are rare. Together with the Syama Tara inscription (Kayastha Sri Sanghesa-gupta) described in the previous session, it confirms the pattern of lay Kayastha-class patronage for Tara devotional imagery in the late Pala period. This inscription likely records a similar votive dedication formula, naming a specific individual's commission of this sculpture for the benefit of themselves and their family — a tangible, personal connection between a named human being of the 11th or 12th century and the goddess whose protection they sought.

Depicts Marichi with multiple arms, goddess of dawn. Marichi is a Buddhist goddess associated with dawn, light, and the sun. She is also a protector against fear and danger. This sculpture shows her with three faces and six arms. Her faces are: one smiling, one fierce (with tusks), and one with a sow’s head (her characteristic attribute). She rides a chariot drawn by seven pigs (representing the seven horses of Surya, the sun god). Her arms hold a needle and thread (to sew up the mouths of demons), a branch of the ashoka tree, a vajra, a noose, and a bow and arrow. The sculpture is highly complex and filled with esoteric symbolism. It reflects the tantric Buddhism (Vajrayana) that flourished in Bengal during the Pala period.

Depicts Vajrasattva holding vajra and bell, symbol of purity. Vajrasattva is a primordial bodhisattva in Vajrayana Buddhism, representing the pure, undefiled nature of the mind. This sculpture shows him sitting in vajrasana (full lotus) on a lotus throne. He holds a vajra (thunderbolt) in his right hand at his heart, and a bell (ghanta) in his left hand on his hip. The vajra represents the masculine principle of method (upaya), and the bell represents the feminine principle of wisdom (prajna). Their union symbolizes enlightenment. Vajrasattva wears a crown and elaborate jewelry. His expression is calm and meditative. This sculpture is not just an icon but also a meditation aid, as Vajrasattva is often visualized during purification practices.

Depicts Padmapani holding lotus, compassionate bodhisattva. Padmapani is another name for Avalokiteshvara, emphasizing his role as the lotus-holder. This sculpture is simpler than ID 49, showing him with just two arms. He stands in a straight posture, holding a long-stemmed lotus in his left hand. His right hand is in the varada mudra (gesture of giving). The lotus is fully bloomed, symbolizing the blossoming of enlightenment in the midst of the mud of samsara (worldly existence). The sculpture is less ornate, perhaps belonging to a monastic complex that emphasized austerity over ornamentation. However, the quality of the carving is still high, with the folds of the garment and the petals of the lotus executed with care.

Fragment depicting Buddha seated in meditation. This is a small panel showing the Buddha in bhumisparsha mudra (earth-touching gesture) under a tree. The scene likely represents the moment of his enlightenment. The Buddha’s right hand touches the earth, calling it to witness his victory over Mara (the demon of desire). The tree above is decorated with leaves and fruits, possibly representing the Bodhi tree. The panel is broken at the edges, but the central figure is intact. It was probably part of a larger narrative cycle depicting scenes from the Buddha’s life, arranged around a stupa or temple. The carving is in low relief, suitable for architectural placement where it would be viewed from a distance.

Fragment with floral motif, decorative temple element. This fragment features a repeating pattern of flowers and vines, known as the ”floral scroll” motif. It would have run along the edge of a temple wall or ceiling as a border decoration. The flowers are stylized lotuses, and the vines curl in interlocking loops. The carving is shallow but precise, designed to be seen from below. Such decorative elements were not merely fillers but were considered auspicious, representing the abundance and beauty of the divine world. The fragment is weathered on one side but still shows the original crispness of the pattern on the other.

Fragment with geometric design, temple ornamentation. This fragment features a geometric pattern of interlocking squares and diamonds, similar to a lattice. Such designs were used in temple floors, ceilings, and window screens (jalis). The geometric precision required careful measurement and carving. This fragment likely came from a floor where the pattern would be seen underfoot. The stone is worn smooth from centuries of foot traffic. Geometric designs in Indian temple architecture are not arbitrary; they are based on sacred geometry and mandalas, representing the ordered structure of the cosmos. This simple fragment thus carries deep cosmological significance.

Fragment with lotus base motif, common in temple architecture. This is the lower portion of a temple pillar or wall, carved with lotus petals arranged in layers. The lotus base (padmapitha) is a standard element in Indian temple architecture; it represents the cosmic ocean from which creation emerges. The petals are thick and fleshy, each one individually carved. The fragment shows only a few rows of petals, but originally there would have been many. The base is wider than the shaft, creating a stable foundation. The polish on this fragment is exceptionally well preserved, indicating it was in an interior space protected from weather.

Fragment of pillar capital with ornate carving. The capital is the topmost part of a pillar, where it supports the beam above. This fragment shows a design of seated lions with foliate tails, arranged in a circle. The lions are stylized, with open mouths and raised paws. Above them is an abacus (flat slab) carved with a lotus motif. Such lion capitals are reminiscent of the famous Ashokan pillars but in a later, more ornate style. The carving is in the round, meant to be seen from all sides. The fragment is heavy and thick, suggesting it supported a significant weight. It likely came from a large temple mandapa (hall).

Fragment of ceiling panel with geometric and floral motifs. This is a square panel that would have been one of many forming a coffered ceiling. The design is a central lotus surrounded by concentric rings of geometric patterns, including triangles and circles. At the corners are small flowers. The panel is deeply recessed, creating a strong play of light and shadow when viewed from below. Such ceilings were common in temple mandapas and were designed to mimic the dome of the sky. The fragment is broken on one corner but the central lotus remains intact. The carving shows evidence of tool marks, giving insight into the stoneworking techniques of the period.

Fragment of temple wall relief showing deity figures. This larger fragment preserves two standing deity figures, probably a male and a female. Only the lower halves of the bodies remain: the male’s legs in a dhoti, the female’s legs in a sari with elegant jewelry on the ankles. Between them is a pilaster (decorative column). The relief is about 30 cm tall, suggesting the original scene was life-size or larger. The style of the carving (slender proportions, delicate jewelry) points to the Sena period (12th century). The fragment is broken unevenly, so the identities of the deities cannot be determined, but it is a valuable piece for understanding temple decoration.

Fragment with decorative border motif from temple ruins. This long, narrow fragment (approx. 15 cm x 60 cm) features a continuous border of intertwined vines and leaves, known as the ”vine scroll” motif. At intervals, a flower or fruit emerges from the vine. This border would have run along the edge of a wall or a door frame. The carving is in low relief and repetitive, suggesting it was done by less skilled craftsmen under the supervision of a master. Despite its simplicity, it effectively frames the larger scenes it once bordered. The stone shows slight weathering, but the pattern is still clear.

Fragment with floral scroll design, ornamental temple element. This fragment is similar to ID 57 but more elaborate. Here, the flowers are larger and the scrolls form loops that enclose small figures of birds and animals. At one point, a monkey hangs from a vine. Such playful additions indicate that temple decorations were not always solemn; they could include elements of humor and observation of nature. The floral scroll motif originated in ancient Indian art (as seen at Sanchi and Bharhut) and continued for over a millennium. This fragment shows the continuity of that tradition into the medieval period.

Fragment with geometric border design, temple ornamentation. This border consists of a repeated diamond pattern, each diamond containing a smaller diamond. The diamonds are created by crossing bands that form a kind of lattice. This is similar to the ”lozenge” pattern found in textile design, and its use in stone may imitate textile borders used in temporary structures. The carving is shallow but precise, each diamond exactly the same size. The fragment is broken at both ends, so the original length is unknown. Geometric borders like this were often used to separate different narrative panels on a temple wall.

Fragment with lotus petal design, symbolic of purity. This fragment shows a series of overlapping lotus petals, similar to the scales of a fish. This motif is often found on the domes of temples, where the petals radiate from the central finial. The petals are thick and fleshy, carved with a central ridge. The fragment is curved, confirming it came from a dome or a circular structure. The lotus petal design symbolizes the unfolding of enlightenment and is one of the most persistent motifs in Buddhist and Hindu architecture.

Fragment of temple cornice with intricate carving. A cornice is the horizontal projection that crowns a wall or roof. This fragment shows a series of small bracket-like shapes (kudus) that are characteristic of Indian temple cornices. Below the kudus is a band of floral decoration, and above is a plain molding. The cornice would have helped water run off the temple roof. The carving is heavily weathered on the top surface (exposed to rain) but well-preserved on the underside. This fragment is important for understanding the architectural forms of Bengal’s medieval temples, many of which have not survived intact.

Fragment of decorative arch element from temple ruins. This curved stone formed part of an archway (torana) or a niche (chandrashala). The surface is carved with a series of miniature arches inside the main arch, each containing a small figure (now worn). The arch motif is called ”chaitya arch” and is derived from early Buddhist rock-cut architecture. Even after Buddhism declined in Bengal, the chaitya arch continued as a decorative element in Hindu temples. This fragment preserves the upper curve of the arch, with a keystone at the top carved with a face (kirtimukha, or ”face of glory”).

Fragment of temple pedestal with carved motifs. A pedestal (vedibandha) is the platform on which the temple walls rest. This fragment is a corner piece, showing two sides meeting at a right angle. Each side is carved with panels depicting dancers and musicians. One panel shows a female dancer with her arms raised, another shows a drummer, another a flute player. These were not deities but celestial beings (apsaras) performing to entertain the gods. The carving is in high relief, and the figures are animated. The pedestal fragment is heavy, indicating the temple was of substantial size. Such scenes of music and dance on the exterior of a temple create a joyful atmosphere for worshippers.

Fragment of decorative panel with deity figures. This panel shows a central deity figure flanked by attendants. The deity is likely a form of Vishnu, as indicated by the remnants of a discus in the upper hand. The figure is seated on a lotus, with legs folded. The attendants are smaller, shown in reverence. The panel is framed by a beaded border. The composition is balanced and symmetrical. The stone is a darker shade of black basalt, almost charcoal. This panel would have been inserted into a larger wall, possibly as part of a series of such panels depicting various deities. The carving style is advanced, with undercutting that creates deep shadows.

Fragment of temple ornament with floral and geometric motifs. This small, intricately carved piece appears to be a finial or a crest from the top of a temple spire (shikhara). It is shaped like an inverted lotus with a pointed tip. Below the lotus are bands of geometric patterns. The tip shows signs of being fitted into something (a hole or socket). This ornament would have been placed at the highest point of a temple, acting as a visual anchor and a symbol of the temple’s connection to the heavens. The carving is in the round, as it would be seen from all angles. Despite its small size (approx. 20 cm tall), it is one of the most refined pieces in the architectural fragments collection.

Fragment with lotus rosette design, symbolic of divinity. A rosette is a circular floral motif. This one shows a central lotus with eight petals, surrounded by an outer ring of smaller petals. The rosette would have been placed in a square panel as a ceiling medallion or as a decoration on a door. The symmetry is perfect, and the carving is deep enough to create a strong relief. The lotus rosette is one of the most common motifs in Indian art, appearing from the Mauryan period (3rd century BCE) to the present. This fragment is in excellent condition, with no visible weathering.

Fragment of temple relief showing narrative scene. This fragment appears to be part of a narrative cycle, possibly from the Ramayana or Mahabharata. Two figures are shown in combat: one raises a sword, the other a shield. Between them is a chariot wheel. The scene is full of action, with flying hair and bent limbs. The identification is uncertain because the faces are damaged, but the quality of the carving is high. Narrative reliefs were often placed on the exterior walls of temples, telling stories from the epics for the edification of the illiterate public. This fragment gives a glimpse of the storytelling tradition in medieval Bengal.

Fragment with decorative motif, temple ornamentation. This is a small piece (approx. 10 cm square) carved with a ”honeycomb” pattern of hexagons. Each hexagon contains a small dot. This motif is often found in the ceilings of Buddhist chaitya halls and later in Hindu mandapas. The hexagons are arranged in a regular grid, and the carving is very shallow, almost like engraving. The fragment likely came from a thin slab that served as a false ceiling. The geometric precision required to create such a pattern suggests the use of measuring tools and compasses. It is a testament to the mathematical knowledge of the medieval stone carvers.

Fragment of temple base with carved lotus design. This is a corner block from the bottommost layer of a temple (the adhishthana). It shows a lotus petal design on both faces, meeting at the corner with a small ornament. The stone is thicker and more massive than other fragments, as it had to bear the weight of the entire temple. The carving is simpler and more robust, suitable for a part that would be near the ground and possibly covered by earth. The base is the most stable part of the temple, and its survival indicates the temple was disassembled rather than collapsed. This fragment is thus evidence of a lost temple that was quarried for building materials.

Fragment of decorative relief with deity figures. This fragment preserves the upper half of a seated deity, likely the goddess Lakshmi. The figure holds two lotuses and has a serene expression. Above her is an umbrella (chhatra) and two flying attendants (vidyadharas) with garlands. The carving is delicate, with fine details in the hair and jewelry. The fragment is broken below the waist, so the lower half is missing. The quality suggests it was part of a major temple funded by royalty or wealthy merchants. The deity’s face is intact and shows the classical Pala-Sena ideal of beauty: full lips, long eyes, and a graceful neck.

Fragment of temple ornamentation with floral motifs. This piece is a curved slab with a design of lotus flowers and buds on stems. The curve suggests it came from a circular pillar or a dome. The flowers are arranged in a spiral, each flower slightly higher than the previous one. The carving is in low relief with a smooth finish. The stone has a greenish-black tint, unusual for the typical black basalt. This could be a different stone source or a result of chemical changes in the soil where it was buried. The motif is simple but elegant, creating a rhythmic pattern around the curved surface.

Fragment of decorative carving from temple ruins. This fragment features a makara (mythical water creature) with an elaborate tail that curls into a scroll. The makara has the head of a crocodile, the trunk of an elephant, and the body of a fish. It is shown facing forward, with its mouth open. The makara is a guardian figure often placed at the entrance of temples or on the ends of archways. The carving is dynamic, with the creature’s tail forming a spiral that fills the available space. The fragment is large (approx. 40 cm wide) and the makara is carved in high relief. It would have been a striking element of the temple’s entryway.

Fragment of temple column with carved motifs. This is a section of a fluted column, with vertical grooves running along its length. At the top of this fragment is a band of carved lotus petals. The column would have been one of many supporting a mandapa ceiling. The fluting is evenly spaced and deeply cut, suggesting the use of a lathe or a carving tool with a gauge. The stone is polished to a smooth finish. Column fragments are valuable for reconstructing the original dimensions of a temple. Based on the diameter (approx. 30 cm), this column would have been about 3 meters tall. The fragment is about 60 cm long, preserving only a small portion of the original column.

Fragment of pedestal with lotus and floral designs. This is a corner block from a pedestal that once supported a deity image. The top surface is smooth with a slight depression (for the deity’s base). The sides are carved with lotus petals and floral vines. The pedestal would have been placed in the sanctum (garbhagriha), so the carving is only on the front and sides that would be visible to worshippers. The back is left rough. This fragment is important because it shows how the deity’s base was integrated into the temple’s architecture. The stone is slightly pinkish, possibly due to iron oxide staining after centuries of exposure.

Fragment of wall panel with deity figures. This large fragment (approx. 50 cm x 40 cm) shows three figures: a central standing deity, possibly Vishnu, and two smaller attendants. The deity’s hands are damaged, but one hand likely held a discus. The deity wears a tall crown and stands on a lotus. The attendants hold fly-whisks. The panel is framed by a thick border with a pearl motif. The carving is in high relief, with figures almost separated from the background. The workmanship is of the highest quality, with intricate details in the jewelry and clothing. This would have been a major decorative element on the temple wall, perhaps placed in a niche.

Fragment of cornice with intricate carvings. This cornice fragment features a row of kudu arches, below which is a frieze of geese (hamsa) in flight. Geese are symbols of purity and spiritual aspiration in Indian art. The geese are carved with outstretched wings, arranged in a continuous line. Below the geese is a band of lotus petals. The cornice would have projected from the wall, and the underside would have been visible to worshippers. The carving on the underside is as careful as on the front, indicating that the cornice was at eye level. The stone is heavily weathered on the top, but the underside is pristine.

Fragment of relief showing narrative temple scene. This fragment shows a palace scene: a king sits on a throne, attended by courtiers. The king is wearing a tall crown and holding a scepter. A queen sits beside him. The scene is likely from a Jataka tale (story of the Buddha’s previous lives) or the Ramayana. The carving includes architectural details like pillars and arches. The figures are small (approx. 10 cm tall), and the relief is shallow, almost like a miniature painting in stone. This suggests the fragment came from a smaller temple or from a part of a larger temple that was viewed from close range, such as a door jamb.

Fragment with lotus panel design, symbolic of purity. This is a large panel (approx. 60 cm x 30 cm) covered entirely with overlapping lotus petals, arranged in rows like scales. This motif is known as ”padma” or ”kamala” and is often used on the ceilings and floors of temples. Walking on such a floor is symbolically walking on a lotus, elevating the worshipper above the mud of the material world. The petals are carved in low relief, with each petal overlapping the one below it. The panel is broken on one side but otherwise intact. The stone is very heavy, suggesting it came from a ground floor.

Fragment of ceiling ornament with floral motifs. This is a large, circular medallion that would have been set into the center of a ceiling. It shows a central lotus with sixteen petals, surrounded by concentric rings of geometric patterns and smaller flowers. The outermost ring is a row of geese (hamsa). The medallion is recessed, creating a deep shadow in the center. The carving is in high relief, and the stone is polished. Such ceiling medallions were status symbols, indicating that the patron could afford not just a temple but one with ornate interior decoration. The medallion is broken into three pieces that have been rejoined, but the missing parts have been filled.

Fragment of temple relief with deity figures. This fragment preserves a goddess figure, possibly Durga, with multiple arms. Only three arms remain, holding a sword, a shield, and a trident. The goddess stands on a lotus and is surrounded by a circular aureole. The background is filled with floral scrolls. The carving is exceptionally fine, with the goddess’s face showing a calm expression despite her martial attributes. The fragment is small (approx. 25 cm tall), suggesting it came from a small shrine or a niche on a larger temple. The stone is a uniform black with no weathering, indicating it was buried soon after the temple’s destruction.

Fragment of temple base with carved lotus motifs. This is a massive block (approx. 40 cm x 40 cm x 20 cm) from the foundation of a temple. The exterior face is carved with a double lotus petal design, while the other faces are rough. The carving is bold and simple, meant to be seen from a distance. The base would have been buried partially in the ground, so only the upper part of the carving would have been visible. The stone is heavily weathered on the exposed face, with lichen growth still present (the museum has not cleaned it to preserve archaeological context). This fragment is important for understanding the scale of temple foundations.

Fragment of temple panel with floral and geometric designs. This panel is a border piece, carved with a meandering vine that produces leaves and flowers at regular intervals. The vine forms loops that contain small rosettes. The design is repeated along the entire length of the panel (approx. 80 cm). The panel would have been placed at the edge of a larger composition, acting as a frame. The carving is in low relief, and the stone has a greenish patina. The panel is unbroken and in excellent condition, suggesting it was carefully removed from the ruins rather than broken in situ.

Fragment of temple base ornament with lotus petals. This is a curved piece that would have wrapped around the corner of a temple wall. The carving on both faces is the same: rows of lotus petals. At the corner, a vertical band with a beaded pattern joins the two faces. The stone is cut at an exact 90-degree angle, demonstrating precise stonecutting techniques. The top and bottom are flat, indicating this block was part of a stacked structure. The lotus petals are crisp and unworn, protected by the overhanging cornice. This fragment shows the three-dimensional thinking required to carve corners in temple architecture.

Fragment of temple cornice with deity figures. This cornice fragment has a row of small niches, each containing a seated deity. The deities are damaged but appear to be the ten avatars of Vishnu (Dashavatara). If so, this cornice would have been placed on a Vaishnava temple. The niches are separated by small pilasters, and the cornice projects forward. The underside is carved with lotus flowers. The deities are only 8 cm tall but are carved with remarkable detail. This fragment is one of the most informative for understanding iconographic programs on temple exteriors. It is broken at both ends, but the existing portion preserves five niches.

Fragment of wall ornament with floral motifs. This fragment features a large lotus flower with a cluster of buds and leaves. The lotus is carved in high relief, almost in the round, while the buds are in low relief. The composition is asymmetrical, with the lotus leaning to one side. This naturalistic treatment is unusual in temple architecture, which tends towards symmetry. The fragment likely came from a less formal part of the temple, such as a garden pavilion rather than the main shrine. The stone has a brownish tint, possibly from being burned in a fire that destroyed the temple.

Fragment of temple base with lotus rosette design. This is a corner block from the base of a pillar or wall. The front face has a large lotus rosette carved into a recessed square panel. The side face has a simpler lotus petal design. The rosette is about 20 cm in diameter and consists of a central lotus with eight petals, surrounded by an outer ring of sixteen petals. The carving is deep, with the petals undercut so they cast shadows. The stone is smooth and polished, and the rosette is in excellent condition. This block would have been at eye level, inviting close inspection.

Fragment of relief panel depicting deity figures. This panel shows Vishnu in his form as Vamana (the dwarf avatar). He is depicted as a short Brahmin with an umbrella, receiving a donation of water from King Bali. The scene is narrative and includes other figures: a priest, a queen, and a water pot. The carving is crowded but detailed. The panel is broken diagonally, losing the upper right corner. The remaining part is about 40 cm x 30 cm. The narrative is rare in stone sculpture; most Vamana images are singular figures. This panel thus provides unique insight into how artists depicted complex stories in relief.

Fragment of temple ornament with floral scroll design. This long, narrow fragment (approx. 15 cm x 100 cm) is a frieze of scrolling vines with flowers and leaves. At intervals, the vine produces a larger flower with a face in the center (kirtimukha). The kirtimukha is a fierce face with bulging eyes and fangs, but it is purely decorative and meant to ward off evil. The carving is repetitive but skillfully done, with each kirtimukha slightly different. The frieze would have run along the top of a wall or below a cornice. It is in two pieces that have been rejoined, with a small missing section in the middle.

Fragment of ceiling relief with deity figures. This is a square panel (approx. 50 cm x 50 cm) that was once part of a coffered ceiling. The relief shows the god Shiva dancing (Nataraja) within a circle of flames. He has four arms, holding a drum and fire, and he tramples a dwarf (Apasmara). The carving is dynamic, with Shiva’s hair flying out. The panel is surrounded by a border of lotus petals. The ceiling relief would have been directly above the central sanctum, with the dancing Shiva as the focal point. The stone is dark and polished, and the relief is so deep that the figure is almost fully three-dimensional.

Fragment of temple carving with floral motifs. This small fragment (approx. 15 cm x 10 cm) is exquisitely carved with a single lotus flower and a bud, surrounded by leaves. The lotus has twelve petals, each with a groove down the center. The bud is shown just beginning to open. The carving is in the round, meaning the entire fragment is sculpted from a block of stone; it is not a relief. This suggests it was a freestanding ornament, perhaps a finial or part of a railing. The stone is a light gray, different from the usual black basalt, indicating a different quarry. The craftsmanship is of the highest order, with every detail carefully rendered.

A large, plain, aniconic Shivalinga — the cylindrical stone column representing Shiva in his unanthropomorphic, purely symbolic form — set within a massive circular gauripatta (yoni-pitha). At 96 cm in height this is one of the larger Shivalingas in the BNM collection and one of the few pieces in the museum that is displayed on the gallery floor rather than on a raised plinth, its sheer size and weight making it a commanding presence in the History and Classical Art gallery.

The linga is perfectly cylindrical and smooth-surfaced — without faces or figural carving — representing the nirguna (without qualities, unmanifest) aspect of Shiva as opposed to the anthropomorphic saguna (with qualities, manifest) forms. This aniconic simplicity is doctrinally deliberate: the linga in its most reduced form embodies the brahman — the absolute, undifferentiated divine reality — before it takes on name, form, and attribute. The smooth, upright, polished column is simultaneously the phallus (linga = sign/mark/phallus), the cosmic axis (axis mundi), the pillar of fire (jyotirlinga) in which Shiva manifested to humble Brahma and Vishnu, and the abstract symbol of creative energy undifferentiated into individual form.

The gauripatta (yoni-pitha) in which the linga rests is notably large — a wide, circular basin with a prominent outer rim and the ribbed drainage spout (pranala) projecting at the front through which ritual ablution water (abhisheka jal) flows away after being poured over the linga. The gauripatta represents the goddess Gauri (Parvati) as the earth-principle, the feminine receptive ground of creation — and the combined linga-yoni composition encodes the union of Shiva and Shakti as the generative principle of the entire universe. As the Bengali text shared by the user explains through the work of Przyluski, the words linga, langul, and langal (plough) share a common etymology — pointing to the pre-Aryan, agricultural origins of linga worship as a symbol of the earth being made fertile.

The Sompara provenance places this within the same Munshiganj / Vajrayogini archaeological zone that has yielded the Astamahabhaya-Tara, the Syama Tara, and other major BNM pieces, confirming the religious pluralism of that area — the same localities producing both the finest Buddhist goddess images and major Shaiva cult objects of the Pala period.

A Panchamukhi Shivalinga — a linga with five faces (mukha) carved on its upper cylindrical portion — representing Shiva in his supreme form as Sadashiva, "the eternally auspicious," whose five faces embody the five cosmic functions (panchakriya) through which the entire universe is created, sustained, dissolved, concealed, and redeemed.

The linga sits within a circular gauripatta (yoni-pitha) — the ritual basin representing the goddess Gauri/Parvati as the earth-principle and creative receptacle — with the characteristic ribbed drainage channel (pranala) at the front. The upper cylindrical section bears four faces visible around the circumference at the cardinal directions, with the fifth face (Ishana) implied at the top or represented by the smooth apex of the linga itself.

The five faces correspond to Shiva's five aspects as enumerated in the Shiva Purana and the Panchavaktra Upanishad:

Sadyojata (west face — creation): the newly born, youthful face associated with the earth element and the function of srishti (creation)
Vamadeva (north face — preservation): the gracious, gentle face associated with the water element and the function of sthiti (maintenance)
Aghora (south face — dissolution): the fierce, terrifying face associated with the fire element and the function of samhara (destruction) — the face that simultaneously destroys and regenerates
Tatpurusha (east face — concealment): the supreme cosmic person face associated with the air element and the function of tirodhana (hiding the divine reality from ordinary perception)
Ishana (zenith — grace): the supreme, all-pervading face associated with the ether (akasha) element and the function of anugraha (bestowing liberation)
The five faces thus encode the entire theology of Shaivism in a single object: Shiva is simultaneously Creator, Preserver, Destroyer, the Concealer of reality (whose maya creates the apparent world), and the Liberator who removes that concealment and grants moksha. The Panchamukhi Shivalinga is therefore not merely a cult object but a complete cosmological system in stone. In Bengal, Panchanana (five-faced Shiva) — popularly called Panchu Thakur — is additionally worshipped as a protector of villages and children, and as a deity of agricultural abundance.

The rough-textured surface of the black basalt, visible in the photograph, is characteristic of the Rajmahal trap basalt used for many Pala-period sculptures from North Bengal and the Munshiganj area, which weathers to a distinctive granular surface texture distinct from the finer-grained polished chlorite used in some Southeast Bengal pieces.

Duplicate of ID 16 – preserved tiger specimen symbolizing Bangladesh’s wildlife. The Royal Bengal Tiger is the apex predator of the Sundarbans. This specimen is a mature male, captured after it became a man-eater. The tiger was euthanized and taxidermied. The mount is displayed in a glass case with a painted background of the Sundarbans. Its roar is sometimes played on a loop. The tiger has become a beloved exhibit for school children, teaching them about wildlife conservation.

Complete skeleton of Asian elephant, educational display. The skeleton is of an adult female Asian elephant (Elephas maximus) that died of natural causes in the Chittagong Hill Tracts. The bones have been cleaned, whitened, and reassembled in a standing posture. The skeleton is suspended from a metal frame, allowing visitors to walk underneath and see the structure of the ribs and spine. The skull includes the tusks (small, as female Asian elephants have small tusks called tushes). This exhibit is used to teach anatomy and the differences between Asian and African elephants. The skeleton is one of the largest objects in the museum, spanning over 3 meters in height and 4 meters in length.

Preserved crocodile specimen from Sundarbans mangrove. This is a saltwater crocodile (Crocodylus porosus), one of the largest reptile species in the world. The specimen is about 4 meters long and is mounted in a lunging pose, mouth open to reveal teeth. The skin is dark green with rough scales. The crocodile was captured in the Sundarbans after it had killed several fishermen. It was killed by forest officials and then taxidermied. The exhibit highlights the danger of human-wildlife conflict in the Sundarbans, where crocodiles and tigers share the habitat with local communities. The specimen is displayed with a mannequin wearing a traditional fisherman's outfit to illustrate the conflict.

Preserved peacock specimen, symbol of South Asian fauna. The peacock (Pavo cristatus) is the national bird of India but is also common in Bangladesh, especially in the Rajshahi and Chapai Nawabganj regions. This specimen is a male with its full train of tail feathers, displayed in a fan-like arrangement. The iridescent blues and greens of the feathers are well preserved. The peacock is mounted on a branch, with its head turned to the side. The exhibit includes a label explaining that the peacock is not native to the Sundarbans but prefers dry deciduous forests. The specimen is a favorite for its beauty and is often photographed by visitors.

Preserved hornbill specimen, highlighting biodiversity. The great hornbill (Buceros bicornis) is a large bird found in the forests of Sylhet and Chittagong. This specimen shows the characteristic casque (hollow helmet) on top of the beak, which is yellow and black. The bird is mounted in flight, with wings spread wide. The feathers are mostly black and white, with a yellow beak. Hornbills are endangered in Bangladesh due to habitat loss, so this specimen serves as a reminder of what is at risk. The label notes that hornbills have a unique nesting habit: the female seals herself inside a tree cavity with mud, leaving only a small slit for the male to feed her.

Preserved king cobra specimen, educational display. The king cobra (Ophiophagus hannah) is the world’s longest venomous snake, reaching up to 5.5 meters. This specimen is about 4 meters long and is coiled around a branch, with its hood expanded. The taxidermy preserves the snake’s pattern of olive-green scales with yellow bands. The king cobra is revered and feared in Bangladesh; it is associated with the snake goddess Manasa. The exhibit includes a warning about snakebite and the importance of antivenom. The snake was collected from the Sundarbans after it died of natural causes, then preserved by the museum’s taxidermist.

Preserved python specimen, large reptile of Bangladesh. The reticulated python (Malayopython reticulatus) is a non-venomous constrictor that can grow over 6 meters. This specimen is about 5 meters long and is displayed in a coiled position, as if resting. The skin has a beautiful geometric pattern of brown, yellow, and black. Pythons are often killed for their skin and meat, but this specimen was donated by a wildlife sanctuary after it died of an injury. The exhibit explains that pythons play a vital role in controlling rodent populations. The python’s jaws are spread open to show how they can swallow prey much larger than their head.

Preserved spotted deer specimen, common Sundarbans fauna. The spotted deer (Axis axis) is the primary prey of the Royal Bengal Tiger in the Sundarbans. This specimen is a male with antlers in velvet. The deer is mounted in a grazing pose, with its head lowered. The coat has the characteristic white spots on a reddish-brown background, which fade with age. The deer was collected from the Sundarbans after it was killed by a tiger; the forest department recovered the carcass and donated it to the museum. The exhibit shows the close relationship between predator and prey in the ecosystem.

Preserved leopard cat specimen, small wild feline. The leopard cat (Prionailurus bengalensis) is about the size of a domestic cat but with a longer tail and more spots. This specimen shows the spotted coat that gives it its name. The cat is mounted in a stalking posture, with its body low to the ground. Leopard cats are nocturnal and are rarely seen in the wild, so this exhibit provides a rare glimpse. The cat was donated by a villager who found it dead on a road (roadkill). The specimen is used to teach about the diversity of wild cats in Bangladesh, which also includes the fishing cat and the jungle cat.

Preserved fishing cat specimen, semi-aquatic feline. The fishing cat (Prionailurus viverrinus) is a medium-sized wild cat adapted to wetlands. This specimen shows the cat’s webbed feet (visible in the mount) and its coarse, olive-grey fur with dark spots. The cat is mounted in a pose reaching into water with one paw, as if fishing. Fishing cats are endangered in Bangladesh due to loss of wetlands. This specimen came from the Sundarbans, where a few remain. The exhibit explains that fishing cats have been observed using their paws to scoop fish out of the water, and they even dive after prey.

Preserved otter specimen, aquatic mammal of Bangladesh. The smooth-coated otter (Lutrogale perspicillata) is a large otter found in the rivers and mangroves of Bangladesh. This specimen shows the otter’s sleek, dark brown fur and its webbed feet. The mount shows the otter sliding on a muddy bank, a typical behavior. Otters are sometimes used by fishermen in Bangladesh to drive fish into nets, a traditional practice known as ”otter fishing” which is now rare. This specimen was donated by a fisherman who no longer used otters. The exhibit discusses the relationship between otters and humans in Bangladesh.

Preserved monitor lizard specimen, reptile of Bangladesh. The Bengal monitor (Varanus bengalensis) is a large lizard that can grow up to 1.5 meters. This specimen is about 1 meter long, with a muscular body, strong claws, and a forked tongue. The lizard is mounted climbing a tree trunk. Monitors are often killed for their skin and meat, and also for use in traditional medicine. This specimen was confiscated from poachers by forest officials and then donated to the museum. The exhibit educates visitors about the ecological role of monitors as scavengers and predators of insects and small animals.

Preserved parrot specimen, colorful bird of South Asia. The rose-ringed parakeet (Psittacula krameri) is a common parrot in Bangladesh, known for its green plumage and the black and rose ring around the neck of males. This specimen is a male, mounted on a perch, with its wings slightly spread. The beak is red and curved. Parrots are popular as pets, but this specimen is wild-caught (from a market seizure). The exhibit discusses the illegal pet trade and the importance of keeping wild birds in the wild. The bright colors make it a favorite with children.

Preserved owl specimen, nocturnal bird of prey. The Indian eagle-owl (Bubo bengalensis) is a large owl with distinctive ear tufts. This specimen is mounted with its eyes wide open, showing the characteristic forward-facing eyes of owls. The plumage is mottled brown and buff for camouflage. Owls are often associated with superstition in rural Bangladesh (considered omens of bad luck), leading to persecution. The exhibit aims to correct these misconceptions by explaining that owls are beneficial because they eat rats and insects. The specimen was collected from a farmer who had killed it; the museum uses it as a teaching tool for conservation.

Preserved eagle specimen, raptor of Bangladesh. The steppe eagle (Aquila nipalensis) is a migratory bird of prey that winters in Bangladesh. This specimen is mounted in a soaring pose, with wings fully extended. The feathers are dark brown, and the beak is hooked. Eagles are apex predators, feeding on small mammals and birds. This eagle was found dead after colliding with a power line, a common cause of death for large birds. The exhibit discusses the threats migratory birds face and the need for international cooperation to protect them. The wingspan of this specimen is about 1.8 meters, making it an impressive sight.

Preserved vulture specimen, scavenger bird. The white-rumped vulture (Gyps bengalensis) was once the most common vulture in Bangladesh, but its population has crashed by over 99% due to the veterinary drug diclofenac. This specimen is a sobering reminder of the crisis. The vulture is mounted standing on the ground, with its wings folded. Its white neck and back contrast with the dark body. The exhibit includes a detailed explanation of how diclofenac causes kidney failure in vultures and what is being done to save them (captive breeding, banning the drug). The specimen is one of the few remaining evidence of a once-thriving population.

Preserved pigeon specimen, common bird of Bangladesh. The rock pigeon (Columba livia) is ubiquitous in cities and villages across Bangladesh. This specimen is mounted on a small platform, showing the typical gray plumage with iridescent neck feathers. While pigeons are common, this specimen is used to teach basic bird anatomy and the differences between wild and domestic species. The pigeon was donated by a breeder who had a surplus. The exhibit notes that pigeons have been domesticated for thousands of years and have been used to carry messages.

Preserved dove specimen, symbol of peace. The spotted dove (Spilopelia chinensis) is a smaller relative of the pigeon, with a distinctive black patch with white spots on the neck. This specimen is mounted on a branch, with its tail feathers spread. Doves are often seen as gentle birds and are mentioned in Bengali literature. This specimen was collected from Dhaka University campus, where doves are common. The exhibit compares the dove to the pigeon, explaining the differences in size, color, and behavior.

Preserved crow specimen, common urban bird. The house crow (Corvus splendens) is one of the most intelligent and adaptable birds in Bangladesh. This specimen is mounted on a railing, mimicking a pose commonly seen in cities. The crow’s black plumage is slightly iridescent. Crows are often considered pests, but the exhibit highlights their intelligence (tool use, facial recognition) and their ecological role as scavengers. The specimen was collected from Old Dhaka, where crows are abundant. It is a familiar sight for visitors, making it an effective teaching tool about urban wildlife.

Preserved mynah bird specimen, songbird of South Asia. The common mynah (Acridotheres tristis) is a brown bird with a yellow beak and yellow eye patches. This specimen is mounted on a branch, with its beak open as if singing. Mynahs are known for their ability to mimic human speech and are popular pets. However, this specimen is wild, collected from a forest. The exhibit explains that mynahs are also invasive species in some parts of the world (like Australia). The specimen is often used in educational programs to teach children about bird calls and mimicry.

Preserved sparrow specimen, common bird of Bangladesh. The house sparrow (Passer domesticus) is a small brown and gray bird that lives closely with humans. This specimen is mounted on a windowsill, a typical habitat. Sparrow populations have declined in many cities due to pollution and lack of nesting sites, including in Dhaka. The exhibit discusses the causes of decline and what people can do to help (put out water, nest boxes). The specimen was collected from a rural area where sparrows are still common. It is a nostalgic exhibit for older visitors who remember sparrows in the city.

Preserved kingfisher specimen, aquatic bird. The white-throated kingfisher (Halcyon smyrnensis) is a brightly colored bird with a blue back, brown head, and white throat. This specimen is mounted on a branch over a painted pond, with a small fish in its beak. Kingfishers are often seen near water bodies, diving for fish. The exhibit explains their hunting technique and their importance in controlling fish populations. The bright colors of this specimen make it one of the most visually appealing in the gallery. It was collected from the wetlands of Sylhet.

Preserved duck specimen, waterfowl of Bangladesh. The mallard (Anas platyrhynchos) is a common duck found in wetlands across Bangladesh. This specimen is a male in breeding plumage, with a glossy green head and a white collar. The duck is mounted in a swimming pose, with its feet tucked under. Ducks are both wild and domesticated in Bangladesh; this specimen is wild. The exhibit explains the difference between mallards and domestic ducks, and also discusses the hunting of waterfowl in Bangladesh (which is regulated). The specimen was donated by a hunter who decided to stop hunting.

Preserved goose specimen, waterfowl of Bangladesh. The greylag goose (Anser anser) is the ancestor of most domestic geese, but wild geese are rare in Bangladesh as they are winter migrants. This specimen is a wild greylag goose that was found injured and later died in captivity. The goose is mounted standing, with its long neck extended. Geese are known for their loud honking and for flying in V-formation. The exhibit discusses the migration routes of geese, which fly from Central Asia to Bangladesh every winter. This specimen is important for teaching about bird migration.

Preserved swan specimen, waterfowl of Bangladesh. The mute swan (Cygnus olor) is not native to Bangladesh; this specimen was donated by a zoo where the swan died. Swans are kept in captivity in parks and zoos for their beauty. This mount shows the swan with its wings slightly lifted, showcasing the large wingspan (over 2 meters). The swan’s orange beak with a black knob is characteristic. While not a wild species in Bangladesh, the swan is included in the gallery as an example of the diversity of waterfowl worldwide and to teach about the care of captive animals. The exhibit also distinguishes between swans, geese, and ducks.
