Preserved crane specimen, wading bird. The sarus crane (Antigone antigone) is the world’s tallest flying bird, standing up to 1.8 meters. This specimen is nearly that tall, with long legs, a long neck, and a red head. The sarus crane is endangered in Bangladesh, with only a few pairs remaining in the wetlands of the north. This specimen was collected in the 1980s, before the population crashed. The mount shows the crane in a courtship display, with its wings spread and head bowed. The exhibit explains the threats to sarus cranes (habitat loss, egg collection) and conservation efforts. It is one of the most spectacular specimens in the gallery.

Preserved stork specimen, wading bird. The painted stork (Mycteria leucocephala) has a distinctive pinkish-white plumage and a long yellow beak. This specimen is mounted standing in shallow water (represented by painted wood). The stork’s wings are folded, but the pink color is still visible. Painted storks are colonial nesters and are found in the wetlands of Dhaka and elsewhere, though they are becoming rare. This specimen was collected from a colony that was destroyed by development. The exhibit discusses the importance of wetlands for migratory and resident birds.

Preserved heron specimen, wading bird. The purple heron (Ardea purpurea) is a large heron with a slate-gray body and a chestnut-colored neck. This specimen is mounted in a hunting pose, standing still with its neck curved. Herons are solitary hunters that stand motionless in water, waiting for fish. The exhibit explains the heron’s hunting technique and its adaptations (long legs, sharp beak). This specimen was collected from the Chittagong Hill Tracts. Herons are common but are often mistaken for cranes; the exhibit clarifies the differences.

Preserved egret specimen, wading bird. The little egret (Egretta garzetta) is a small, all-white heron with black legs and yellow feet. This specimen is mounted with its wings spread, showing the delicate plumes (aigrettes) that were once prized for the feather trade. The exhibit discusses how the feather trade almost drove egrets to extinction in the late 19th century, leading to the first conservation movements. This specimen is a reminder of the impact of fashion on wildlife. It was donated by a former feather trader who turned conservationist.

Preserved pelican specimen, aquatic bird. The spot-billed pelican (Pelecanus philippensis) is a large water bird with a massive throat pouch. This specimen is mounted with its pouch inflated, showing the elastic skin that can hold up to 13 liters of water. Pelicans are found in the wetlands of Bangladesh, but their populations have declined. This specimen was collected from a zoo where the pelican died of old age. The exhibit explains how pelicans use their pouch to scoop up fish and how they work together in groups to herd fish. The large size and unusual appearance make it a crowd-pleaser.

This copperplate charter issued by King Sri Chandra of the Chandra dynasty records a land grant to a Brahmin. The inscription is in Sanskrit and the script is a variant of northern Gupta. The plate is one of the most important sources for the history of the Chandra dynasty, which ruled over eastern Bengal and the Samatata region. The copperplate is well preserved, with the text legible. It is displayed with a transliteration and translation, allowing visitors to read the original grant, which includes details about the donor, donee, boundaries of the land, and witnesses. This is a key artifact for understanding the administrative and legal systems of early medieval Bengal.

A silver rupee (square shape) issued by the Mughal Emperor Akbar from the mint of Dhaka. The coin is inscribed with the Arabic kalima on one side and the name of Akbar on the other. This coin is evidence of Mughal control over Bengal and the integration of Bengal into the Mughal monetary system. The square shape is unique to Akbar's coins and reflects his innovative approach to administration. The coin is in excellent condition, with the inscriptions clearly legible. It was part of a hoard discovered near Old Dhaka.

One of seven Sher Shahi cannons held at the Bangladesh National Museum. These distinctive light bronze cannons bear Persian inscriptions dated 948 AH (1541–1542 CE), naming the manufacturer as Saiyad Ahmad Rumi and recording that they were cast under the command of Khwaja Basharat Sultani, Sher Shah's governor of Jannatabad (present-day Gaur in Bengal). The most striking feature is the tiger-head-shaped muzzle — the open jaws of a tiger form the mouth of the barrel, reflecting Sher Shah Sur's royal emblem and the Persian 'Sher' (lion/tiger) in his name. The barrel is narrow and cylindrical, approximately 4 ft 5 in (135 cm) long with a bore diameter of roughly 1 inch at the muzzle, with trunnions positioned near the mid-point. A long rear handle allowed the cannon to be steadied or repositioned. Sher Shah famously deployed 4,000 such light zarb-zan (swivel guns), each weighing 60–100 kg, in his campaigns to briefly displace the Mughal emperor Humayun (1540–1545). The BNM specimens are classified as 'Pre-Mughal cannons of Bengal' and are key to understanding the transfer of artillery technology from the Middle East, Central Asia, and Portugal into Bengal during the 16th century.

Artifact_Name: Rāma Breaking the Bow — Terracotta Relief Panel
Finding_Place: Palashbari, near Mahasthangarh, Bogra District (in the vicinity of Govinda Bhita temple complex)
Description: One of a celebrated series of Rāmāyaṇa narrative relief panels recovered from Palashbari, close to the ancient Govinda Bhita temple site at Mahasthangarh, representing the peak of terracotta sculpture in Bengal during the late Gupta period. This particular panel depicts the pivotal svayamvara scene from the Rāmāyaṇa in which Rāma masters and breaks the great bow of Janaka to win Sītā as his wife. The composition shows Rāma as the central figure engaged dynamically with the bow, accompanied by the sage Viśvāmitra on the left — who places his right hand on Rāma's shoulder in admiration — and Lakṣmaṇa standing to the right watching in wonder. Each figure is carved in very high relief, practically freed from the background, and the characters partially overlap or hide the broad frame surrounding the panel — a hallmark of this school. The faces display wide open eyes and vivid individual expressions that convey the emotional charge of the scene with exceptional strength. Bodies are full-volumed and dynamically posed, with nervously energetic but elegant lines; movement and feeling are expressed through varied gestures and facial expression to a degree not easily achieved in stone. The panels from Palashbari — almost certainly once distributed in horizontal rows across the outer brick walls of the Govinda Bhita temple — represent the unsurpassed achievement of Bengali artists in narrative terracotta, absorbing the Gupta aesthetic tradition and transforming it into something distinctly regional and dynamic

Period_Dating: 8th–9th century CE (early Pala period, Samatata / Southeast Bengal school)
Description: A significant bronze icon of Sitātapatrā — a protective Buddhist goddess whose name means "she of the white parasol" — recovered from Comilla district and representing the distinctive early cast-image tradition of Southeast Bengal. The surface of the figure reflects the smooth, soft modelling characteristic of the Lalmai-Mainamati atelier: a gentle, harmonious rendering of the body in which the dress clings to the limbs without any fold being indicated, underlining the shapes beneath. The face, unfortunately partially rubbed, originally displayed the tender and slightly compassionate smile typical of this school, with half-open eyes in the lotus-petal form. The deity is elegantly silhouetted in front of a plain back-slab adorned with rows of pearls and flames running along its edge, the whole composition bearing the umbrella (chattra) at the top — from which the goddess takes her name — though often broken away in surviving examples. The pedestal is elaborately worked, with lions and elephants on either side of the hanging drapery, and is widely open, creating internal iconographic space in contrast to the more compact northern examples. This image stands as an important representative of the highly refined Buddhist bronze-casting tradition centered on the Lalmai-Mainamati ridge, whose influence extended as far as Java (Indonesia) and Bihar in the 8th–9th centuries, attesting to the role of Southeast Bengal as a major centre for Buddhist art and maritime trade.

Artifact_Name: Air Force Badge, Uniform & Pen of Bir Shreshtha Matiur Rahman
Material: Wool/cotton uniform fabric; metal badge (brass/bronze); ink pen
Finding_Place: Bangladesh Air Force, Dhaka; recovered posthumously
Gallery_No: Gallery 38 — Bangladesh's Struggle for Independence: Bengali Bangladesh Liberation War
Description: The service uniform, rank badge, and personal pen of Flying Officer Matiur Rahman, the only air force officer among the seven Bir Shreshtha — Bangladesh's highest gallantry award recipients. Born in 1941 in Norsingdi, Matiur joined the Pakistan Air Force and was stationed at Masroor Air Base in Karachi at the outbreak of war in 1971. On 20 August 1971, he hijacked a Pakistani T-33 jet trainer with trainee pilot Mintu Mia, planning to defect to India and join the resistance. During a struggle in the cockpit, the aircraft crashed in Thatta, Sindh, killing both men. He was 29. The uniform on display is a dark olive PAF service dress with his Flying Officer rank insignia; the brass wing-and-propeller badge marks his aircrew qualification. The pen — a modest everyday object — sits alongside as a quiet contrast to the dramatic circumstances of his death, humanising the hero. Pakistan returned his remains to Bangladesh in 2006; his name is among the most recognised of 1971 and the display is one of the most visited spots in the liberation war galleries.

Artifact_Name: Standing Woman (architectural panel with female figure)
Material: Wood (species unspecified; likely teak or sal)
Finding_Place: Uttar Kazi Qazba (North Kazi Qasba), Dhaka District
Description: One of an extremely small number of surviving medieval wood carvings from Bengal, this panel depicting a standing female figure is among the rarest artifacts in the Bangladesh National Museum collection. The climate of the Bengal delta is hostile to the preservation of organic material, making such survivals exceptional. The panel, recovered from a domestic or temple architectural context in Dhaka district, belongs directly to the 11th–12th century stone sculpture school of Southeast Bengal — sharing its stylistic vocabulary in form, proportion, and ornamental treatment, while exploiting the particular advantages of wood as a medium. The female figure stands in a measured, slightly tribhanga (three-bend) pose, carved in the niche of a decorative panel. The movements of the body and limbs are extremely restrained but quietly animated with a subtle inner energy and life; wood permits a far smoother, more sensuous and detailed surface rendering than stone, and this is fully exploited in the delicate modelling of the face, jewellery and dress. Carved either fully in the round or nearly so, the figure expresses perhaps the highest level of refinement achieved by the artists of the Delta. Together with a handful of comparable surviving pieces — wooden pillars from Rampal, a capital from Sonarang, and a lintel from Vikrampur — this panel testifies to a rich tradition of architectural wood sculpture in medieval Bengal that has been almost entirely lost to time and humidity.

Artifact_Name: Bloodstained Blazer, Shirt & Shoes of Language Martyr Shafiur Rahman
Material: Wool blazer, cotton shirt, leather shoes; bloodstains preserved
Description: The bloodstained blazer, shirt, and shoes worn by Shafiur Rahman on the day he was killed, making them among the most emotionally charged relics in the museum. Shafiur was a court employee and student activist who joined the massive Bengali-language protest march in Dhaka on 21 February 1952, when the Pakistani government had banned public assembly. Police opened fire on the crowd near the Dhaka Medical College, killing several demonstrators. Shafiur Rahman was shot and died on that day, becoming one of the primary martyrs of the Language Movement — the struggle to have Bengali recognised as an official language of Pakistan that would ultimately contribute to the 1971 independence movement. The dark fabric of the blazer retains visible dark bloodstains, preserved over seven decades. These garments function less as clothing than as physical testimony: tangible, irreducible proof of the violence of that day. The 21 February is now observed globally as International Mother Language Day, a UNESCO designation since 1999.
The map is made using soil of 64 districts of Bangladesh

Gallery_No: Natural History or Economic Botany section
Description: A three-part interpretive display documenting the rubber industry in Bangladesh, centred on the Chittagong Hill Tracts where rubber (Hevea brasiliensis) cultivation was introduced during the British colonial period. The display comprises three elements shown together in a single case. On the left stands a realistic model of a tapped rubber tree stump with the characteristic diagonal slash marks on the bark from which white latex flows into a small clay collection bowl at its base, alongside a young rubber sapling growing from sandy soil. On the wall hangs a composite photograph panel labelled লাভার তৈরি / Rubber Making in Bengali and English, showing five historical black-and-white photographs illustrating the full production process: the rubber plantation canopy, bark tapping in progress, workers processing raw latex on long tables, and the drying and smoking racks where sheets are cured. On the right wall hang two sheets of processed rubber — amber-brown, textured, waffle-patterned — representing the finished raw commodity exported from Bangladesh. The display contextualises rubber as one of the significant commercial plantation crops of the Chittagong Hill Tracts economy, alongside tea and bamboo.

Material: Wood veneer cabinet, metal chassis, vacuum tubes, fabric grille
Dimensions: Height ~18 cm, Width ~37 cm, Depth ~17 cm (approx. from label)
Description: A vintage tabletop valve radio receiver manufactured by the Shanghai Radio Factory in China, model Type 161-1 — one of the most widely exported Chinese consumer radios of the 1960s. The set is housed in a warm brown wood-veneered rectangular cabinet with a large woven fabric speaker grille occupying most of the front face, behind which a small decorative shield badge identifies the manufacturer. The control panel below carries the brand name SHANGHAI in gold lettering across a black fascia, with two large rotary knobs — one for tuning, one for volume — flanking a multi-band frequency scale marked with three wavebands: Medium Wave (MW, 650–1600 kHz) and two Shortwave bands (SW.I and SW.II), along with a row of four white preset buttons. The Type 161-1 was capable of receiving international shortwave broadcasts, making it a significant object in the context of Bangladesh's Liberation War of 1971 — when radios of exactly this type were used by ordinary families to follow news from Swadhin Bangla Betar Kendra (Free Bengal Radio Station) and the BBC Bengali Service. The museum label notes it was used for listening to various broadcasts. Donated to the BNM in 2019.

A working cargo-and-sail river boat from Kushtia district, with a shallow flat-bottomed hull, a small roofed wooden cabin at the stern for the boatman, a central mast with cross-spar for sail rigging, and long bamboo oars for manoeuvring in calmer water. The Bachari is a multi-purpose craft widely used on the rivers of central and western Bangladesh for transporting goods and people. The model shows the practical carpentry of rural Bengali boat-building with no ornamentation — every element is functional.

Material: Vellum or early paper, iron-gall ink Script: Early Arabic — Kufic style
Dimensions: Length 10 inches, Width 22 inches, Height 34 inches; Weight 4 kg; Pages: 372
Description: A handwritten manuscript of the Holy Quran described on the museum label as a shadow copy (ছায়ালিপি) of the Mushaf-e-Usmani — the authoritative recension of the Quran compiled under the third Caliph Hazrat Uthman ibn Affan (RA) (644–656 CE), who standardised the text and dispatched copies to major Muslim cities. The script visible in the photograph is an early angular Arabic hand consistent with the Kufic tradition — one of the oldest calligraphic styles of the Arabic script, characterised by bold horizontal strokes, angular letterforms, and absence of diacritical vowel marks (tashkil), which is typical of the earliest Quranic manuscripts. The pages are of a warm cream-ivory colour showing significant age browning and foxing, and the ink — likely iron-gall — has darkened to near-black. The manuscript is displayed open at what appears to be an interior sura, written in a dense two-column layout of approximately 15–17 lines per page with no illuminated headings visible on this opening. At 372 pages and weighing 4 kg, this is a substantial full-text codex. Whether it is an authentic pre-modern manuscript or a scholarly facsimile reproduction of a Uthmanic original, it represents an important object in the BNM's Islamic heritage collection and in documenting the history of Quranic transmission.

Artifact_Name: Women Tea Pickers in the Hill Garden (Life-size Diorama)
Description: A large-scale, immersive diorama depicting the labour of women tea garden workers in the hill tea estates of the Sylhet region — the heart of Bangladesh's tea industry. Two life-size female mannequins, dressed in working saris with head coverings, are positioned among a dense planting of realistically rendered tea bushes (Camellia sinensis), their hands extended in the act of two-leaves-and-a-bud plucking, the standard harvesting technique for quality tea. The nearer figure carries a large wicker basket suspended from a headband across her forehead — the jhuri — the traditional carrying method in which the weight of the full basket of plucked leaves is borne by the neck and forehead rather than the hands, keeping both hands free for picking. Behind them a sweeping panoramic painted mural backdrop depicts the characteristic landscape of the Sylhet tea estates: terraced hillsides of vivid green tea bushes rolling across rounded hills beneath a cloud-filled sky, with additional worker figures visible in the middle distance. This diorama documents the lives of the largely female, predominantly Adivasi (indigenous) tea garden workforce — a community that has maintained the tea industry since the British colonial period but has historically faced significant social and economic marginalisation.

Three ornate full-length garments are displayed on mannequins within a glass case, with additional textile panels visible at the sides.Left — Choka (চোগা): A long flared outer robe in olive-gold silk with an overall small floral or boteh (paisley) brocade pattern woven across the body, and a broad, heavily embroidered dark border running along the hem and cuffs. The Choga is a traditional overgarment of Mughal and Persian origin worn by men of rank across the Indo-Persian cultural world. It falls to the ankle, is open at the front, and has long full sleeves.Centre — Chapkan (চাপকান): A fitted, knee-to-ankle-length coat in bright magenta silk with a dense woven gold zari (metallic thread) brocade of small repeating motifs across the entire surface, finished with a particularly heavy and elaborate gold border along the lapel, front opening, and hem. The Chapkan is a close-fitting garment derived from the Mughal court tradition — more structured and formal than the Choga — historically worn by nobles, officials, and grooms in wedding ceremonies. The vivid magenta with gold zari is a bridal or festive ceremonial combination.Right — Choka (চোগা), second example: A darker, slate-grey or charcoal outer robe with an extremely dense all-over surface of floral and arabesque embroidery covering practically the entire garment in a technique consistent with zardozi (gold and silver thread work) or fine block-printed resist-dyed fabric. The heavily worked surface would have required months of skilled handwork and represents a prestige garment of the highest order.

A bronze portrait bust of Rabindranath Tagore (7 May 1861 – 7 August 1941) — Nobel Laureate in Literature (1913), poet, philosopher, composer, and the author of Amar Shonar Bangla, the national anthem of Bangladesh. The bust depicts Tagore in his characteristic elderly appearance, the form by which he is universally recognised: a broad, noble forehead framed by thick, wavy hair swept naturally back from the face, deepset and contemplative eyes under strong brows, a prominent straight nose, and the full, long flowing beard that became his most iconic physical feature. The sculptor has rendered the beard with considerable detail — individual locks and strands are modelled with sensitivity, giving the mass of hair an organic, living quality rather than a rigid sculptural convention. The drapery of the upper garment falls in broad, loosely worked folds across the chest and shoulders, suggesting the simple traditional chadar or shawl he habitually wore. The facial expression is meditative and inward — calm, wise, and gently melancholic in the way that characterises many of his most admired portraits. The surface of the bronze has developed a natural patina of warm brown and green oxidation, which gives the bust an aged, authoritative presence consistent with Tagore's standing as one of the defining figures of Bengali civilisation. Tagore's connection to present-day Bangladesh is direct and deep: he managed his family's zamindari estates at Shilaidaha (Kushtia), Shahjadpur (Sirajganj), and Patisar (Naogaon) for many years and composed some of his greatest works on the rivers and countryside of Bengal.

A bronze portrait bust of Kazi Nazrul Islam (25 May 1899 – 29 August 1976) — the National Poet (Jatiya Kabi) of Bangladesh, revolutionary lyricist, composer, novelist, and the most celebrated rebel voice in Bengali literature. Unlike the Tagore bust displayed nearby, this work depicts Nazrul in his youth — as the defiant, passionate young poet of the 1920s rather than the stricken older man of his later years. The face is full and youthful, with high, prominent cheekbones, wide eyes gazing upward and outward with an air of restless energy and defiance, and a slightly open, determined mouth. The hair is thick, wavy, and swept back from the forehead in loose natural curls that fall at the sides — a style consistent with his appearance in photographs from his most productive years. He wears an open-collared shirt, the collar loosely arranged, contributing to the impression of an unconventional, free-spirited personality. The bust is placed in front of a display panel that reproduces in large Bengali script one of Tagore's poems, alongside a historical photograph of Nazrul as a young man, creating a deliberate curatorial pairing of the two poets who together define the two great pillars of Bengali literary culture. The background poem, dated ২৬ চৈত্র ১৩০২ (26 Chaitra 1302 BS — 9 April 1896 CE), appears to be Tagore's Banga Mata — underscoring the thematic unity of both figures as voices of Bengali identity. Nazrul's body is interred at the Dhaka University campus mosque, making Bangladesh the country of his final rest and the primary custodian of his legacy.

Matsya — Sanskrit for "fish" — is the first of the ten principal avatars (Dashavatara) of Vishnu and the first intervention of divine preservation in Hindu cosmology. The myth exists in multiple versions across the Mahabharata, Shatapatha Brahmana, and the Puranas, but its essential structure is constant: at the end of a cosmic age, the demon Shankhasura stole the sacred Vedas — the divine knowledge that sustains the order of the universe — from the sleeping Brahma and concealed them in the depths of the primordial ocean. Vishnu descended in the form of a great fish to recover the Vedas from the cosmic deep and simultaneously guided the sage-king Manu and his family through the universal deluge (pralaya) in a great boat, thereby preserving the seed of humanity and all living beings for the new creation cycle to follow. The Matsya avatar thus carries a triple symbolic weight: it is an act of cosmic preservation (rescuing the Vedas), an act of civilisational salvation (guiding Manu through the flood — a narrative structurally parallel to the Mesopotamian and Biblical flood myths), and a cosmological marker (the transition between dissolution and new creation). As the first avatar it establishes the entire principle of Vishnu's avatarhood — that the divine descends into the world in embodied form whenever cosmic order (dharma) is threatened.The BNM Matsya Avatara from Vajrayogini, Munshiganj is carved in the fine-grained black basalt (Rajmahal black chlorite) that characterises the innumerable beautiful sculptures in Rajmahal Black Basalt Stone at the Bangladesh Museum from the Pala period. The stone's hardness permitted the extraordinarily fine surface detail — individual scales on the fish body, minute jewellery elements, subtle facial modelling — that distinguishes the best Pala carving from all contemporaneous Indian regional schools. 
Wikipedia

The upper human portion of the figure displays Vishnu in his standard four-armed manifestation, the body rendered with the full, smoothly modelled volumes of the Pala style — broad shoulders, a defined chest, a relatively narrow waist. The face carries the serene, inward-looking expression characteristic of Vaishnava images of the period: eyes slightly downcast and half-closed in the meditative yogic mode, brows gently arched, lips curved in the barely perceptible smile of divine composure. The kiritamukuta (tall cylindrical crown) rises above the head, and the standard Vaishnava ornaments — vanamala garland, kaustubha jewel on the chest, yajnopavita sacred thread, girdle, armlets, anklets — are rendered with careful attention to detail. The four hands hold the canonical Vaishnava attributes in their respective positions.

The transition between the human torso and the fish body is handled with the technical assurance of the mature Pala atelier — the transformation reads as natural and inevitable rather than awkward, the divine nature of Vishnu encompassing both forms simultaneously without contradiction. The fish body curves behind and below, its tail fin spreading at the base, the scaled surface texture providing a visual counterpoint to the smooth planes of the human torso above.

The sculpture is set against a prabhavali back-slab in the standard Bengal form, with flame borders running along the edge. Given its recovery from Vajrayogini in Munshiganj — the region of ancient Vikramapura — it belongs to the Southeast Bengal stylistic tradition and its characteristic clarity of composition and sensitivity of line.

A damaged stone image of Kusumavahana recovered from Niyamatpur, Naogaon, now preserved in the Bangladesh National Museum. Kusumavahana — "he whose vehicle is flowers" — is an epithet associated with Kamadeva (the god of love) or with a specific form of a deity whose mount or vehicle is identified with blossoms. The damaged condition of the image prevents full iconographic reading, but the recovery from the Naogaon region places it within the North Bengal artistic tradition of the Pala period, characterised by the fine black basalt carving of the Rajmahal stone workshops.

Artifact_Name: Khadiravani Tara (Standing, with Ashokakanta-Marici and Ekajata)
Description:
A later and more elaborate standing Tara image from Rampal, Munshiganj — the same site that yielded the magnificent dancing Chamunda (Fig-21) described earlier — confirming Rampal as a major centre of religious sculptural production in the Vikramapura region. The goddess stands gracefully, two-armed, in the standard Tara iconographic mode: varada-mudra in the right hand and nilotpala stalk in the left. The composition is distinguished from the earlier Sukhabashpur example by the presence of two named attendant goddesses flanking the central Tara: Ashokakanta-Marici to her right and Ekajata to her left.

This specific triad — Tara with Ashokakanta-Marici and Ekajata — corresponds precisely to the form of Tara described in the Sadhanamala (the Vajrayana liturgical compendium of goddess iconographies) as Khadiravani Tara — literally "Tara of the Acacia forest" (khadira = Acacia catechu), a form of the goddess associated with a specific forest grove and with the particular protection she offers to those who practise her sadhana (meditation ritual) within such a setting. The Sadhanamala identification of this specific triad as Khadiravani Tara gives the sculpture a precise textual anchor in the liturgical literature of late Pala Vajrayana Buddhism, confirming it was produced not merely as a devotional image but as the material focus of a specific contemplative and ritual practice.

At the apex of the composition, five Transcendent Buddhas are arranged with Amoghasiddhi — the Buddha of the north, whose name means "infallible accomplishment" — placed in the central position. This confirms the family affiliation stated in the source text: Tara belongs to the family of Amoghasiddhi, and her presence within his mandala as the active, protective feminine principle of his enlightened activity is the cosmological statement that the sculpture's composition makes visible.

Two sculpture of this exceptionally rare goddess are now in the BNM — one from Vajrayogini, Munshiganj and one from Naynanda — making the museum the primary repository of Parnashabari imagery in the world. The Scribd source text itself flags the iconographic significance precisely: this is "a unique figure of the Buddhist goddess only available from East Bengal" — meaning Parnashabari as a sculptural type is geographically exclusive to this specific region and cannot be found in the Buddhist art of North Bengal, Bihar, or any other centre of Pala period production.

Parnashabari — Sanskrit for "she who wears leaves as her garment" (parna = leaf, shabara = tribal/forest-dweller) — is a forest deity of tribal origin who was absorbed into the Vajrayana pantheon as a goddess of healing, specifically as a protectress against contagious diseases and epidemics. Her tribal identity is declared by her garment of leaves rather than the silks and jewels of all other deities in the Pala sculptural tradition — a deliberately non-courtly iconographic statement that marks her as belonging to the margins of the social order and to the raw, unmediated power of the forest rather than the refined world of the monastery or palace.

The goddess is depicted standing in pratyalidha — the dynamic battle-lunge stance with the right leg advanced — trampling two male figures beneath her feet, these figures representing personified diseases (vyaadhis) that her worship conquers. She is three-headed and eight-armed. The source text specifies that in six of her hands she holds clockwise: elephant-goad (ankusha), arrow (bana), thunderbolt (vajra), leaves (parna — her defining attribute), bow (dhanu), and the threatening pointing gesture (tarjani-mudra). Two of the remaining hands are engaged in the trampling posture or in additional gestures not specified in this passage. She is pot-bellied — an iconographic feature associated with abundance and the earth's fertility — and is accompanied by two attendant figures, one of whom rides a donkey, a distinctly humble and non-royal mount consistent with her tribal, non-courtly identity.

On the pedestal below the main composition, a crawling figure with an elephant head holds a sword and shield — identified in the source text as an obstacle-demon (vighna), a supernatural being representing impediments that the goddess overcomes. At the apex of the composition, five Transcendent Buddhas (Dhyani Buddhas) are arranged with Amoghasiddhi — the Buddha of the north, associated with fearlessness and the wisdom of accomplished action — placed in the central position. This cosmological crown elevates Parnashabari from a tribal healing deity to a fully integrated figure within the Vajrayana mandala system, her healing power framed as an expression of Amoghasiddhi's indestructible compassionate activity.

A three-headed, eight-armed image of Pratisara — also called Mahapratisara, "the Great Protectress" — the foremost of the five Pancaraksha ("Five Protective Goddesses") of Vajrayana Buddhism. The source text makes an observation of critical regional significance: "the cult of these Five Protective deities was prevalent only in this area of Bengal" — meaning eastern Bangladesh, specifically the Vikramapura / Munshiganj / Comilla zone. This geographical exclusivity mirrors the pattern seen with Parnashabari and confirms that the tantric Buddhist communities of Southeast Bengal developed specific goddess cults that had no parallel in the Buddhism of North Bengal, Bihar, or beyond.

The deity is seated in satvaparyankasana — the posture of heroic ease, with one knee raised — a posture of dignified, settled power appropriate to a great protectress. She is three-headed, the heads shown in relief-sculpture format, and eight-armed, though the upper portion of the image is damaged. The eight hands hold clockwise the following eight attributes as specified in the source: discus (cakra), trident (trishula), arrow (bana), sword (khadga), bow (dhanu), thunderbolt (vajra), hatchet (parashu), and noose (pasha) accompanied by the threatening pointing gesture (tarjani-mudra). This arsenal of eight weapons — spanning the attributes of Vishnu, Shiva, Indra, and the directional guardians — identifies Mahapratisara as a cosmic protectress capable of defeating threats from all directions and of all categories.

The combination of the three heads, the eight weapons, and the satvaparyankasana posture follows the iconographic prescription for Mahapratisara found in the Pancaraksha tantric texts — a class of protective literature whose practical application in ritual was the conferral of immunity from disease, poison, fire, flood, evil spirits, and all dangerous supernatural forces. The presence of this image from Vikrampur confirms that the Vikramapura monastery complex — capital city of the Candra, Varman, and Sena dynasties — sustained an active tradition of Pancaraksha worship alongside its better-documented Shaiva and Vaishnava religious life.

A sculpture of Heruka in his two-armed manifestation, recovered from Shubhapur in Devidvar, Comilla district. Heruka is one of the principal wrathful (krodha) deities of Vajrayana Buddhism — a fierce, ecstatic deity of the anuttarayoga-tantra class whose terrifying form represents the transformation of negative emotions into liberating wisdom. In his two-armed form he is typically depicted standing in a dynamic posture, naked or minimally clothed, adorned with bone ornaments (ashtamudrabhushana), displaying an expression of fierce compassion. The recovery from Comilla district — the region of the Lalmai-Mainamati ridge and Vikramapura — confirms the presence of advanced Vajrayana tantric practice in Southeast Bengal, consistent with the documented role of the Mainamati monasteries as centres of esoteric Buddhism from the 7th century onward and their artistic connections to Java and Bihar

The goddess sits in vajraparyankasana — the cross-legged adamantine posture — inside a chaitya: the characteristic horseshoe-arched architectural frame of a Buddhist shrine, whose pointed arch and distinctive profile identifies the entire composition as a sacred space, a sanctuary within a sanctuary. This setting within a chaitya arch is consistent with other late Pala period images from Southeast Bengal in which the deity is shown residing within a miniature architectural structure, as documented by Bautze-Picron in the paper you uploaded.

She is three-headed — the three faces arranged frontally with the lateral heads in three-quarter profile, a compositional convention for multi-headed deities established throughout the Pala sculptural tradition — and twelve-armed, the twelve arms fanning symmetrically around the body, each hand holding a specific attribute. The twelve-armed configuration corresponds to the standard Namasamgiti description in the Dharmakosasamgraha and reflects the fullness of the deity's cosmological reach — twelve being a number of cosmological completeness in the Vajrayana system, corresponding to the twelve members of dependent origination (pratityasamutpada) and to the twelve-spoked wheel of the dharma.

While the specific attributes held in the twelve hands are not enumerated in the source text, the standard Namasamgiti attribute programme — drawn from the Sadhanamala and the Nispannayogavali — would include the sword of wisdom (khadga), the blue lotus (nilotpala), the bow and arrow, the vajra (thunderbolt), the book (pustaka — representing the Namasamgiti text itself), and various gestures of teaching, protection, and boon-giving. In the female form, some of these attributes would be modified to reflect her closer alignment with the Prajnaparamita and Tara traditions.

A Pala-period blackstone sculpture of Brahma — the Creator god of the Hindu trinity (Trimurti) — seated in padmasana (lotus posture) on a large lotus throne, his characteristic four faces (caturmukha) arranged at the cardinal directions, with the principal face frontal and the three subsidiary faces visible in three-quarter profile to the left and right and implied at the back. The four faces reflect the theological identity of Brahma as the deity who presides over all four directions of space and whose creative speech (Vak) — the sacred syllable Om — resounded in all four directions simultaneously at the moment of cosmic creation.

The figure is four-armed, holding in his hands the standard Brahma iconographic attributes: a water vessel (kamandalu), associated with the primordial waters from which creation arose; prayer beads (akshamala), marking his status as the lord of cosmic time measured through ritual; and the Vedas (pustaka), the sacred texts that he holds as their ultimate author and guardian. His body is ornamented with jewellery consistent with the 10th-century Pala stylistic idiom — a necklace, armlets, and a girdle — rendered with the careful, restrained detail of the mature North Bengal school.

Beneath the lotus throne, Brahma's vahana (divine vehicle) the hamsa — the goose or swan, symbol of discriminating wisdom (viveka) and of the brahman in its unmanifest form — is visible, providing the cosmic mount upon which the Creator rides. Two small worshipping figures are positioned at the base of the pedestal, while two celestial attendant figures (vidyadharas) are carved in the upper corners of the composition carrying garlands in devotion. The back-slab shows various attendant deities and ornamental elements consistent with the 10th-century North Bengal compositional tradition.

The recovery from Kalihar in Rajshahi district places this within the North Bengal Pala school. Brahma, often a minor deity elsewhere, was notably popular in Bengal, evidenced by numerous 8th–9th century stone images identified in various museums. This 10th-century Kalihar Brahma extends that tradition into a slightly later period, showing the continued vitality of Brahma worship in North Bengal even as the major sculptural energy of the Pala period shifted toward Vishnu and Shaiva imagery in the 11th–12th centuries.

Finding_Place: Bangarh, West Dinajpur District (Balurghat), India (now South Dinajpur)
Description:
A nibedon stupa — literally a "dedicatory stupa" (nibedan = offering/dedication in Bengali, from Sanskrit nivedana) — is a miniature architectural monument in stone, functioning as a votive offering placed within a temple precinct or monastery as an act of religious merit-making. It is a condensed, sculptural version of a full-scale Buddhist or Hindu religious tower, offered by a donor as a permanent act of devotion rather than built at full scale. This BNM example, recovered from Bangarh in West Dinajpur, is a remarkable specimen of this relatively rare genre of Pala-period religious art.

The monument takes the form of a tapering tower of octagonal or square plan rising from a broader base, the entire exterior surface elaborately carved in horizontal registers of diminishing width as the monument ascends. The lower section of the tower has deep-set arched niches on each face, within each of which stands a small carved figure of a deity — from the photograph, figures that appear to be standing male deities in the Vaishnava or Brahmanical tradition, each within its own miniature arched frame. Above the niche register, multiple horizontal bands of dense foliate and scrollwork ornament cover the tapering body of the tower — interlaced floral arabesque, lotus patterns, and geometric banding of the type characteristic of the mature Pala architectural ornamental vocabulary. The entire composition is crowned at the apex by a large amalaka — the ribbed melon-shaped finial of the Hindu rekha deul (curvilinear shikhara tower) — confirming that the monument's overall form is modelled on the North Indian temple tower rather than the hemispherical Buddhist stupa proper, despite its name. To the left in the photograph a second, plainer pillar of similar form is visible, suggesting the BNM holds at least two such votive pillars from Bangarh.

Dimensions: Length 71 cm (Daily Star source confirms 74.93 × 33.02 cm)
Description:
One of the rarest and most theologically unusual sculptural types in the entire BNM collection — and indeed among the rarest iconographic types in all of Bengal's medieval sculpture — this horizontal relief slab depicts an extraordinarily intimate and tender mythological scene: the goddess Gauri (Parvati) reclining on her daybed as a new mother, with the infant Lord Shiva in the form of Sadyojata nursing at her breast.

The composition inverts the usual hierarchical relationship between Shiva and Parvati in Indian iconography — in which Shiva is the senior, omnipotent deity and Gauri his devoted consort — and instead shows the great god of destruction and dissolution as a newborn child, entirely dependent on the nurturing body of the goddess. This inversion encodes a profound and specifically tantric theological statement: that the male divine principle (Purusha / Shiva) is ultimately born of and sustained by the female divine principle (Prakriti / Shakti / Gauri), and that the goddess in her maternal aspect is cosmologically prior and causally supreme. Sadyojata — "just born," the western face of Shiva associated with creation and the earth element — is here literally just born, the great Creator-Destroyer as an infant at the breast of the Mother of the Universe.

Reclining on her day bed with her newborn, bejeweled Gauri enjoys a foot rub from a lady-in-waiting. The baby nursing at her breast is Lord Shiva in the form of Sadyojata. The divine mother is healthy, conveyed by her contented smile and sensuous waist. Various offerings are laid below, and a host of diminutive deities assemble above to make this votive image more auspicious by their presence. They are comprised of Shiva in his aniconic form as the lingam, Shiva's sons Ganesha and Kartikeya, and the nine planetary bodies in Indian astronomy — the navagraha

A stone epitaph (mazarlipi or qabrlipi) bearing the tombstone inscription of Haji Shariatullah (c. 1781–1840 CE), founder of the Faraizi Movement (Faraezi Andolan) — one of the most significant Islamic reform movements in 19th-century Bengal and a major precursor to the broader social and anti-colonial consciousness that eventually shaped the independence movements of South Asia.

The inscription is engraved in dense naskh Arabic script on a rectangular black stone slab, beginning at the top with the Bismillah — Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim ("In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful") — in an ornamental cartouche, followed by multiple lines of Arabic text recording the death, identity, and religious standing of the deceased. The date 1255 AH / 1840 CE is visible in the lower registers of the inscription. The clarity of the engraving and the density of the text suggest this was the work of a skilled professional calligrapher-stonemason, likely in the Persian-Arabic epigraphy tradition that flourished in Bengal under Mughal and later Nawabi patronage.

Haji Shariatullah was born in Bahadurpur, Faridpur district. He spent approximately twenty years studying in Mecca, where he came under the influence of the Wahhabi reform movement of Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab and the broader movement for returning Islamic practice to its scriptural fundamentals. Returning to Bengal around 1820, he founded the Faraizi movement — named for its central emphasis on the faraiz (obligatory duties/pillars of Islam) — which called for:

Strict adherence to Quranic obligations and rejection of what he considered un-Islamic innovations (bid'ah) that had entered Bengali Muslim practice
The declaration that Friday prayers and Eid prayers were not obligatory in Bengal as it was Dar al-Harb (territory under non-Muslim rule) — a controversial ruling that distinguished his movement from others
Opposition to exploitative indigo planters and zamindars — making the Faraizi movement simultaneously a religious reform and a peasant resistance movement against British colonial economic oppression
Shariatullah died in Bahadurpur, Faridpur in 1840 and was buried there. His son Dudu Miyan (Muhammad Muhsinuddin) continued and radicalised the movement after his death. The removal of his tombstone inscription from Faridpur to the BNM has preserved what would otherwise be a vulnerable outdoor epigraphic record, making the museum the primary custodian of this material document of one of Bengal's most important 19th-century religious and social leaders.

Finding_Place: Bangarh, West Dinajpur District, India (now South Dinajpur)
Description:
A monumental inscribed black stone pillar, standing 255 cm tall, erected in 966 CE by order of a king of the Kamboja dynasty — making it one of the most precisely dated pieces of monumental stone architecture from 10th-century Bengal in any museum collection, and a primary historical document of one of the least studied dynasties of early medieval Bengal.

The pillar is octagonal in plan — its eight faces carrying the continuous decorative programme around its circumference — and tapers slightly from a broader square base to a more slender shaft and an elaborately carved capital. The carved decoration is organised in horizontal registers of diminishing height as the pillar ascends. The lower section bears figural carved panels — divine or royal figures within arched niches. The middle shaft carries bands of floral and geometric ornament in the mature Pala-period North Bengal idiom. The capital is the most elaborately worked section, with multiple stacked bands of dense interlaced foliage, kirtimukha (monstrous face of glory), and pearl borders beneath the broad flat top of the capital. The inscription — confirming the date of 966 CE and the Kamboja dynastic identity — would be carved on one or more faces of the shaft or base.

The Kamboja Dynasty in Bengal: The Kambojas were a people of northwestern origin — associated in ancient sources with the Kamboja country of the northwest frontier — who established a ruling dynasty in North Bengal in the 10th–11th centuries, displacing the weakened Pala rulers. The Kamboja-Pala dynasty, known by this name in the 10th and 11th centuries, established control over North and East Bengal after defeating the Pala rulers. Rajyapala was the founder of this dynasty, and the history of this dynasty is found in the Irda copper plate inscription. The 966 CE date on this pillar would place it in the reign of one of the earliest Kamboja rulers of Bengal — contemporary with or immediately following Rajyapala's consolidation of power — making it a primary epigraphic witness to the Kamboja takeover of North Bengal. The Bangarh provenance is significant: Bangarh (ancient Kotivarsya) was the most important administrative centre of North Bengal under successive dynasties, and the erection of a monumental inscribed pillar there was a deliberate act of political legitimation — claiming the ancient capital and its authority for the new Kamboja rulers.

Period_Dating: 13th century CE (late Sena / early Sultanate transitional period)
Dimensions: 71.6 cm (label measurement — likely diameter or section height; full column considerably taller)
Description:
A sandstone temple pillar of the 13th century from Barisal district — one of the very few stone architectural elements in the BNM collection from South Bengal and from the period immediately preceding the Muslim Sultanate's consolidation of power over Bengal. The warm buff-grey colour and granular texture of the sandstone contrasts sharply with the fine black basalt of the Pala-period sculptures surrounding it in the gallery, immediately signalling a different geological source, a different regional tradition, and a different historical moment.

The pillar is composed of three clearly differentiated sections. The base is square in plan with deeply carved ornamental panels on each face — small standing deity figures in arched niches are visible on two faces of the base in the photograph, each figure richly detailed despite the smaller scale, representing the guardian deities or dvarapalas that conventionally flank temple entrances and structural supports. Above the base, a concave moulding marks the transition to the shaft, which is circular in plan and carries multiple horizontal bands of carved ornament: a band of elongated pendant forms (alambi) in the lower shaft, above which a band of interlaced or knotted floral ornament fills the mid-section, and above that a further band of scrollwork. The capital is a large, fluted bell or cushion form (ghata-pallava or kalasa capital) of substantial diameter, with a beaded ring at its junction with the shaft and a flat abacus on top.

The 13th-century dating places this pillar at the most turbulent transitional moment in Bengal's cultural history — the period of the initial Muslim conquests of Bengal under Bakhtiyar Khilji (1203 CE) and the subsequent establishment of the Bengal Sultanate. The construction of a stone temple in Barisal in the 13th century — using the indigenous sandstone architectural tradition rather than the black basalt of the North Bengal school — indicates that Brahmanical temple construction continued in South Bengal even as political authority was transitioning, and that regional stone-carving traditions distinct from the Pala mainstream persisted into this period. The pillar is among the rare physical survivals of this transitional architectural moment in the BNM collection.

This sculpture depicts Vishnu in his Varaha (boar-headed) incarnation, rescuing the Earth Goddess from cosmic waters. Vishnu stands in alidha posture, with his right foot pressing upon the serpent Adisesa and his left bent upon a lotus upheld by the Naga king’s consort. His four hands hold the traditional attributes — gada (mace), chakra (discus), padma (lotus), and shankha (conch) — though the upper right hand and mace are broken.

The upper left hand supports a small female figure in anjali mudra, identified as the Earth Goddess (Prithvi). Vishnu is richly adorned with ornaments: necklace, earrings, armlets, girdle, and sacred thread (upavita). A vanamala garland flows down to his knees.

At the pedestal, Garuda is shown at the center, while worshippers kneel on either side in reverence. The prabhavali (back-slab) rises behind him, crowned with an inverted lotus and a kirtimukha at the top. Two vidyadharas approach with garlands. Despite slight mutilation on the left edge, the sculpture retains its grandeur.

This Varaha image embodies the Pala dynasty’s mastery of iconography, blending mythological narrative with refined stone carving. It symbolizes Vishnu’s cosmic role as preserver, saving the Earth from chaos and reaffirming divine kingship.

This sculpture represents Devi Gauri, a serene and auspicious manifestation of Parvati/Durga, revered as the embodiment of purity, fertility, and maternal power. The figure is carved in chaturbhuja (four-armed) form, holding symbolic attributes: rosary (japamala), lotus flower, water pot (kamandalu), and one hand in abhaya mudra (gesture of reassurance). In some iconographic traditions, she may also hold a trident (trishula).

The goddess is adorned with bright ornaments — necklaces, bangles, mangalsutra, and nose-ring — and wears a richly carved sari, reflecting the Pala-Sena style of sculpture. Her face is calm and luminous, symbolizing her transformation from ascetic Parvati to radiant Gauri after penance and divine blessing.

At her feet, depictions of her vahana (vehicle) vary: sometimes a lizard (godha), sometimes a lion, linking her to Durga’s martial aspect. The back-slab (prabhavali) often features a crescent moon and accompanying deities such as Lakshmi, Saraswati, Kartikeya, and Ganesha, emphasizing her role as mother and cosmic matriarch.

This sculpture is a rare and significant example of Mahagauri iconography in Bengal, combining local stylistic features with pan-Indian goddess traditions. It highlights the Pala-Sena period’s devotion to Shakti and the artistic mastery of black basalt carving.

Artifact_Name: Devi Chandi (চণ্ডী) — Fierce form of Parvati/Durga
Description:
This sculpture represents Devi Chandi, the fierce manifestation of Parvati/Durga, revered as the embodiment of Shakti. According to the Markandeya Purana, Chandi is the slayer of demons such as Shumbha, Nishumbha, Chanda, and Munda, and in her Durga form she defeats Mahishasura.

The figure is carved in black basalt, standing with powerful posture and adorned with ornaments — necklaces, earrings, armlets, and a sacred thread. Her multiple arms (depending on iconographic variation) hold weapons and symbols of divine power, including trident, sword, lotus, and conch, while one hand is often in abhaya mudra (gesture of protection).

The back-slab (prabhavali) is decorated with celestial motifs, including kirtimukha at the top, symbolizing the warding off of evil. Chandi’s fierce yet protective expression embodies her dual role as destroyer of demons and guardian of devotees.

Among the oldest coins found in the Indian subcontinent, these irregular silver punch-marked coins were cut from bars and stamped with symbols — sun, moon, hill, elephant, tree — each representing a specific authority. Thousands were excavated at Wari-Bateshwar, Narsingdi, pointing to an advanced ancient trading center. The museum's collection spans several types representing the earliest chapter of monetary history in Bengal.

Cowry shells served as small-denomination currency in Bengal for thousands of years, imported from the Maldive Islands through ancient Indian Ocean trade. Durable, uniform, and difficult to counterfeit, they were used for everyday low-value transactions alongside metal coins, remaining in use in rural areas well into the early 20th century. The display traces the longest-serving currency medium in Bengal's monetary history.

Finding_Place: Bactria / Northwest India (trade finds in Bengal)
Description: Coins of the Greek kings who ruled in Bactria following Alexander's conquests, with Hellenistic portraits of kings on the obverse and Greek deities on the reverse. Their appearance in Bengal demonstrates long-distance trade connections. These are among the most artistically refined coins of the ancient world, and among the most unusual artifacts in the collection.

Gold and copper coins of the Kushan Empire — the powerful Central Asian dynasty controlling Silk Road trade. Kushan coins are iconographically diverse: emperors standing or on horseback on the obverse; Shiva, Buddha, Mithra, and fire-altar deities on the reverse, reflecting a multi-religious empire. Kushan-period coins found across the Bengal delta evidence active trade with overland routes through Kushan-controlled territory.

Finding_Place: Coastal Bengal — Sylhet, Noakhali, Mainamati (Comilla), Chittagong
Description: Harikela silver coins were the dominant currency of coastal Bengal, circulating widely in Bay of Bengal maritime trade zones with Southeast Asia, Sri Lanka, and the Arab world. Bearing stylized symbols derived from Gupta-period traditions, a major cache was excavated at Mainamati. This display is the most significant assembly of Harikela coins in Bangladesh.

Gold coins of Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya) — described by the museum's keeper as one of Gallery 1's main attractions. Among the most beautifully designed ancient coins in the world, Gupta coins show the king hunting lion from horseback, playing the vina, or standing with a bow; the reverse shows goddess Lakshmi. Their presence underscores Bengal's participation in the Gupta imperial economic and cultural zone.

Gold tankas of Delhi Sultanate sultans — specifically mentioned among the museum's prize exhibits. Issued under Iltutmish, Alauddin Khalji, and Muhammad bin Tughluq, these coins bear the sultan's name and titles in Arabic naskh calligraphy, the kalima, and the mint name. The Sultanate-period tanka became the basis of subsequent Bengali monetary systems.

Artifact_Name: Bengal Sultanate Coins — Silver & Gold Tanka
Finding_Place: Bengal Sultanate mints: Firuzabad, Pandua, Sonargaon
Description: A comprehensive display covering coins of major Bengal sultans including Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah, Alauddin Hussain Shah, and Nusrat Shah. Silver tankas bear fine Arabic calligraphy with the sultan's name, titles, kalima, and mint city. The gold tankas are especially rare. The series documents nearly two centuries of independent Bengali Muslim rule, and the mint cities reveal the geography of the sultanate's capitals.

Artifact_Name: Mughal Empire Coins — Gold Mohur & Silver Rupee
Finding_Place: Mughal imperial mints: Akbarpur, Rajmahal, Dhaka (Jahangirnagar)
Dimensions: Gold mohur: ~20 mm; Silver rupee: ~19 mm
Description: A display of Mughal gold mohurs and silver rupees — the standardized imperial coinage dominating Bengal's monetary economy from 1576 until the mid-18th century. The obverse bears the emperor's name in Persian nasta'liq; the reverse carries the mint city, regnal year, and sometimes a Persian poetry couplet. Special focus on Dhaka (Jahangirnagar) mint coins — the Mughal provincial capital of Bengal — representing the economic output of Bangladesh's most important historical city.

Artifact_Name: Coin Minting Dies — Kremnica, Japan & Germany
Credit_Donor: Donated by respective mints to Bangladesh Bank
Description: A special display of master coin-minting dies from three of the world's most celebrated mints — specifically highlighted as major attractions by the museum's keeper. The Kremnica Mint (founded 1328, Slovakia) is one of the world's oldest continuously operating mints. The Japan Mint (Osaka) is renowned for extraordinary precision and artistic quality. The German die represents European minting tradition. Displayed together, they allow visitors to understand the mechanical core of coin production across different national traditions.

Artifact_Name: Ancient Coin Storage Pot & Wooden Coin Boxes
Description: Clay pots and wooden boxes used to hoard and conceal coins — displayed alongside their associated coin finds. Hoards buried in pots are among the most important sources of ancient and medieval coins in Bangladesh: people buried savings during political instability, intending to recover them later. The display shows several vessel types matched to the coin types they contained, from ancient punch-marked silver to Sultanate tankas. Iron coin chests used by banks and money-lenders are also shown.

Artifact_Name: British India Coins — East India Company & Crown Series
Description: A comprehensive display of East India Company and British Crown coins issued for India from 1757 to 1947 — covering Queen Victoria, Edward VII, George V, and George VI. Includes silver rupees, 8 annas, 4 annas, 2 annas, 1 anna, and pice denominations. The display documents the colonial monetization of Bengal, the displacement of local tanka currency, and a special 1947 series issued in the year of independence. These were the everyday coins of Bangladesh's territory for nearly two centuries.

A complete display of Pakistani rupee coins and banknotes that served as the official currency of East Pakistan (present-day Bangladesh) from 1947 to 1971. The banknotes' bilingual evolution — Urdu and Bengali — reflects the Language Movement's political impact on currency design. The collection includes all denominations from 1 paisa to 100 rupees, providing a full visual record of the monetary tokens of an era that ended with Bangladesh's independence in 1971.

Finding_Place: Government of Bangladesh / Security Printing Press
Description: The first official currency note of independent Bangladesh — the 1-taka 'Map Series', issued on 4 March 1972, just over three months after independence. The obverse features a map of Bangladesh; the reverse shows guilloche patterns. This note bears the Finance Secretary's signature (not the Bangladesh Bank Governor's), as the 1-taka is a government instrument. It remained legal tender until 30 March 1974. The most historically charged object in the museum: the moment Bangladesh expressed sovereignty through its own currency.

Artifact_Name: First Bangladesh 10-Taka Note with Bangabandhu Portrait (1972)
Description: The first 10-taka note issued by Bangladesh Bank (2 June 1972), featuring a portrait of Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman — the Father of the Nation — on the obverse. This was the first Bangladesh Bank note to carry his portrait, making it a founding document of the nation's currency visual identity. Its introduction six months after independence, while Bangladesh was still rebuilding from the Liberation War, represents an extraordinary institutional achievement.

Finding_Place: Bangladesh Security Printing Press / Foreign mints
Description: The first coins of independent Bangladesh — the 5, 10, 25, and 50 paisa denominations of 1973, bearing the national emblem of Bangladesh (a water lily flanked by rice sheaves, surmounted by three jute leaves, encircled by two stars). These were the first metal coins to carry the national emblem. Introducing coinage was a critical step in establishing Bangladesh's monetary system alongside paper notes.

Artifact_Name: Commemorative Notes — Mujib Centenary, Golden Jubilee, Nazrul
Description: Three landmark commemorative notes: (1) Polymer note for the Birth Centenary of Bangabandhu (17 March 2020), featuring his portrait and Liberation War scenes; (2) Polymer note for the Golden Jubilee of Independence (26 March 2021), depicting 50 years of national development; and (3) Paper note honoring Kazi Nazrul Islam, the National Poet. These notes document how Bangladesh Bank uses currency as a medium of national commemoration and cultural identity.

Artifact_Name: Rare Banknotes — USSR, Germany, Japan Military Yen
Finding_Place: USSR; East & West Germany; Imperial Japan
Description: Specifically highlighted by the museum's keeper as major attractions: Soviet ruble notes spanning the 1920s to 1991, documenting socialist iconography and the eventual collapse of the USSR; East and West German Deutsche Mark and Ostmark notes showing how one divided nation maintained two ideologically distinct currencies (1948–1990); and pre-WWII Japanese military yen and occupation currency from Southeast Asian territories. Together they illustrate currency as an instrument of political power and ideology.

Artifact_Name: Currencies of Extinct Nations — Yugoslavia, Czechoslovakia
Description: Banknotes from Yugoslavia and Czechoslovakia — nations that no longer exist. Yugoslav dinar notes span a monarchist federation through socialist Yugoslavia to catastrophic hyperinflation (500 billion dinar notes among the most dramatic documents of monetary collapse). Czechoslovak koruna notes reflect a stable socialist economy that peacefully divided in 1993. These illustrate the theme of currency as witness to political transformation.

Artifact_Name: Dolphin Coin of Ancient Olbia (Greek Colony, Black Sea)
Finding_Place: Olbia, Greek colony, Black Sea (present-day Ukraine)
Description: Cited as one of the museum's most remarkable exhibits: a dolphin-shaped cast bronze coin from ancient Olbia, over 2,500 years old. Rather than disk-shaped, Olbia's early currency took the form of miniature dolphins — believed to derive from earlier arrow-shaped proto-currency and the dolphin's sacred significance in Greek maritime culture. Extremely rare in South Asian collections, this coin represents one of the world's most distinctive early monetary forms.

Finding_Place: Left wall, museum entrance, Mirpur, Dhaka
Credit_Donor: Commissioned by Bangladesh Bank; artists Hashem Khan, Shyamal Chowdhury, Shantanu Khan
Description: A 'money tree' (taka gaach) mural on steel embedded with coin replicas from different historical periods, created by three prominent Bangladeshi artists. The tree's branches hold coins from ancient punch-marked silver through modern taka, providing a visual timeline of the entire collection before visitors enter. The concept draws on a universal folk motif of wealth and organic growth.

Credit_Donor: Excavation find, transferred from Dept. of Archaeology
Description: Display of coins and related artifacts from the extraordinary Wari-Bateshwar hoard — described as 'several thousand artifacts' pointing to ancient Bengal's trade routes. Wari-Bateshwar was a major trading city connected to the Roman world and Southeast Asia. The hoard includes punch-marked silver coins, rouletted ware pottery, and semi-precious stone beads. It is the most important archaeological numismatic find from Bangladesh.

Credit_Donor: Donated by central banks and governments; collected by Bangladesh Bank
Description: Gallery 2 houses paper, polymer, and hybrid notes and coins from approximately 200 countries — the museum's most internationally diverse exhibit. Includes currencies from Switzerland, Germany, Australia, Japan, USA, England, Spain, Argentina, India, Pakistan, China, Vietnam, Bulgaria, Cambodia, Mauritius, Kazakhstan, Syria, Bahrain, Oman, Philippines, Sri Lanka, Qatar, UAE, Kuwait, South Africa, and many more. Some were donated directly by central banks or diplomatic missions. Also includes currencies of defunct nations, making it a comprehensive archive of 20th-century world monetary history.

Finding_Place: Gallery 1 & 2, Bangladesh Bank Taka Museum, Mirpur
Description: 3D television and LCD display panels providing audio-visual interpretation of currency history, installed at the museum's 2013 inauguration per Governor Dr. Atiur Rahman's directive for a 'modern digital' museum. The digital kiosk allows visitors to print a souvenir note bearing their own face for Tk 50 — a popular feature especially with school groups. Animated sequences show the evolution of coins and banknotes, the mechanics of coin-minting, and the global spread of monetary systems.

Artifact_Name: Ancient Hindu Stone Sculpture — Deity Figure
Description: A black stone deity sculpture recovered from an archaeological site within Barisal Division, representing the strong Hindu religious traditions of the ancient Chandradwip kingdom. The figure is carved in the typical Bengal style of the Pala-Sena period, with elaborate jewelry, headdress, and multiple arms holding iconographic attributes. Stone sculptures from this region document the sophisticated artistic traditions of ancient South Bengal before the arrival of Islam.

Terracotta plaques with decorative motifs — floral scrolls, geometric patterns, lotus flowers, and mythological scenes — recovered from medieval temple and mosque sites across Barisal Division. The Barisal region, known historically as Chandradwip, was an independent Hindu-Buddhist kingdom before coming under Muslim rule, and its terracotta decorative tradition reflects that layered cultural heritage. These plaques are among the most visually striking exhibits in Gallery 3.

A collection of intricately crafted bricks from medieval structures in Barisal Division — specifically mentioned as signature exhibits of the museum. Some bricks bear stamped or incised decorative patterns; others are notable for their large Sultanate-period dimensions and dense firing. The Chandradwip kingdom was a prosperous region noted for its brick construction, and these specimens document the region's building traditions across the medieval period.

Period_Dating: Sultanate to British colonial period (14th–20th century CE)
Description: A collection of coins spanning from the Bengal Sultanate period through the Mughal and British colonial eras, recovered from various sites within Barisal Division. The collection includes Bengal Sultanate silver tankas, Mughal rupees, and British India coins. The region's position as a major trading hub of South Bengal made it a center of monetary circulation, and coins from multiple periods and dynasties have been recovered from its soil.

A collection of ancient pottery and ceramic utensils — water storage vessels, cooking pots, serving bowls, and storage jars — recovered from excavations across Barisal Division. These everyday objects document the material culture of the people who lived in the Chandradwip kingdom and its successor polities. The forms range from plain utilitarian ware to finely finished vessels with geometric incised decoration.

Artifact_Name: Traditional Musical Instruments of South Bengal
Material: Wood, bamboo, animal skin, metal strings
Credit_Donor: Donated by local cultural organizations and folk artists
Description: A collection of traditional musical instruments from the folk music tradition of South Bengal (Barisal Division): the dotara (two-string lute), the dhol (double-headed drum), the ektara (one-string drone lute), the bashi (bamboo flute), and the khamak (plucked percussion). Barisal Division has a rich folk music tradition including baul songs, bhatiali (river songs), and jari music associated with Muharram. These instruments document the living musical heritage of the region.

Credit_Donor: Donated by local families and cultural foundations
Description: Displays of traditional costumes and textiles from Barisal Division's diverse communities — including the white cotton sari worn by Hindu women, the embroidered kameez of Muslim women, the lungi and panjabi of men, and samples of locally woven fabrics. Barisal was historically a major center of cotton cultivation and hand-loom weaving, and these textiles document the material culture of its communities before industrial textile production transformed everyday dress.

Credit_Donor: Department of Archaeology and donated items
Description: A mixed display of religious artifacts reflecting the multi-religious history of Barisal Division: Hindu deity images in stone and bronze; a small bronze Buddha figure from the Buddhist period of the Chandradwip region; Islamic calligraphic tiles and a mosque lamp from the Sultanate-Mughal period; and a brass Hindu puja set from the 19th century. The collection documents the successive religious traditions that shaped the culture of South Bengal across 1,500 years.

Credit_Donor: Donated by families, National Archives of Bangladesh
Description: A collection of historical documents and photographs relating to Barisal Division's administrative, cultural, and political history: colonial-era revenue maps of the Chandradwip region, photographs of the historic Barisal Collectorate Building (now the museum itself), documents from the Language Movement of 1952, photographs of the 1971 Liberation War in Barisal, and portraits of prominent personalities from the region including poets, educators, and freedom fighters.

Artifact_Name: Geographic & Natural History Displays — Barisal Division
Credit_Donor: Department of Archaeology / Ministry of Cultural Affairs
Description: Gallery 1 of the museum presents the geography and natural environment of Barisal Division — one of the most hydrologically complex regions of Bangladesh, composed almost entirely of river delta formed by the Meghna, Tetulia, Arial Khan, and hundreds of smaller rivers. The exhibit includes topographic maps, hydrological diagrams, satellite images, and natural specimens — flora and fauna of the southern delta and the mangrove fringe adjacent to the Sundarbans. The Barisal Division is known as the 'Venice of Bengal' for its thousands of river channels.

Artifact_Name: Portraits & Biographies — Prominent Personalities of Barisal
Material: Oil and tempera on canvas; photographic prints
Credit_Donor: Donated by families and cultural institutions
Description: Gallery 2 is dedicated to prominent personalities of Barisal Division — the region that produced an remarkable concentration of Bengali intellectuals, writers, scientists, and politicians. The display includes portraits and biographies of poet Jibanananda Das (one of the most celebrated Bengali poets of the 20th century, born in Barisal), Aghor Nath Guha, Ashwini Kumar Dutta (educator and nationalist leader), Surendranath Haldar, and others. The gallery documents Barisal's exceptional contribution to Bengali intellectual and cultural life.

Artifact_Name: The Collectorate Building — Colonial Architectural Heritage
Credit_Donor: Government of Bangladesh / Department of Archaeology
Description: The museum building itself — the historic Barisal Collectorate Building, constructed in 1821 during the British colonial period — is displayed and interpreted as a heritage artifact. Gallery 9 presents the architectural history, construction techniques, and administrative significance of the building. Declared a protected archaeological site in 2003, it was abandoned by the Public Works Department in 1984 and transferred to the Department of Archaeology in 2005 for museum conversion. The Neoclassical colonial administrative architecture represents a significant layer of Barisal's physical heritage.

The Dakmanda (women's lower garment) and Dakmaro (chest wrap) form the traditional dress of Garo women, woven from cotton on back-strap looms in bold horizontal stripes of red, black, white, and green. The Garo people (also known as the Achik) are one of the major indigenous groups of northern Bangladesh, living along the foothills of the Garo Hills (Meghalaya border) in Netrokona and Mymensingh districts. This hand-woven garment is a living tradition maintained by Garo women and represents both technical skill and cultural identity. The museum's collection includes several examples in traditional patterns.

A Mingre — a traditional Garo hand-woven bag used for carrying everyday items, tools, or agricultural produce. Woven in bold geometric patterns on a back-strap loom using cotton and jute thread, the Mingre is both a functional object and a carrier of Garo aesthetic tradition. The geometric patterns carry cultural meaning — certain patterns are reserved for specific occasions or social groups. The Garo are a matrilineal society, and women's weaving is a central element of cultural transmission between generations. The museum holds several examples demonstrating the range of traditional Garo weaving patterns.

Traditional costumes and silver jewelry of the Hajong people — one of the indigenous groups of northern Bangladesh living alongside the Garo in the Durgapur area. The Hajong women's costume consists of a wrapped cotton sari in indigo and white with a characteristic border pattern. The jewelry display includes necklaces of silver coins and beads, ear ornaments, and wrist cuffs. The Hajong community has a distinct language (related to Bengali), a tradition of oral poetry, and a history of resistance against forced labor that culminated in the Hajong Revolt of the late 19th century.

Artifacts representing the culture of the Koch people — one of the ancient indigenous groups of northern Bangladesh. The display includes Koch ceremonial objects, hunting and agricultural tools, traditional storage vessels, and musical instruments. The Koch are believed to be among the earliest inhabitants of the Bengal-Assam borderland region. Their culture blends animist religious practices with later Hindu influences. The museum's Koch collection provides important documentation of a community whose traditional way of life is under pressure from modernization and cultural change.

Credit_Donor: Donated by farming families of Garo, Hajong, Koch communities
Description: A collection of traditional agricultural tools used by the indigenous communities of Durgapur Upazila: wooden plows, bamboo seed-carriers, iron weeding tools, hand-operated rice-threshing implements, and bamboo water-carrying poles. The indigenous communities of northern Bangladesh practice wet rice cultivation, shifting cultivation (jhum), and forest-based subsistence alongside settled agriculture. These tools document the ecological knowledge and farming practices of communities that have cultivated the foothills of the Garo Hills for centuries.

Artifact_Name: Garo Musical Instruments — Dama, Aduri & Bangsi
Credit_Donor: Donated by Garo musicians and cultural organization
Description: Traditional Garo musical instruments: the Dama (double-headed drum made from hollowed wood and animal skin), the Aduri (a gourd-resonated lute), and the Bangsi (a bamboo flute). These instruments are central to Garo musical performances associated with their festivals, particularly the Wangala harvest festival (celebrated in November to thank the sun-god Saljong for agricultural abundance) and the Sangrama festival. The Wangala is the most important Garo festival and its music is inseparable from the Dama drum, which leads the procession.

Hunting bows and arrows, bamboo fish traps (polo), cast nets (jal), hand-line fishing equipment, and small animal traps representing the traditional subsistence practices of the indigenous communities of the Durgapur area. The Someshwari River and its tributaries, along with the forested foothills bordering Meghalaya, have sustained Garo, Hajong, and Koch communities through fishing and hunting alongside agriculture. These implements document the ecological knowledge that has sustained life in this region across generations.

Traditional pottery made by the indigenous communities of the Durgapur area, including water storage pots, cooking vessels, grain storage jars, and ritual bowls. Pottery-making in this region uses hand-building techniques (coil and paddle) rather than the potter's wheel, producing vessels with a characteristic surface texture. Some vessels bear incised geometric decorations applied with a pointed tool before firing. The pottery traditions of the Garo Hills foothills are distinct from the mainstream Bengali terracotta tradition.

Finding_Place: Tribal Cultural Academy, Birisiri, Durgapur, Netrokona
Description: A collection of research publications and field documentation produced by the Tribal Cultural Academy's Research Section — one of the four institutional sections (Culture, Research, Library, Museum) of the academy.
