Publications include monographs on Garo language and grammar, studies of Hajong oral literature, documentation of traditional agricultural practices, and cultural surveys of Koch, Banai, Hadi, and Mandai communities. The Research Section has been documenting the intangible cultural heritage of northern Bangladesh's indigenous peoples since the academy's founding in 1977.

Artifacts representing the smaller indigenous communities of the Netrokona region — the Banai, Hadi, and Mandai peoples — alongside the Garo, Hajong, and Koch. These communities maintain distinct languages, belief systems, and material cultures. The display includes weaving samples, personal ornaments, ritual objects, agricultural implements, and everyday utensils. The Tribal Cultural Academy was specifically founded to serve all ethnic groups of northern Bangladesh, and its museum collection reflects this inclusive mandate to document the full diversity of indigenous cultural heritage in the region.

Dimensions: Various sizes (bound volumes and single folios)
Credit_Donor: Founded by Mahesh Chandra Bhattacharya (1912); donated by scholars over generations
Description: The Rammala Library and Museum's most important asset: a collection of approximately 9,000 rare Sanskrit, Bengali, and Prakrit manuscripts produced between 1500 and 1900 CE. The collection spans Vedantic scriptures, Puranas, Smritis, poetry, drama, grammar, philosophy, astronomy, Ayurvedic texts, economic treatises, and translations of sacred literature. Many manuscripts are illuminated with miniature paintings. Scholars have noted that rare books available here are not found even in Kolkata. The manuscript collection is one of the largest and most significant in Bangladesh and represents an irreplaceable repository of pre-modern Bengali intellectual life.

A collection of ancient coins recovered from the Comilla region — including 7th-century specimens specifically cited in national encyclopedic references as among the museum's most important archaeological holdings. The Comilla region (ancient Samatata) was a major kingdom of early medieval Bengal, and its coins provide primary evidence for the economic history of southeast Bengal before the arrival of Sultanate power. The collection also includes later Sultanate-period and British colonial coins found in the region.

Credit_Donor: Department of Archaeology transfers and donations
Description: Pottery and ceramic vessels from excavation sites in the Comilla region — representing the everyday material culture of the ancient and medieval population of Samatata (southeastern Bengal). The collection includes cooking vessels, storage pots, and decorated serving ware in forms ranging from simple utilitarian pieces to finely crafted examples with incised geometric decoration. These objects are particularly significant given the proximity of the major Buddhist site of Mainamati, where extensive ceramic sequences have been documented.

Credit_Donor: Department of Archaeology and private donations
Description: Stone sculptures from the medieval period recovered from the Comilla region, representing the Hindu and Buddhist sculptural traditions of ancient Samatata. The region's artistic production was connected to both the Pala Buddhist tradition (centered at Mainamati/Lalmai) and the later Hindu Sena period. These stone sculptures join the museum's terracotta artifacts and coins as primary archaeological evidence for the sophisticated artistic culture of pre-Islamic southeastern Bengal.

Artifact_Name: Rare Bengali Periodicals — Bangabasi, Hitabadi, Probasi
Dimensions: Various sizes (bound volumes and single issues)
Credit_Donor: Original collection of Mahesh Chandra Bhattacharya; preserved by successive librarians
Description: Rare original copies of landmark Bengali periodicals that are unavailable elsewhere in Bangladesh, including: Bangabasi (one of the most influential Bengali weekly newspapers, founded 1881); Hitabadi; Sanjibani; Sahitya Parishad Patrika (journal of the Bangiya Sahitya Parishad); Probasi (the prestigious literary journal founded by Ramananda Chattopadhyay, 1901); and Shanibarer Chithi. These periodicals were the primary vehicles for the Bengali cultural renaissance of the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Old copies of Sanskrit Aryaprabha are also preserved. The collection is described as irreplaceable for the study of Bengali language and culture.

Credit_Donor: Collected by Mahesh Chandra Bhattacharya and successors
Description: An unparalleled multi-faith collection assembled by founder Mahesh Chandra Bhattacharya representing ancient and modern religions: Hindu, Muslim, Buddhist, Christian, Sikh, Jain, Jewish, Zoroastrian, Egyptian, Babylonian, and Assyrian religious texts. The collection includes both printed books and manuscripts. Mahesh Chandra's father was a Sanskrit scholar, and his ecumenical approach to religious knowledge shaped the Rammala collection's extraordinary breadth. This comparative religious collection is unique among Bangladeshi libraries and reflects a 19th-century Bengali intellectual ideal of universal scholarly inquiry across religious boundaries.

Artifact_Name: Founder's Personal Collection — Mahesh Chandra Bhattacharya Memorabilia
Description: Objects and documents related to Mahesh Chandra Bhattacharya (born in Brahmanbaria district), the homeopath and philanthropist who founded the Rammala Library in 1912 in memory of his devout mother Rammala Devi. His father Ishwardas Tarkasiddhanta was a Sanskrit scholar, and Mahesh Chandra inherited a love of learning. The display includes his portrait, personal correspondence, documents from the founding of Ishwar Pathsala Tol (the Sanskrit school that became the library), and early donation records. Mahesh Chandra's vision of an open, free library serving all readers — religious, secular, rich, poor — is documented in his personal papers.

Artifact_Name: Ancient Coins — From 7th Century CE (Core Archaeological Collection)
Credit_Donor: Archaeological finds and donations, Comilla Heritage organization
Description: The museum's core numismatic collection specifically cited in the Nations Encyclopedia reference to the museum: '7th-century archaeological finds'. These include coins from the ancient kingdom of Samatata, coins associated with the Harikela tradition of coastal southeast Bengal, and later Sultanate and Mughal period coins from the Comilla area. Together they trace the monetary history of one of Bangladesh's most historically significant districts, where the Mainamati Buddhist complex was a major center of civilization from the 7th to 12th centuries CE.

Finding_Place: Baliati Palace, Rang Mahal, Saturia, Manikganj
Credit_Donor: Original palace inventory, Department of Archaeology
Description: One of fifteen iron safes (tijori) preserved in the Rang Mahal museum, used by the Baliati zamindars to store cash, jewelry, land deeds, and other valuables. The safe is of heavy cast iron construction with a double-lock steel mechanism and decorative cast-iron handles on the sides. Such safes were imported from British manufacturers — likely from Calcutta agents — during the height of the zamindari system in the late 19th century. The Baliati zamindars, descended from salt merchant Gobinda Ram Shaha, accumulated enormous wealth through salt trade and land revenues, and these vaults held the tangible instruments of that wealth. The museum's collection of 15 vaults is one of the largest in-situ collections of zamindari safes in Bangladesh.

Material: Brass horn, steel needle arm, wooden cabinet, shellac record
Finding_Place: Baliati Palace, Rang Mahal, Saturia, Manikganj
Description: A wind-up gramophone with a large flared brass horn, preserved from the zamindars' collection. The gramophone cabinet is of polished dark wood with a spring-wound motor; the horn is of heavy-gauge brass, now showing a natural patina of dark gold-green. Gramophone machines were among the most prestigious consumer goods in early 20th-century Bengal, and their ownership was a marker of elite status and Western cultural aspiration. The Baliati zamindars were known as progressive landlords who embraced modern technology and education — the family endowed Jagannath College in Dhaka. This gramophone would have played shellac 78 rpm records of Bengali classical music, film songs, and operatic performances for guests in the Rang Mahal (entertainment hall).

A decorative iron cash box with brass fittings, used for storing daily-use cash and petty revenues by the zamindari household. The box has a hinged lid with a brass hasp lock and a brass ring handle on each end for carrying. The exterior is plain iron with a faint scrollwork pattern pressed into the lid panel. Such cash boxes were kept in the counting room (ganjipura) of zamindari establishments, used by the nayeb (estate manager) to handle daily transactions with tenants, workers, and traders. The Baliati estate was one of the most prosperous zamindari operations in Manikganj district, and objects like this cash box were central to its day-to-day financial management.

Material: Glass chimney, tin body, brass fittings, cotton wick
Description: A hurricane paraffin lamp (hariken) in good condition, with its original glass chimney intact. The base is of pressed tin with a brass fuel reservoir and a wick-adjustment wheel. Hurricane lamps were the primary source of portable artificial lighting in Bengali households before the introduction of electricity, and remained in use in rural areas long after. The Baliati Palace complex would have required hundreds of such lamps to illuminate its over 200 rooms, corridors, ghats, and grounds. This example represents the everyday material culture of the palace during its active years in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, before the zamindari system was abolished by the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act of 1950.

Finding_Place: Baliati Palace, Rang Mahal ceiling, Saturia, Manikganj
Description: A multi-armed hanging chandelier (jhalar bati) from the Rang Mahal of the Baliati Palace, with brass arms and cut-glass pendant drops. The central column is of turned brass with a ceiling hook; six arms branch outward, each holding a glass oil font with a brass collar. The cut-glass drops refract the lamp light into prismatic sparkles, creating the festive ambiance expected of an entertainment hall (rong mahal) where the zamindars received guests, hosted musical performances, and celebrated festivals. Chandeliers of this type were manufactured in Calcutta by European firms and imported to zamindari establishments throughout Bengal in the late Victorian era. This example is original to the palace and has been in the museum collection since the Department of Archaeology's acquisition of the site in 1987.

Material: Teak wood frame, Italian white marble top
Finding_Place: Baliati Palace, dining hall, Saturia, Manikganj
Description: A large dining table with a teak wood frame and an Italian white marble top, from the main dining hall of the Baliati Palace. The teak frame is carved with decorative moldings on the apron and has eight turned legs joined by stretchers. The marble top is a single slab of pale white Carrara-type marble with faint grey veining, slightly chipped at one corner. Marble-top furniture was a hallmark of prosperous Bengali zamindari households in the late 19th century: marble was cool, easy to clean, and a conspicuous symbol of wealth and Western taste. This table would have been used by the zamindar family for formal meals and ceremonial feasts for guests. Its survival in reasonable condition makes it one of the most evocative pieces of furniture in the collection.

Material: Teak wood, beveled glass mirror, brass fittings
Finding_Place: Baliati Palace, Andarmahal (inner quarters), Saturia, Manikganj
Description: A tall teak wood almirah (wardrobe/cabinet) with a large central beveled glass mirror set into the door, from the Andarmahal (inner residential quarters) of the Baliati Palace. The almirah has two lower drawers, two cupboard sections with carved panel doors, and a central mirrored section flanked by narrow shelf cupboards. The brass fittings — hinges, drawer pulls, and keyhole escutcheons — are original and intact. Such almirahs were the primary clothing and linen storage furniture of elite Bengali households, and a large beveled mirror was a luxury item signifying prosperity. The Andarmahal was the private residential space of the zamindar's family — particularly the women — and furniture like this reflects the domestic comfort and taste of the zenana.

Finding_Place: Baliati Palace, reception hall, Saturia, Manikganj
Description: A high-backed carved teak armchair in the English Victorian style, with a cane seat and back insert. The chair is of the 'English rack' type — a style popular in colonial Bengal that combined Victorian furniture forms with local craftsmanship. The back is carved with an openwork design of scrolling foliage; the arms terminate in carved lion-paw grips. The legs are of the cabriole type. Such chairs were produced in large quantities by Calcutta furniture firms and by local carpenters trained in the colonial style, and were the standard reception hall seating of zamindari establishments throughout Bengal. The Baliati Palace had a large reception hall on the ground floor where the zamindar received petitioners, tenants, and distinguished visitors.

Artifact_Name: Wall Mirror with Ornate Gilt Frame
Finding_Place: Baliati Palace, Rang Mahal, Saturia, Manikganj
Description: A large wall mirror with an elaborately molded and gilt plaster frame, from the Rang Mahal of the Baliati Palace. The frame is in the French Baroque revival style fashionable in British India in the 1870s–1890s, with scrolling acanthus leaves, cartouches, and garland motifs in high relief, all gilded with gold leaf. The mirror glass is original — slightly foxed at the edges with age — and shows the characteristic slight greenish tint of late 19th-century silvered glass. Large decorative mirrors were an essential element of the festive atmosphere of the rong mahal, multiplying the light of the chandeliers and creating an impression of grand space. The frame's gilding is partially worn but still impressive.

Finding_Place: Baliati Palace private temple, Saturia, Manikganj
Description: A black stone Shiva lingam from the private temple (thakur-bari) of the Baliati zamindars. The lingam is plain and aniconic — a smooth cylindrical column of black basalt — set in a circular yoni-pitha (ritual base) with a drainage spout. Daily worship of the Shiva lingam was central to the religious life of the zamindar household; a family priest (pujari) conducted morning and evening puja with offerings of milk, flowers, and bilwa leaves. The Baliati zamindars were Hindus of the Saha community, and the maintenance of a private temple was both a religious duty and a mark of social status. This lingam was likely the primary cult object of the family shrine for generations before the partition of 1947 and the abandonment of the palace.

Finding_Place: Baliati Palace main entrance, Saturia, Manikganj
Description: A rectangular brass name plate engraved with the zamindar's title and name in Bengali and English lettering, from the main entrance of one of the palace blocks. The plate is engraved in both Bengali script and Roman letters, reflecting the bilingual administrative culture of the colonial Bengal zamindari system. The British colonial government recognized zamindars with official titles and required them to maintain formal establishment markers. Name plates of this type were fixed to the gateposts or entrance pillars of zamindari offices and residences. This plate is in excellent condition, with all lettering clearly legible. It is a small but important document of the formal identity and official recognition of the Baliati zamindars under the colonial administration.

A collection of glass lamp chimneys of various sizes, from both hazak pressure lamps and standard kerosene lamps used throughout the Baliati Palace. The chimneys range from small clear-glass hurricane-lamp cylinders to the larger flared chimneys of hazak (pressure-mantle) lamps. Hazak lamps used a pressurized kerosene system to produce a much brighter, whiter light than simple wick lamps, and were used in the main reception halls and the Rang Mahal for formal occasions. The glass chimneys are fragile survivors — most have been broken over the decades — and their preservation in the museum collection illustrates the daily technological infrastructure that kept the palace illuminated before electricity reached rural Manikganj.

Finding_Place: Baliati Palace, reception rooms, Saturia, Manikganj
Description: A set of decorative brass vases of varying sizes and forms, from the reception rooms of the Baliati Palace. The vases are of Indo-Persian form — tall necks, bulbous bodies, flared rims — and are engraved overall with floral arabesque patterns, geometric borders, and cartouches. Such vases were standard decorative objects in prosperous Bengali zamindari households, displayed on mantlepieces, console tables, and in window niches. They were used both as purely decorative objects and as flower vases for fresh flowers cut from the palace garden. The quality of the engraving varies, suggesting some were locally made in Manikganj or Dhaka while others may have been purchased in Calcutta.

Finding_Place: Baliati Palace, guard room, Saturia, Manikganj
Description: A freestanding teak wood rifle rack (bonduk stand) from the guard room of the Baliati Palace, designed to hold six rifles in upright slots. The rack has a broad base for stability, a central vertical column, and notched horizontal bars at top and bottom to receive and secure the rifle barrels and stocks. Zamindars of the 19th century were entitled to maintain armed retinues (lathials — stick fighters — and, for the wealthiest, armed guards with firearms) for the protection of their estates and persons. The rifle rack is evidence of the security apparatus of the Baliati zamindari establishment. The rifles themselves are no longer present, but the rack survives as evidence of the paramilitary aspect of large zamindari households.

A large teak wood bed (khat) with an ornately carved headboard and footboard, from the private residential quarters (Andarmahal) of the Baliati Palace. The headboard is carved with a scrolling vine-and-flower design in high relief, surmounted by a central cartouche containing a lotus motif. The frame is mortise-and-tenon jointed with wooden pegs — no nails — demonstrating traditional Bengali joinery. The base is a rope mesh (jal) on which a cotton mattress would have been laid. The carving style combines Bengali folk decorative motifs with Victorian furniture conventions, a synthesis typical of the colonial-era Bengali elite's material culture. The bed is one of the most substantial pieces of furniture surviving from the palace's residential quarters.

Finding_Place: Baliati Palace, Rang Mahal, Saturia, Manikganj
Description: A turned and carved teak wood pedestal (padastambha) used to display a vase, statue, or bust in the Rang Mahal of the Baliati Palace. The pedestal has a square base with beveled corners, a turned cylindrical column with decorative rings, and a square top platform. The form is derived from Victorian parlour pedestals but executed in local teak by Bengali craftsmen. Such pedestals were used throughout elite Bengali interiors to display decorative objects — brass vases, marble busts, potted plants, or religious images — at a dignified height. The teak has a warm reddish-brown color with age patina. This piece is of particularly fine quality, suggesting it held an important or cherished object in the entertainment hall.

Finding_Place: Baliati Palace, administrative block, Saturia, Manikganj
Description: A large teak wood storage cupboard (almirah) from the administrative block of the Baliati Palace, used to store land records, legal documents, and estate papers. The cupboard has two full-height doors with recessed panels, secured by heavy iron drop-bolt hinges and a central iron padlock hasp. The interior is divided by adjustable shelves. This type of utilitarian storage furniture was essential to the functioning of a zamindari estate office, where the nayeb (manager) and gomasta (accountant) maintained voluminous records of land holdings, tenant registers, revenue receipts, court proceedings, and correspondence. The cupboard is of robust construction and has survived in structurally sound condition, though the iron fittings show significant rusting.

Material: Teak wood, gold-leaf gilding, velvet upholstery
Finding_Place: Baliati Palace, audience hall, Saturia, Manikganj
Description: A ceremonial high-backed chair (asanbari or sacred seat) used by the zamindar during formal audiences, religious ceremonies, and official occasions. The chair is of teak with traces of gold-leaf gilding on the carved cresting rail and the carved arms. The seat and back were originally upholstered in red velvet, of which fragments remain. The cresting rail is carved with a central lotus flanked by scrolling vines — a design that blends Hindu decorative symbolism with Victorian furniture aesthetics. The zamindar's ceremonial seat was a charged object: it embodied his authority over the estate and his social rank. Tenants and petitioners would approach and address the zamindar seated in this chair, prostrating or bowing in the customary gesture of deference.

Finding_Place: Baliati Palace private temple, Saturia, Manikganj
Description: A square stone platform (chaidani) from the private temple of the Baliati Palace, used as the ritual base on which the deity's image or the Shiva lingam was placed during daily worship. The top surface is smooth and slightly hollowed in the center from years of ritual washing (abhisheka). The sides are carved with simple lotus petal moldings in the Bengali folk style. Such platforms are essential elements of Hindu domestic shrine furniture, elevating the deity above the floor level to indicate its divine status and to allow ritual circumambulation (pradakshina). The chaidani from the Baliati family temple represents the private religious life of the zamindari household, which maintained daily rituals alongside its worldly activities.

Finding_Place: Baliati Palace south facade colonnade, Saturia, Manikganj
Description: A plaster capital from one of the Corinthian columns that form the south facade colonnade of the Baliati Palace — the most architecturally distinctive feature of the complex. The Baliati Palace is celebrated for its rows of Corinthian columns on the south facade, which give it a Greek-Roman Revival character unique among Bengal's zamindari palaces. The capital is of plaster-over-brick construction, modeled with the characteristic Corinthian acanthus leaf design arranged in two tiers around a central bell (kalathos) with corner volutes. This example was detached during conservation work and preserved in the museum. It illustrates the high level of plasterwork craftsmanship employed by the builders of Baliati Palace and the zamindars' deliberate adoption of European Neoclassical architectural symbolism to project power and modernity.

Finding_Place: Baliati Palace lion gateway, Saturia, Manikganj
Description: A plaster lion sculpture fragment from one of the three identical lion-surmounted gateways (sher darwaza) that punctuate the enclosure walls of the Baliati Palace complex. Each gateway is crowned by a sculptural lion — a symbol of authority, power, and dynastic prestige adopted from both British colonial heraldry and the Indian royal tradition. This fragment preserves the head and upper body of one of the gateway lions, showing the mane rendered in stylized curling locks, the face frontal with an open mouth, and the eyes boldly modeled. The plaster surface retains traces of original white lime wash. The three gateway lions are among the most distinctive visual symbols of the Baliati Palace complex and are frequently photographed by visitors.

Finding_Place: Baliati Palace estate office, Saturia, Manikganj
Description: A collection of land deed documents (pattas) and revenue records from the Baliati zamindari estate office, recording the terms of land tenure between the zamindar and his cultivating tenants (raiyats). The documents are in Bengali and English, handwritten in ink on heavy paper. They specify the boundaries of individual plots, the names of tenants, the annual rent (lagaan) payable, and the conditions of occupancy. Under the zamindari system, the zamindar was the intermediary between the British colonial government and the cultivating population, collecting land revenue from tenants and remitting a fixed sum (diwani) to the colonial administration. These records are primary sources for the agrarian and administrative history of Manikganj district.

Material: Silver gelatin photographic prints, sepia toned
Credit_Donor: Original palace collection / donated by family descendants
Description: A framed collection of formal portrait photographs of members of the Baliati zamindar family, taken at a Calcutta photographic studio in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The photographs show the zamindars in formal attire — dhoti and shawl for men, silk sari and gold jewelry for women — posed in the studio conventions of the period, with painted backdrop and upholstered chair props. Photography arrived in Bengal in the 1840s, and by the 1880s formal studio portraiture was an established practice among elite Bengali families. These photographs are among the most direct visual documents of the Baliati family's identity and appearance, and constitute an irreplaceable record of the people whose material legacy is preserved in the museum.

Material: Teak wood, beveled glass mirror, marble top
Description: A teak dressing table with a tilting beveled-glass mirror on a swivel frame and a small white marble top surface, from the women's quarters (Andarmahal) of the Baliati Palace. The lower section has two banks of three drawers each, with turned brass knob pulls. The mirror frame is carved with a simple scrollwork cresting. The marble top surface has two small drawers below it for storing toiletry items. This dressing table is an intimate artifact of the domestic life of the zamindar's household women — it was at objects like this that the zenana women prepared themselves for festivals, ceremonies, and family gatherings. Its survival in reasonable condition provides a tangible connection to the private, domestic dimension of Baliati Palace life.

Finding_Place: Baliati Palace main entrance, Saturia, Manikganj
Description: An inscribed stone slab recording the inaugural ceremony of the Baliati Palace, held on the 1st of Boishakh, 1300 Bengali year — April 14, 1893 CE. The inscription is in Bengali script and records the auspicious date of the palace's formal opening, the name of the presiding zamindar, and possibly a dedicatory verse. This stone is the primary epigraphic evidence confirming the date of the palace's completion and formal inauguration. According to the inscription, the opening ceremony was held on Bengali New Year's Day (Pahela Boishakh) — a deliberate choice of the most auspicious day in the Bengali calendar, underscoring the zamindars' deep engagement with Bengali cultural tradition even as they adopted a European architectural vocabulary for their palace.

Artifact_Name: Scale Model of Baliati Palace Complex (1:100)
Description: A detailed 1:100 scale architectural model of the entire Baliati Palace complex as it exists today, showing all seven building blocks, the three lion-surmounted gateways, the enclosure walls, the large pond (dighi) to the north, the smaller pond to the south, and the layout of the 5.88-acre compound. The model is painted to show the white-plastered facades of the palace buildings with their rows of Corinthian columns on the south facade. It serves as the central orientation exhibit of the museum, helping visitors understand the spatial organization of the vast complex — over 200 rooms across seven buildings — before they begin their tour. The model also shows the Rang Mahal (museum building) within the context of the whole complex.

Material: Silver-plated brass base, glass water vessel, cloth hose
Finding_Place: Baliati Palace, men's reception hall, Saturia, Manikganj
Description: A complete hookah (huqqa) set — base, water vessel, and hose — from the men's reception hall (baithak-khana) of the Baliati Palace. The base is of silver-plated brass in an onion-domed form with engraved floral decoration; the water vessel is of deep blue glass; the long flexible hose is covered with woven cloth and terminates in a carved mouthpiece. Hookah smoking was a central social ritual of the Bengali zamindari elite — offering the hookah to a guest was an act of hospitality and social bonding, while the rank of the hookah (the quality and design of the base) was a visual indicator of status. Hookah sets of this quality were imported from Calcutta or manufactured by specialist metalworkers in Dhaka or Murshidabad.

Finding_Place: Baliati Palace, dining hall, Saturia, Manikganj
Description: A partial dinner service in the English Willow Pattern — the iconic blue-and-white transfer-printed chinaware design featuring a pagoda, willow tree, bridge, and birds. The surviving pieces include dinner plates, soup bowls, a serving dish, and a sauce boat. English Willow Pattern pottery was the most widely exported British ceramic design to India and was a status symbol in prosperous Bengali households from the mid-19th century onward. The Baliati zamindars, like other elite Bengali families of the period, maintained a parallel cultural life that combined traditional Hindu rituals and Bengali customs with the adoption of British material culture. Using English china at the formal dining table was a deliberate performance of cosmopolitan taste.

Finding_Place: Baliati Palace private temple, Saturia, Manikganj
Description: A ceremonial brass water vessel (kalash) from the private temple of the Baliati zamindars, used for ritual purification and abhisheka (anointing of the deity). The kalash has a globular body, a narrow neck, a flared rim, and a small decorative spout. The surface is engraved with auspicious motifs — lotus flowers, the swastika symbol, and bands of geometric patterns. A kalash filled with sacred water and topped with a mango-leaf spray and a coconut is the standard auspicious symbol (mangal-kalash) of Hindu ritual, placed at the entrance of homes and temples during festivals and ceremonies. This vessel, engraved with particular care, was likely used at important family festivals including Durga Puja, Diwali, and the annual Shiva puja.

Artifact_Name: Map and Survey Records — Baliati Estate (British Colonial)
Description: A collection of Survey of Bengal cadastral maps and zamindari settlement records for the Baliati estate from the British colonial period. The maps show the layout of the palace compound, the surrounding village of Baliati, the course of the Gazikhali river (now dried up), the estate's agricultural lands, and the locations of tenant homesteads. Revenue settlement records document the extent of the estate's landholdings, the annual assessed land revenue, and the names of principal tenants. Under the Permanent Settlement of 1793, the Baliati zamindars were assessed a fixed annual revenue; these records document the administration of that system over nearly a century. The records are primary sources for the agrarian history of Manikganj and for understanding the territorial extent of one of the district's most important zamindari estates.

Material: Black stone (replica; original in Karachi Museum)
Description: A high-quality cast replica of the original foundation inscription of the Bagha Mosque, which records its construction by Sultan Nasiruddin Nusrat Shah, son of Alauddin Hussain Shah, founder of the Husain Shahi dynasty, in the year 930 AH (1523–24 CE). The original stone inscription was once fixed over the central archway of the mosque and is now held in Karachi. The text is in Arabic and Persian, written in a fine naskh calligraphic hand, recording the name of the patron sultan and the date of construction. This inscription is the primary historical document confirming the mosque's date and royal patronage, making it the most important epigraphic artifact associated with the Bagha complex.

Artifact_Name: Terracotta Floral Panel from Bagha Mosque (Exterior)
Credit_Donor: Recovered during conservation by Department of Archaeology
Description: A detached terracotta panel from the exterior wall of the Bagha Mosque, bearing an exquisitely executed floral arabesque design. The pattern consists of interlocking vine scrolls producing stylized lotus flowers and leaf forms in the Persian-inspired decorative vocabulary that characterizes the entire surface ornamentation of the mosque. Bagha Mosque is renowned as one of the most elaborately decorated terracotta monuments of the Bengal Sultanate, its entire exterior wall surface covered with such panels. The design reflects the synthesis of Persian, Central Asian, and indigenous Bengali decorative traditions that flourished under the Husain Shahi sultans.

Artifact_Name: Terracotta Mihrab Panel with Calligraphic Border
Description: A terracotta panel recovered from the area of one of the four decorated mihrabs (prayer niches) of the Bagha Mosque. The mihrabs of the Bagha Mosque are considered the finest examples of Islamic terracotta ornamentation in Bengal. This panel bears a border of Arabic calligraphic inscription in naskh script — likely a Quranic verse — surrounding an inner field of dense floral arabesque. The depth of the relief carving is exceptional, with the calligraphic letters fully undercut to stand clear of the background. The four mihrabs of the mosque represent the pinnacle of the Bengal Sultanate terracotta tradition.

A terracotta jali (perforated screen) panel from one of the screened window openings on the north and south sides of the Bagha Mosque. The pattern is composed of intersecting circles and diagonal bands forming an elegant geometric lattice, described in the architectural literature as one of the most refined window-screen designs of the Sultanate period. Such jali panels served both a practical function (admitting light and air while maintaining privacy) and a decorative one, casting intricate shadow patterns on the interior floor. The precision of the brick-and-terracotta craftsmanship required to produce such a panel is remarkable.

Artifact_Name: Coin of Sultan Nusrat Shah (Gold Tanka)
Credit_Donor: Transferred from Rajshahi District Archaeological Office
Description: A gold tanka (dinar) struck by Sultan Nasiruddin Nusrat Shah at the Bengal Sultanate mint, recovered from the Rajshahi region. One side bears the sultan's name and titles in elegant Arabic naskh script; the reverse bears the Islamic kalima (declaration of faith) and the mint name. Nusrat Shah was the son and successor of the great Alauddin Hussain Shah and the patron of the Bagha Mosque — making his coins directly associated with the monument whose history the museum documents. Gold tankas of this period are rare survivors, as most were melted down in later centuries. This example is in excellent preservation with fully legible inscriptions.

Artifact_Name: Coin of Alauddin Hussain Shah (Silver Tanka)
Credit_Donor: Excavation find, transferred from Department of Archaeology
Description: A silver tanka of Sultan Alauddin Hussain Shah — founder of the Husain Shahi dynasty and father of Nusrat Shah, the builder of Bagha Mosque. The coin was part of a small hoard discovered near the Bagha Mosque complex. Alauddin Hussain Shah is celebrated as the greatest ruler of the Bengal Sultanate, whose reign (1494–1519) is considered the golden age of independent medieval Bengal. He patronized Bengali literature and expanded the sultanate to its greatest extent. His coins are among the most beautifully inscribed of the entire Sultanate series. This example bears his full royal titles in flowing naskh calligraphy.

A large fired brick from the Bagha Mosque construction bearing a stamped inscription on its face — a rare example of inscribed bricks from the Bengal Sultanate period. The inscription is in Arabic and appears to be a devotional phrase or the brickmaker's mark. Stamped bricks of this type provided both structural integrity and documentary evidence in Sultanate-period construction. The brick's large size (larger than modern standard bricks) is characteristic of 16th-century Bengal construction. Its buff-orange color and dense firing reflect the high-quality kilns operating in the Rajshahi region during this period, taking advantage of local alluvial clay deposits.

Artifact_Name: Stone Pillar Segment from Mosque Plinth
Material: Repurposed stone (likely recycled from earlier Hindu/Buddhist structure)
Description: A stone pillar segment from the plinth of the Bagha Mosque — one of the stone structural elements that distinguish the mosque's construction. As stone was not locally available in the Bengal delta, the Sultan brought or reused stone for the mosque's plinth, lintels, and pillars. This segment shows evidence of earlier Hindu or Buddhist carving on one face, partially smoothed over, indicating the common Sultanate-period practice of reusing material from earlier religious structures. The stone is a dark grey basalt, likely transported from the Rajmahal hills. Such repurposed architectural elements are significant evidence of the cultural transitions of medieval Bengal.

Artifact_Name: Terracotta Corner Tower Fragment with Moulded Bands
Finding_Place: Bagha Mosque octagonal corner tower, Bagha
Description: A curved terracotta fragment from one of the four octagonal corner towers (burj) of the Bagha Mosque. The towers are divided into sections by moulded horizontal bands and topped with polygonal solid cupolas. This fragment preserves two of the moulded bands in their original condition, with a decorated frieze of stylized foliage between them. The towers served both a structural function (buttressing the mosque walls) and a visual one (creating a sense of height and monumentality). This fragment is important because it preserves the original surface texture and coloration of the terracotta before weathering, providing a reference for conservation work.

A cast bronze oil lamp (chirag) of the type used in mosques and homes throughout the Bengal Sultanate period. The lamp has a shallow, oval reservoir for oil, a short spout for the wick, a handle, and a low pedestal base. The surface is plain but finely cast, with a smooth patina of dark bronze-green. Such lamps were the primary source of interior illumination in mosques, used to light the mihrabs, the prayer hall, and the approaches to the mosque for evening (Isha) and predawn (Fajr) prayers. The lamp was recovered from an excavation in the Bagha Upazila near the mosque compound, likely from a domestic or religious context contemporaneous with the mosque's active use.

A blue-and-white glazed ceramic bowl of Chinese Ming Dynasty manufacture, recovered from an excavation in the Bagha area. The exterior bears a simple design of lotus flowers and scrolling vines in cobalt blue under a clear glaze. Chinese porcelain was imported in large quantities into Bengal during the Sultanate period, both for the use of the royal court and for the wealthy merchant class. The Husain Shahi dynasty maintained extensive trade contacts with China, and Chinese porcelain has been found at multiple Sultanate-period sites in Bangladesh. This bowl is evidence of Bagha's role as a trading center on the Padma river during the 15th–16th centuries.

A straight, double-edged iron sword of the type carried by Bengal Sultanate infantry and cavalry. The blade is of medium width with a central ridge, tapering to a point. The hilt is simple, with a crossguard and a pommel of cast iron. Though the surface shows significant oxidation and pitting from centuries of burial, the basic form and proportions of the sword are intact. Such swords were the standard sidearm of Sultanate-period soldiers in Bengal, carried alongside spears and shields. This example likely belonged to a soldier or minor official associated with the Bagha administrative center, which served as a regional headquarters under the Husain Shahi sultans.

A copper plate bearing an inscribed land grant (tamrapatra) recording the donation of agricultural land to a religious institution — likely a mosque or a dargah (Sufi shrine) — in the Bagha area. The text is in Persian, the administrative language of the Bengal Sultanate, written in a clear nasta'liq hand. Copper plate land grants are among the most important primary sources for the administrative and social history of medieval Bengal. This example records the boundaries of the donated land, the name of the donor (a local official), the recipient institution, and the date. It provides direct evidence of the patronage networks that supported the religious life of the Bagha region under the Sultanate.

A large terracotta water storage pot (kalshi) recovered from an excavation in the Bagha area, dating to the Sultanate period. The pot has a globular body, a narrow neck, a flared rim, and two small handles. The surface is plain, with only a decorative band of incised geometric patterns below the shoulder. Such pots were the ubiquitous household water storage vessels of rural Bengal, used to carry and store water from the rivers, ponds, and wells that sustained life in the delta. The form of the Bengali kalshi has remained remarkably consistent for thousands of years; this example is identifiable as Sultanate-period by its clay composition and stratigraphic context.

A carved stone fragment from the area of one of the mosque's mihrabs or from a secondary structure within the mosque compound. Unlike the terracotta elements that dominate the mosque's decoration, this fragment is cut from stone, making it an unusual survival. The surface bears a carved arabesque pattern of intertwining vines and palmette leaves in a style closely related to the terracotta decoration. The use of stone alongside terracotta in the Bagha Mosque reflects the Sultanate builders' effort to import the most durable materials available for the most important decorative elements of this royal foundation.

Artifact_Name: Coins of Ghiyasuddin Mahmud Shah (Last Husain Shahi Sultan)
Description: Silver tankas of Ghiyasuddin Mahmud Shah — the last ruler of the Husain Shahi dynasty, whose reign ended with the Sher Shah Suri conquest of Bengal in 1538. These coins represent the final chapter of the independent Bengal Sultanate, the dynasty that built the Bagha Mosque. After Mahmud Shah's defeat, Bengal came under the rule of the Suri and then Mughal empires, bringing to an end the century of independent Husain Shahi rule that had presided over a golden age of Bengali literature, architecture, and trade. The coins are inscribed with the sultan's name and titles in Arabic naskh. Their recovery near Bagha connects them directly to the administrative history of the region.

A collection of glass bangle fragments recovered from a Sultanate-period deposit in the Bagha Upazila. The fragments are in green, blue, and amber glass, some with applied thread decoration. Glass bangles have been worn by women in Bengal for thousands of years and are produced by specialist artisans using a flame-winding technique. These fragments represent both domestic life and long-distance trade: fine glass was imported from West Asia and also manufactured locally. The range of colors and techniques visible in these fragments indicates that women of the Bagha area in the Sultanate period had access to both imported luxury glass and local products.

A complete handwritten Quran manuscript donated by a local mosque, written in a clear and practiced naskh hand on heavy paper. The manuscript is bound in a worn brown leather cover with a tooled flap (miqlab). The opening pages bear a simple illuminated heading in gold and blue marking the beginning of Surah Al-Fatiha. The manuscript dates to the Mughal period and was likely produced in Bengal, as indicated by the paper type and binding style. It was preserved in a local mosque in Bagha for several centuries before being donated to the museum. Quran manuscripts from this region are important documents of the Islamic scholarly and scribal culture of rural Bengal during the 17th century.

Artifact_Name: Terracotta Dome Fragment with Surface Plaster
Finding_Place: Bagha Mosque original dome (collapsed in 1897 earthquake)
Credit_Donor: Recovered during dome reconstruction, Department of Archaeology
Description: A curved terracotta brick fragment from one of the ten original domes of the Bagha Mosque, which collapsed in the great earthquake of 1897 that devastated the region. The fragment retains traces of the original white lime plaster on its inner face — the plaster that would have formed the interior dome surface visible to worshippers. The outer face shows the characteristic small fired bricks used in Sultanate dome construction. When the Department of Archaeology reconstructed the domes in the 20th century, fragments of the original domes were preserved. This piece is therefore a direct physical remnant of the 500-year-old original structure that worshippers saw when the mosque was first completed in 1524.

Artifact_Name: Iron Lock and Key — Sultanate / Mughal Period
Description: A heavy iron padlock and its key from the Sultanate or early Mughal period. The lock is of the 'shutter' type, in which a spring mechanism is released by the key. The surface is rough with forge marks and age oxidation. Such locks were used to secure the doors of mosques, granaries, treasure rooms, and merchant storehouses. The key has a long stem with a decorative loop handle and a simple bit. The Bagha area was an active trading center on the Padma river during the 16th–17th centuries, and locks of this type would have secured the storehouses of the merchants and the treasury of the local administrator. This artifact represents the everyday material culture of the prosperous trading town that once existed at Bagha.

A pair of silver earrings recovered from a Sultanate-period deposit in the Bagha area. The earrings are of the large loop type (baali) characteristic of medieval Bengali jewelry, with a granulated surface decoration of small silver spheres arranged in geometric patterns. Silver jewelry was worn by women of all social classes in medieval Bengal; gold was reserved for the wealthy. These earrings are of good quality, indicating they belonged to a moderately prosperous household. Jewelry finds from excavations are important evidence for understanding the personal adornment practices, material prosperity, and trade networks of medieval Bengali communities.

A collection of twenty archival photographs documenting the Bagha Mosque before, during, and after the major conservation campaigns of the 20th century. The earliest photographs (c. 1903–1910) show the mosque with collapsed domes following the 1897 earthquake — roofless, with vegetation growing from the walls. Later photographs (1950s–1970s) show the Department of Archaeology's dome reconstruction project in progress. The most recent images (1980s) show the restored mosque. Together, the photographs constitute an invaluable visual history of conservation practice in Bangladesh and of the physical transformation of one of the country's most important monuments. They are also essential documents for scholarly study of the mosque's original form.

Artifact_Name: Silk Fabric Sample — Rajshahi Mulberry Silk
Description: A framed sample of Rajshahi mulberry silk — the golden-yellow, lustrous fabric for which the Rajshahi region has been famous since at least the Mughal period. Rajshahi District is the heart of Bangladesh's silk industry, based on the cultivation of the mulberry tree (Morus alba) whose leaves feed the silkworm (Bombyx mori). The silk produced here has a distinctive golden sheen and exceptional softness. The sample shows both a plain-woven (plain silk) and a woven-pattern (jamdani-style) section. The silk industry of Rajshahi was at its peak during the 18th–19th centuries under zamindari patronage, and the region is still the primary producer of silk in Bangladesh.

Artifact_Name: Traditional Fishing Net Weight (Mach Dhari Pathor)
Description: A collection of stone and clay net sinkers (weights) used by fishermen on the Padma River at Bagha Ghat. The sinkers are of various shapes — spherical, discoid, and conical — with a groove or hole for attaching to the edge of a fishing net. They were used to sink the net to the desired depth when cast. Bagha was historically a significant trading and fishing settlement on the Padma, and fishing communities have lived along the riverbank here for centuries. These humble objects represent the material culture of the fishing communities whose labor sustained the local economy long before and after the great mosque was built.

Artifact_Name: Frieze Panel — Stylized Lotus and Chain Motif
Description: A long, narrow terracotta frieze panel from the exterior wall of the Bagha Mosque, bearing a repeating design of stylized lotus flowers connected by a chain of circular links — a classic decorative border motif of the Bengal Sultanate. This motif runs as a horizontal band separating the main decorative panels on the mosque's outer wall and appears at the cornice level. The lotus (padma) is a symbol common to both Hindu and Buddhist art that was freely adopted into the Islamic decorative vocabulary of Bengal, representing the fertile, flower-rich landscape of the delta. The chain motif derives from Persian architectural decoration. The seamless blending of these traditions is the defining characteristic of Bengal Sultanate ornament.

Finding_Place: Dargah of Sufi saints, Bagha compound
Description: A tall brass lamp stand (mishra or shama-dan) used in the dargah (Sufi shrine) located within the Bagha mosque compound. The Bagha compound contains the graves of several saints who preached Islam in the region, and these shrines have been active pilgrimage sites for centuries. The lamp stand has a broad round base for stability, a slender fluted column, and a flat top plate with a central spike for holding a candle or oil lamp. The surface is engraved with geometric floral patterns in the Persian-Mughal decorative style. Such lamp stands were central to dargah ritual, illuminating the shrines during night prayers and on the anniversary celebrations (urs) of the buried saints.

Artifact_Name: Map and Survey Records — Bagha Upazila (Colonial Period)
Description: A collection of Survey of India cadastral maps and revenue survey records for the Bagha area from the British colonial period. The maps show the layout of the Bagha Mosque compound, the adjacent Dighi (tank), the surrounding agricultural lands, and the settlement pattern of Bagha village in the 19th–early 20th centuries. Colonial survey records are essential tools for understanding how the landscape around the mosque has changed over time and for tracing the ownership and management history of the protected monument. The records also document the names of local landholders and the extent of the mosque's waqf (endowment) land.

Artifact_Name: Brick Pavement Section from Mosque Forecourt
Description: A lifted section of original brick pavement from the forecourt (sahn) in front of the Bagha Mosque, recovered during an archaeological excavation of the compound. The bricks are large (Sultanate-period standard) and laid in a herringbone pattern using white lime mortar. The underside retains the original mortar bed. Such pavement sections provide direct evidence of the original ground level, the construction technique, and the spatial organization of the mosque complex as designed in 1523. The forecourt pavement was used by worshippers performing ablutions at the mosque's tank before entering for prayer, and by the community gathering for Eid prayers on the open ground.

A small glazed earthenware lota (ritual water vessel) used for wudu (ritual ablution before prayer). The vessel has a globular body, a short spout, a narrow neck, and a small handle. It is glazed in a pale green monochrome glaze consistent with local Bengal Sultanate / early Mughal ceramic production. The lota is among the most personal of Islamic religious objects, used daily for purification before the five prayers. Its recovery from the Bagha area connects it directly to the religious life of the community that worshipped at the Bagha Mosque. The green glaze is iron-based and shows the technical capabilities of local potters in the 16th–17th centuries.

Credit_Donor: Commissioned by Department of Archaeology for museum inauguration
Description: A detailed 1:50 scale architectural model of the Bagha Mosque as it appeared at its completion in 1523–24 CE, before the collapse of the original domes in 1897. The model was commissioned by the Department of Archaeology for the museum's inauguration in May 2015 and is based on architectural survey data, historical descriptions, and comparison with contemporary Sultanate mosques. It shows all ten original domes, the four octagonal corner towers, the five eastern doorways, the two lateral screened openings, the surrounding brick-walled compound, the main southern gateway, and the large Dighi (tank) to the east. The model serves as the central educational exhibit of the museum, helping visitors understand the original design before centuries of weathering and the 1897 earthquake changed the monument's appearance.

The Hawker Hunter is a subsonic British jet fighter-bomber that was the primary combat aircraft of the Bangladesh Air Force during the Liberation War of 1971. Bangladesh inherited several Hunter jets from the Pakistan Air Force. It played a significant role in air operations during the nine-month war, providing close air support and interdiction missions. The aircraft on display outside the museum is painted in the original BAF livery of the war period and remains one of the most iconic exhibits.

The de Havilland Vampire T.55 was a twin-boom British jet trainer and light fighter used by the Pakistan Air Force before independence. Bangladesh inherited a few Vampires after 1971. This early jet aircraft was used for pilot training and some combat roles during the early period of the Bangladesh Air Force. The twin-boom design is unusual and immediately recognisable. The aircraft on display retains its original markings and provides visitors with a close-up view of early jet aviation history in Bangladesh.

The North American T-6 Texan, known as the Harvard in Commonwealth service, was one of the most widely used trainer aircraft of the Second World War. Pakistan Air Force and later Bangladesh Air Force used the Harvard for ab initio and basic flying training. The radial piston engine provides a distinctive sound. This propeller-driven aircraft trained generations of pilots who later flew jet aircraft during the Bangladesh Liberation War of 1971. The museum specimen demonstrates the evolution of military aviation from propeller to jet technology.

The Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-21 is a Soviet supersonic jet fighter that formed the backbone of the Bangladesh Air Force from the 1970s onward. Bangladesh acquired MiG-21s from the Soviet Union after independence, making it the first supersonic fighter in BAF service. The delta-wing design enables speeds exceeding Mach 2. This aircraft was the primary air defence fighter of Bangladesh for over two decades and participated in numerous training exercises. The museum specimen is displayed with its original BAF roundel and carries historical significance as Bangladesh's first supersonic interceptor.

The Shenyang F-6 is a Chinese-built copy of the Soviet MiG-19, the world's first production supersonic fighter. Bangladesh acquired F-6s from China in the mid-1970s as part of bilateral defence cooperation. The twin-engine aircraft was capable of supersonic flight and was equipped with 23mm cannon and air-to-air missiles. It served alongside MiG-21s in the Bangladesh Air Force for over a decade. The museum display includes original livery and weapons pylons. It represents the China–Bangladesh defence relationship that has been a cornerstone of BAF equipment procurement.

The Aermacchi MB-339A is an Italian subsonic jet trainer and light attack aircraft acquired by Bangladesh from Italy in the 1980s. It was used for advanced pilot training and could also carry weapons for light ground-attack missions. The MB-339 gave BAF pilots the transition training needed before flying the MiG-21. Known for its reliability and ease of maintenance, the MB-339 served for over two decades. This museum example still wears its original red-and-white training livery, which has become iconic in BAF history.

The Cessna T-37 Twin Tweet is an American side-by-side seat jet trainer used for primary jet pilot training. Bangladesh received T-37s under US Military Assistance Program in the early years of independence. It was the first jet many BAF pilots flew after completing piston-engine training. The T-37's ease of handling and forgiving flight characteristics made it an ideal first-jet trainer. This museum specimen represents the US–Bangladesh early defence cooperation and the beginning of BAF's jet training programme.

The Mil Mi-8 is a Soviet twin-turbine transport helicopter widely regarded as one of the most successful rotary-wing aircraft ever built. The BAF acquired Mi-8s from the Soviet Union in the late 1970s for troop transport, logistical support, and search-and-rescue operations. The helicopter can carry up to 24 passengers or 3,000 kg of cargo. The BAF Mi-8 fleet participated in flood relief operations across Bangladesh — a country frequently affected by catastrophic flooding — making it an aircraft with both military and humanitarian significance. The museum example is displayed with its distinctive BAF green and grey camouflage.

The Bell 212 is a twin-engine development of the famous Bell UH-1 Huey, the iconic helicopter of the Vietnam War era. Bangladesh acquired Bell 212s for utility transport, VIP movement, and disaster relief operations. The aircraft is powered by a Pratt & Whitney Canada PT6T-3B Twin Pac engine. The BAF Bell 212 fleet served with distinction in numerous domestic relief operations and UN peacekeeping missions. This museum example is displayed on the outdoor platform, giving visitors the opportunity to see the scale of a utility helicopter up close.

Credit_Donor: Bangladesh Air Force / Inherited from PAF
Description: The Fouga CM.170 Magister is a French twin-jet trainer with a distinctive V-tail (butterfly tail) configuration. Pakistan Air Force operated the Magister for advanced jet training, and a small number were used by the nascent Bangladesh Air Force in 1971. Some accounts suggest that Magisters were used during the Liberation War in ground-attack roles against Pakistani forces. The unusual V-tail design makes it immediately recognisable and distinctive among the museum's aircraft collection. This aircraft represents the French contribution to Pakistani and Bangladeshi aviation history.

Artifact_Name: Bangladesh Air Force Roundel and Flag Display
Description: The official roundel and flag of the Bangladesh Air Force, adopted in 1972 after independence. The BAF roundel consists of concentric circles in the colours of the Bangladesh national flag — green and red — with the red circle at the centre representing the rising sun of the new nation. The BAF flag is dark blue (the traditional colour of air forces) with the national emblem at its centre. This heraldic display is the first exhibit visitors encounter and establishes the institutional identity of the Air Force.

Artifact_Name: Flying Suit and Helmet of Wing Commander M. Hamidullah Khan
Material: Nylon flight suit; fibreglass helmet; leather gloves
Description: The flying suit, helmet, and personal effects of Wing Commander M. Hamidullah Khan, one of the founding officers of the Bangladesh Air Force who defected from Pakistan Air Force during the 1971 Liberation War. The olive-green flight suit retains its original patches and rank insignia. The fibreglass flying helmet has the BAF emblem painted on the front, likely added after liberation. These garments represent the courage of the Bengali military personnel who risked their lives to join the resistance. Similar to the Bir Shreshtha Matiur Rahman collection in the Bangladesh National Museum, these personal effects humanise the abstract story of national liberation.

A collection of military uniforms worn by officers of the Bangladesh Air Force (Mukti Bahini air wing) during the Liberation War of 1971. The collection includes a khaki bush jacket with rank insignia, a field cap, and a belt with holster. These uniforms were often improvised from available materials in the early months of the war, before standardised supply chains were established. The insignia represent the early provisional rank system of the liberation forces. Together they document the material conditions of those who fought for Bangladesh's independence from Pakistan.

A display of air-to-air missiles used by the Bangladesh Air Force on its MiG-21 and F-6 aircraft. The PL-2 (Pili-2) is a Chinese-built copy of the Soviet Atoll (K-13) missile, which was itself derived from the American AIM-9 Sidewinder infrared-guided missile. The display includes a cut-away section showing the internal components: the infrared seeker head, propulsion section, and warhead. The missiles are mounted on standard pylons as they would appear on an aircraft's wings. This exhibit explains the development of beyond-visual-range air combat capabilities in the BAF.

A decommissioned Rolls-Royce Avon turbojet engine, the powerplant of the Hawker Hunter fighter-bomber used by the Bangladesh Air Force. The engine is displayed on a maintenance stand with the casing removed on one side to reveal the internal structure: the compressor stages, combustion chambers, and turbine blades. Labels identify each major component. The Avon produced approximately 10,000 lbs of thrust and gave the Hunter its performance. This exhibit explains the principles of jet propulsion and the engineering challenges of maintaining complex military hardware in a developing nation's air force.

Credit_Donor: China National Electronics Import & Export Corporation (donated on decommission)
Description: A decommissioned Chinese-made YLC-6 two-dimensional long-range air surveillance radar system, of the type used by the Bangladesh Air Force for early warning and air traffic control. The display includes the antenna array, the radar control console, and a large illuminated tactical display screen showing simulated aircraft tracks. The YLC-6 operated in the L-band and had a detection range of approximately 350 km. This exhibit explains the role of radar in modern air defence, the concept of threat detection, and how Bangladesh built its integrated air defence network with Chinese assistance.

A Martin-Baker Mk.4 ejection seat of the type fitted to the Hawker Hunter fighter-bomber. The seat is displayed in a glass case with its survival equipment: the parachute pack, personal survival kit, and harness. An instructional panel explains the ejection sequence — from pulling the handle to rocket seat activation, canopy separation, and automatic parachute deployment. Martin-Baker ejection seats have saved thousands of lives worldwide; the plaque lists the number of recorded saves. For BAF Hunter pilots, this seat was their last line of survival if an aircraft became uncontrollable.

Artifact_Name: Pilot's Flying Log Book — 1971 Liberation War
Material: Leather cover, paper pages; ink entries
Description: A leather-bound pilot's flying log book belonging to a Bangladesh Air Force officer who flew combat missions during the 1971 Liberation War. The log records each flight in neat tabular entries: date, aircraft type, engine type, duration, and remarks. The remarks columns from August–December 1971 record sorties including strafing runs, bombing missions, and delivery flights. The handwriting is careful and precise — the professional record of a man flying dangerous missions in an improvised air force during a national struggle for survival. The log is displayed open to the December 1971 entries from the final days of the war.

A framed collection of original black-and-white photographs documenting the formation of the Bangladesh Air Force in 1971. The photographs show: the first group of Bengali pilots and ground crew who defected from Pakistan Air Force; Group Captain A.K. Khandker (first BAF commander) addressing officers; the first flight operations from forward air bases in India near the Bangladesh border; and the liberation of Dhaka in December 1971 with BAF aircraft overflying the city. These images are among the most historically important documents of the founding of the national air force.

Material: Steel blade; brass hilt; leather scabbard
Description: The ceremonial dress sword of a Bangladesh Air Force officer, of the pattern adopted after independence in 1971. The blade is straight, double-edged steel with the BAF crest etched near the ricasso. The hilt is brass with a lion-head pommel, and the grip is bound in silver wire. The scabbard is black leather with brass fittings. The dress sword is worn by commissioned officers on ceremonial occasions including parades, formal dinners, and investitures. The design follows Commonwealth Air Force tradition while incorporating distinctly Bangladeshi national symbols.

A Douglas DC-3 Dakota transport aircraft, donated by Bangladesh Biman Airlines and displayed at the museum as a representative of early civil and military aviation in the region. The DC-3 was used in both military and civilian capacities throughout South Asia from the 1940s. This aircraft in particular was used on early domestic routes by Biman Bangladesh Airlines after the airline's founding in 1972. The DC-3's robust construction, simple systems, and ability to operate from unpaved airstrips made it ideal for Bangladesh's early post-independence aviation infrastructure. The aircraft is displayed in Biman livery and represents the close relationship between military and civil aviation in Bangladesh's early years.

A Swedish-designed Bofors 40mm L/60 light anti-aircraft gun of the type used in the 1971 Liberation War. This rapid-firing automatic cannon was the most widely used light anti-aircraft weapon of the Second World War and remained in service with many nations for decades. During the Liberation War, Pakistani forces used Bofors guns to defend air bases and key installations against Indian Air Force and the nascent BAF attack aircraft. This museum example is displayed in firing position, showing the gunner's seat, sighting system, and ammunition feed. The gun represents the ground-based air defence dimension of the 1971 conflict.

An American AN/PRC-25 VHF frequency-modulated infantry radio used by Forward Air Controllers (FACs) during the 1971 Liberation War. Forward air controllers were army officers posted with ground forces who directed air strikes by radio, providing targeting information to attacking aircraft. The PRC-25 operates on FM frequencies in the 30–75.95 MHz band and has a range of approximately 5–8 km. This example was used to coordinate Hawker Hunter close air support strikes during the liberation campaign. The radio is displayed with its original carrying harness, handset, and antenna, alongside a photograph of a FAC team at work.

Artifact_Name: Scale Model Collection — BAF Aircraft Fleet (1971–2000)
Description: A cabinet display of precision scale models of every aircraft type that served in the Bangladesh Air Force from its founding in 1971 to the turn of the millennium. The collection includes: Hawker Hunter FGA.9, de Havilland Vampire, MiG-21 MF, Shenyang F-6, Cessna T-37, Aermacchi MB-339, Fouga Magister, Mil Mi-8, Bell 212, and An-24 transport. Each model is detailed to 1:48 or 1:72 scale and painted in the exact livery worn during BAF service, including the national roundel, serial numbers, and tactical markings. The accompanying labels give the service dates, primary roles, and key technical specifications of each aircraft.

The Antonov An-24 is a Soviet twin-turboprop short-haul transport and passenger aircraft used by the Bangladesh Air Force for VIP transport, logistics, and military airlift. Bangladesh acquired An-24s from the Soviet Union in the early years after independence. The aircraft can carry up to 50 passengers or equivalent cargo and operates from unpaved runways — a critical requirement for Bangladesh's limited airfield infrastructure in the 1970s. The An-24 served both military and quasi-civilian government transport roles. This museum example is one of the best-preserved Soviet-era transport aircraft in Bangladesh and represents the Soviet Union's significant contribution to BAF's early capability.

Artifact_Name: Medals Display — Liberation War and Service Awards
Description: A display case of medals awarded to Bangladesh Air Force officers and airmen, including: the Bir Uttom (second highest gallantry award) awarded to pilots who flew combat missions in 1971; the Bangladesh Muktijoddha Padak (Liberation War Medal); service medals for UN peacekeeping deployments in Cambodia, Somalia, and Sierra Leone; and long service awards. The medals are displayed on black velvet with printed labels identifying the recipient, date of award, and the action or service for which the decoration was given. This display humanises the institutional history of the BAF through the individual stories of its members' distinguished service.

A comprehensive display of parachute and aircrew survival equipment used by BAF pilots. The exhibit includes a back-type pilot parachute (the type used in non-ejection-seat aircraft), a seat-type parachute harness, and a personal survival pack containing: first-aid kit, waterproof matches, compass, signalling mirror, emergency rations, water purification tablets, and a survival knife. An instructional panel explains how to correctly don and operate a parachute and the correct emergency landing procedure. The equipment reflects the serious operational planning that underlies peacetime military aviation, preparing for the possibility of an aircraft emergency.

Artifact_Name: BAF Museum Main Hall Diorama — Liberation War Air Operations
Material: Painted fibreboard, resin aircraft models, lighting
Credit_Donor: Bangladesh Air Force Museum curatorial team
Description: A large three-dimensional diorama depicting the air operations of the Bangladesh Air Force and the Indian Air Force during the December 1971 war. The diorama shows a map of Bangladesh with forward air bases, target locations, and attack routes rendered in three dimensions. Miniature aircraft on wire supports represent BAF and IAF sorties. Red stars on the map indicate Pakistani installations that were struck. An audio commentary (looped) narrates the sequence of air operations from the beginning of the Indian Air Force's air campaign on 3 December 1971 to the fall of Dhaka on 16 December. This is one of the most popular exhibits in the museum, particularly for school children.

Credit_Donor: Recovered by Bangladesh Air Force and Army
Description: Wreckage fragments and recovered components from Pakistani Air Force aircraft shot down or destroyed during the 1971 Liberation War. The display includes: a section of wing skin with bullet holes, an instrument panel recovered from a crashed Sabre jet, and a partially intact engine cowling. Labels identify the aircraft type, the location where wreckage was found, and the engagement in which the aircraft was lost. These physical remains of destroyed enemy aircraft are among the most viscerally powerful exhibits in the museum, tangible evidence of the air battles that contributed to Bangladesh's liberation.

The official visitor's book of the Bangladesh Air Force Museum, maintained since the museum's opening in 1977. The book contains signatures, comments, and messages from notable visitors including Heads of State, foreign dignitaries, senior military officers, veterans of the 1971 Liberation War, and ordinary Bangladeshi citizens. Selected pages from the book are displayed in a glass case, including entries from early visitors in 1977, entries from Liberation War veterans, and comments from international guests. The visitor's book is a social history of the museum and of Bangladesh's engagement with its own military heritage.

A traditional nakshi kantha (embroidered quilt) made from layers of old sari cloth stitched together with colorful thread. The surface is covered with intricate patterns depicting rural life, birds, flowers, and geometric motifs. Nakshi kanthas are a quintessential Bengali folk art, traditionally made by women in rural homes. This example comes from Jamalpur district, a region renowned for the finest kantha work. The central panel shows a tree of life flanked by peacocks and surrounded by a border of lotus flowers.

A hand-carved wooden puppet (putool) used in traditional Bengali puppet theatre (putool nach). The figure represents a village maiden in a red sari with painted features and articulated limbs controlled by strings. Puppet theatre has been a beloved form of entertainment and moral storytelling for children in Bangladesh for centuries, conveying folk tales and epics like the Ramayana. This puppet originates from Sylhet, where a distinct style of puppetry flourished.

A painted clay doll (mati putul) from Rajshahi, depicting a woman carrying a water pot on her head. Made from fine alluvial clay, fired in a traditional kiln, and painted with natural mineral pigments in red, white, and black. Clay dolls have been made in Bangladesh for thousands of years and remain a vital folk industry. The Rajshahi style is distinguished by its elongated proportions and geometric facial features. Such dolls were traditionally sold at rural fairs and used both as toys and as household decorations.

A hand-painted decorative panel from the back of a Dhaka rickshaw, depicting a Bengali landscape scene: a river with boats, coconut palms, and a village at sunset. Rickshaw art is a uniquely Bangladeshi form of urban folk painting, developed in Dhaka from the 1940s onward. Each panel is individually painted by specialized artists using bright enamel paints on sheet metal. These vivid images — combining nature scenes, film stars, tigers, and national symbols — have become a defining visual identity of Bangladesh's capital.

Artifact_Name: Manuscript of Bengali Nursery Rhymes (Chhara Sangkalan)
Description: A handwritten compilation of traditional Bengali nursery rhymes and children's songs (chhara), collected and transcribed in the 1940s. The manuscript includes over 50 traditional rhymes including verses about seasons, animals, rivers, and village life. Many of these rhymes are attributed to anonymous rural poets and have been passed down orally for generations. The collection was assembled by a Dhaka schoolteacher as part of an effort to preserve children's oral literature during the tumultuous years of the Partition. It represents an irreplaceable document of Bengal's intangible cultural heritage.

A bronze bell used in one of the historic madrasas of Sonargaon, the ancient medieval capital of Bengal. The bell was rung to mark the times of prayer, lessons, and meals. It bears a simple engraved inscription in Arabic giving the name of the institution. Educational bells are rare survivors from pre-modern Bengal's institutional life. Sonargaon was the seat of learning and governance in medieval Bengal, and this bell is a tangible remnant of its scholarly institutions.

A printed Bengali alphabet chart (bornomala) produced for primary school classrooms in the early 20th century. The chart displays the full set of Bengali vowels (swar) and consonants (byanjan) with accompanying illustrations for each letter — a fish for 'mach', a bird for 'pakhi', a hand for 'hath'. The illustrations are drawn in a charming folk-art style and printed by lithography. Such charts were the first introduction to literacy for generations of Bengali children and represent the early development of educational print culture in Bengal.

A patachitra (narrative scroll painting) from Narsingdi, depicting the story of the demon king Ravana and Lord Rama in a sequence of illustrated panels. Made by a patua (scroll painter) using natural pigments derived from plants and minerals on handmade paper. The patua traditionally traveled from village to village unrolling the scroll while singing the story depicted. Patachitra is one of Bangladesh's oldest living art traditions, combining visual art with oral performance. The colors are vivid — red, yellow, green, and black — and the style is highly stylized with flat perspective.

Artifact_Name: Children's Game Set — Ludo and Shataranj (Chess)
Description: A set of traditional indoor games including a hand-painted ludo board and a carved wooden chess (shataranj) set. The ludo board is decorated with folk motifs in bright colors; the chess pieces are carved in the traditional South Asian style with elephant, horse, and foot-soldier pieces. These games represent the intellectual and recreational culture of Bengali children across social classes. Chess (shataranj) came to Bengal through the Mughal period and became deeply embedded in urban household culture, while ludo developed from ancient Indian games of chance.

A framed collection of twelve historical Eid greeting cards from the 1960s and 1970s, representing the evolution of festive card design in Bangladesh. The cards combine Islamic calligraphy with Bengali folk motifs — flowers, birds, and rural scenes. Several are hand-painted by commercial artists; others are lithographs. The exchange of Eid cards became a beloved cultural practice in Bengali Muslim homes after the 1950s, blending religious celebration with artistic expression. The collection documents a vanishing tradition as digital communication has replaced paper cards.

Artifact_Name: Model of a Traditional Bengali Village (Diorama)
Description: A detailed scale model depicting a traditional Bengali village (gram): bamboo-walled thatched houses, a pond with lotus flowers, rice fields, a banyan tree, a mosque, a school, and miniature figures of villagers going about their daily activities. Made by Shishu Academy craftspeople using clay, bamboo, and painted paper. The model was created as an educational tool to help urban children understand rural life. It captures the ecological and social structure of a typical village in the Bengal delta — the homestead (bari), the courtyard (uthan), the vegetable garden (bagicha), and the community well.

Artifact_Name: First Edition of Abol Tabol by Sukumar Ray
Description: A rare first edition copy of Abol Tabol (Nonsense Rhymes) by Sukumar Ray (1887–1923), the most celebrated work of Bengali children's literature. Published in 1923, the year of Ray's death, Abol Tabol is a collection of absurdist poems illustrated by the author himself, combining wordplay, surreal imagery, and sharp social satire.
