The book created an entirely new genre of children's literature in Bengali and remains the most read and memorized collection of verse by Bengali children worldwide. This copy is in remarkably good condition, with the original cloth binding and all illustrations intact.

A hand-modeled terracotta horse with rider, made in the tradition of the Bisnupur ceramic toys of Bengal. The horse is painted in red and white with geometric decorations. Such terracotta horses were offered at village shrines and sold at rural fairs as toys and votive objects. They are among the most ancient forms of Bengali folk art, with parallels stretching back to the Harappan civilization. The modeling is bold and simplified, capturing the essence of movement in a few expressive forms. The rider carries a sword and wears a peaked hat, possibly representing a folk hero.

Credit_Donor: Donated by musicians and folk artists
Description: A display of ten traditional bamboo flutes (bashi) of varying sizes, from different regions of Bangladesh. The bashi is the most iconic instrument of Bengali folk music, associated with the legendary flute-player Lord Krishna and with the baul (wandering mystic) musical tradition. Each flute is hand-crafted from a single bamboo internode, with finger holes bored by a heated iron rod. The examples here come from Sylhet and the Chittagong Hill Tracts, where distinct local playing styles have developed. Several are decorated with carved geometric patterns or wrapped with colored thread.

Credit_Donor: Donated by Press Institute of Bangladesh
Description: A collection of twelve black and white photographic prints documenting the participation of school children in the Bengali Language Movement protests of February 1952. The photographs show young students marching in Dhaka, gathering near Dhaka Medical College, and participating in memorial ceremonies. Children were among the most active participants in the Language Movement, and their courage contributed to making Bengali an official language of Pakistan in 1956. These photographs are among the most important documentary records of children's role in Bangladesh's political history.

Artifact_Name: Illustrated Story Book — Thakurmar Jhuli (Grandmother's Bag of Tales)
Description: A facsimile reproduction of the first edition of Thakurmar Jhuli (1907) by Dakshinaranjan Mitra Majumder — the most important collection of Bengali fairy tales and folk stories. The book contains stories of princes and princesses, demons (rakshas), magical birds, and enchanted forests drawn from the oral storytelling tradition of rural Bengal. The original illustrations in this edition are woodcuts in the folk style. Thakurmar Jhuli has been the primary source of magical folk narratives for Bengali children for over a century and was later made into an iconic animated film.

Credit_Donor: Donated by master weaver family, Rupganj
Description: A framed sample of authentic Dhakai muslin — the legendary woven cotton so fine it was called 'woven air' (bafta hawa) by Mughal emperors and 'running water' (rogan pani) by European traders. This sample, woven in the 1950s by one of the last master weavers of the tradition, demonstrates the extraordinary fineness: a full sari of this fabric, 6 meters long, could be folded into a matchbox. The muslin is woven from the thread of Phuti karpas cotton grown only in a narrow strip of land along the Meghna river. The tradition was nearly destroyed by colonial policies and the advent of machine textiles.

Material: Gourd, bamboo, metal string, animal skin
Description: An ektara (one-string drone lute) and a dotara (two-string melody lute) belonging to a baul singer from the Kushtia region — the heartland of the baul tradition associated with the mystic poet Lalon Shah (1774–1890). The ektara consists of a dried gourd resonator with a bamboo neck and a single metal string, played by squeezing the bamboo to change pitch. The dotara is a more complex plucked lute with two wire strings and a wooden body. These instruments are inseparable from baul philosophy, which sees music as the path to the divine. The baul tradition of Bangladesh and West Bengal was inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2008.

Credit_Donor: Donated by children's war memorial project
Description: A collection of fifteen drawings made by Dhaka schoolchildren in 1972, one year after independence, depicting their memories and imaginings of the 1971 Liberation War. The drawings show Pakistani soldiers, freedom fighters (muktijoddha), burning villages, the national flag, and portraits of Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman. Made with crayons and pencils, the works are raw and deeply moving documents of how children processed the trauma and triumph of the war. They were collected as part of an early Shishu Academy project to document children's responses to independence.

A tall brass hookah (huqqa) decorated with engraved scenes of children at play — flying kites, spinning tops, swimming in ponds, and catching fish. While hookahs were adult objects, this example is unusual in that its decorative program is entirely devoted to childhood scenes. The engraving is of the highest quality, with each scene framed in floral cartouches in the Mughal decorative tradition. The glass water vessel at the base is original, preserved intact. This object illustrates how childhood was conceptualized and depicted in late 19th-century Bengali decorative arts.

A detailed scale model of a traditional dingi fishing boat used in the rivers and coastal waters of southern Bangladesh. The model shows the flat-bottomed hull, the small covered cabin, the single mast with a cotton sail, and fishing nets coiled at the stern. River boats (nauka) are central to the culture and economy of Bangladesh, where thousands of rivers create the arterial system of a nation. The model was made by a master boatbuilder from Barisal and represents the craft knowledge of boat-building communities that has sustained life on the Bengal delta for millennia.

A hand-embroidered jute schoolbag (pothi bag) made by a rural woman for her child to carry books to school. The bag is embroidered with a scene of a schoolhouse, trees, children playing, and the Bengali letters 'ba' for 'boi' (book). Made from locally grown jute cloth with cotton thread embroidery in red and green. Such bags were a labor of love, each one unique, representing the aspirations of rural families for their children's education. Jute — Bangladesh's golden fiber — forms the material base of this humble but touching artifact.

A original offset lithograph poster produced by Children's Museum (Shishu Academy) for International Children's Day 1974 — the second year of Bangladesh's independent existence as a nation. The poster shows a group of children of different backgrounds playing together under a rainbow, with the Bengali text 'Amader shishu, amader asha' (Our children, our hope). Designed by a prominent Dhaka graphic artist, the poster represents the early nation's aspirations for children as the foundation of the new Bangladesh. It is among the earliest graphic design artifacts in the Shishu Academy's collection.

A collection of twelve traditional Bengali kites (ghuri) in various shapes and sizes — diamond kites, bird-shaped kites, and the large 'pataug' display kite. Made from split bamboo frames covered with colored tissue paper, decorated with cut-paper patterns. Kite-flying (ghuri ura) is one of the most beloved seasonal pastimes in Bangladesh, particularly during the winter months and at the Sakrain festival in Old Dhaka. The competitive sport of kite-fighting (ghuri kata) — cutting opponents' strings with glass-coated 'manja' thread — has been a defining feature of Dhaka's cultural life for centuries.

Artifact_Name: Certificate of the First National Children's Literature Award (1976)
Description: The original certificate awarded at the first Children's Museum (Shishu Academy) National Children's Literature Award ceremony in 1976, presented to a pioneering author of Bengali children's fiction. The certificate is hand-calligraphed in Bengali on cream parchment with gold borders and bears the official seal of Children's Museum (Shishu Academy) and the signature of the cultural minister. The establishment of a national children's literature prize in 1976 — just five years after independence — reflected the new nation's commitment to building a distinct cultural identity for its youngest citizens. The award continues to be presented annually.

Artifact_Type: Traditional Watercraft / Boat Model or Specimen
Finding_Place: Collected from riverine communities of Bangladesh
Description: The Dingi is one of the most common and traditional small boats of Bangladesh, used widely across rivers and canals for everyday transport, fishing, and household use. A small, narrow, flat-bottomed rowboat typically made of wood, it is found throughout riverine Bangladesh. Explicitly named in the CholoZai source listing the museum's collection.

Artifact_Type: Traditional Watercraft / Boat Model or Specimen
Description: The Ekmalai is a traditional Bangladeshi boat type preserved and displayed in the museum. Listed among the boat types in the museum's collection in the CholoZai source. Specific details about its use and origin region are not stated in the available sources.

Artifact_Type: Traditional Watercraft / Boat Model or Specimen
Description: The Pansi is a traditional Bangladeshi sailing and rowing boat with a distinctive long, narrow hull. It is historically used for transport of goods and passengers along rivers in southern Bangladesh, including the Barisal and coastal regions. Listed among the boat types in the museum's collection.

Artifact_Type: Traditional Watercraft / Boat Model or Specimen
Description: The Gayna (also Gaina) is a traditional decorated Bangladeshi boat, often associated with ceremonial or festive use. Listed among the named boat types in the museum's collection in the CholoZai source. Specific regional details not stated in available sources.

Artifact_Type: Traditional Watercraft / Boat Model or Specimen
Description: The Keraya is a traditional Bangladeshi boat type included in the museum's collection. Listed by name in the CholoZai source among the variety of boats displayed. No further details are available in the cited sources.

Artifact_Type: Traditional Watercraft / Boat Model or Specimen
Description: The Kosha is a traditional narrow, wooden fishing and transport boat used in Bangladesh's riverine waterways. Listed among the named boat types in the museum's collection. Also known as a dugout-style craft in some regions.

Artifact_Type: Traditional Watercraft / Boat Model or Specimen
Description: The Konda is a traditional Bangladeshi boat type included in the museum's collection. Listed by name in the CholoZai source. No further details available in the cited sources.

Artifact_Type: Traditional Watercraft / Boat Model or Specimen
Description: The Ghasi is a traditional Bangladeshi boat type preserved and displayed in the museum. Listed among the named boat types in the CholoZai source. Specific regional or use details are not stated in the available sources.

Artifact_Type: Traditional Watercraft / Boat Model or Specimen
Finding_Place: Collected from coastal and riverine communities
Description: The Sampan is a flat-bottomed wooden boat widely used along the rivers and coastal areas of Bangladesh and Southeast Asia. It is used for fishing, transport, and daily life along waterways. Listed in the museum's collection by name in the CholoZai source (listed twice in the original source text, suggesting possibly multiple variants or regional types of Sampan were displayed).

Artifact_Type: Traditional Watercraft / Boat Model or Specimen
Description: The Lambapadi is a traditional Bangladeshi boat type included in the museum's collection. Listed by name in the CholoZai source. 'Lamba' in Bengali means long, suggesting a long-hulled vessel design. No further details are available in the cited sources.

Artifact_Type: Traditional Watercraft / Boat Model or Specimen
Description: The Kathami, also called 'Export' boat, is a traditional Bangladeshi boat type included in the museum's collection. The CholoZai source lists it as 'Kathami or Export', indicating these are local names for the same vessel type. No further details are stated in the available sources.

Artifact_Type: Traditional Watercraft / Boat Model or Specimen
Description: The Bachari is a traditional Bangladeshi boat type preserved and displayed in the museum. Listed among the named boat types in the CholoZai source. TripMonarch also mentions the goal of preserving 'extinct Bahari shaped boats', suggesting Bachari/Bahari may be among the extinct types documented in the museum.

Artifact_Type: Traditional Watercraft / Boat Model or Specimen
Description: The Patam is a traditional Bangladeshi boat type included in the museum's collection. Listed by name in the CholoZai source. No further details on its region of use or status are stated in the available sources.

The Baich boat is the traditional Bangladeshi racing boat, used in the famous Naukabai (boat race) festivals, which are an integral part of Bengali culture and heritage. Boat races (Naukabai) have historically been associated with Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman and Bengali cultural identity, making this a symbolically significant exhibit. Listed among the named boat types in the CholoZai source.

Finding_Place: Established 31 December 2020 within the museum complex
Description: A dedicated section within the museum documenting the connection between Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, the Bangladesh Liberation War, and the cultural/historical significance of boats to Bangladesh. The museum was named in honor of Mujib Year (birth centenary of Bangabandhu). Explicitly mentioned in Wikipedia as a facility inside the museum complex.

Finding_Place: Established 31 December 2020 within the museum complex
Description: A research center within the museum complex dedicated to the study and documentation of traditional Bangladeshi boats. The museum aimed to preserve portraits, information, and specimens of boats from different regions of Bangladesh. Explicitly mentioned in Wikipedia as a facility of the museum.

Finding_Place: Established 31 December 2020 within the museum complex
Description: A modern library within the museum complex, aimed at housing books, research materials, and documentation related to Bangladesh's boat heritage and riverine history. Explicitly mentioned in Wikipedia as a facility of the museum.

Finding_Place: Established 31 December 2020 within the museum complex
Description: A children's recreation and entertainment center within the museum complex, aimed at making the museum accessible and engaging for younger visitors. Explicitly mentioned in Wikipedia as a facility of the museum.

Finding_Place: Established 31 December 2020 within the museum complex
Description: A food court facility within the museum complex, designed to make the museum a self-contained visitor destination. Explicitly mentioned in Wikipedia as a facility of the museum.

A bronze image of the goddess Tārā, one of the most revered female Bodhisattvas in Vajrayana Buddhism. Tārā is the compassionate saviour deity and her form is found in multiple variants at Mainamati. This piece is part of the rich bronze collection of the museum.

A bronze image of Avalokiteśvara (Lokeśvara), the Bodhisattva of infinite compassion — one of the most frequently depicted deities in the Mainamati bronze corpus. A colossal example was found at Ānanda Vihāra, and a large bronze head near Kutila Mura.

Manasā, the Bengali folk goddess of serpents, depicted surrounded by cobras. She is one of the most distinctive deities found in the Mainamati region, reflecting the syncretic blend of Buddhist and Hindu folk worship characteristic of early medieval southeast Bengal.

Naṭarāja — Śiva as the Lord of Dance — depicted in his cosmic Āṇanda Tāṇḍava dance posture. This multi-armed form of Śiva symbolises the eternal cycles of creation, preservation and destruction. Found at Mainamati-Lalmai ridge, it reflects Brahmanical influence alongside Buddhist art.

Umā-Maheśvara — Śiva and his consort Pārvatī (Umā) depicted together seated on Mount Kailāsa in a scene of divine domestic bliss. Reflects the Brahmanical patronage coexisting with Buddhism at Mainamati.

A standing image of Pārvatī, the Hindu goddess and consort of Śiva, depicted in elegant tribhaṅga posture with her characteristic attributes. Reflects the Hindu sculptural tradition that flourished alongside Buddhism in the Mainamati region.

The magnificent colossal bronze Vajrasattva — 1.10 m high in seated position — considered one of the finest examples of bronze casting from the Indian subcontinent. Vajrasattva represents all five Tathāgatas simultaneously. Found at Bhoja Vihāra; the donor was clearly a very wealthy merchant or royal dignitary of the Candra dynasty.

Cāmuṇḍā, the fierce goddess and one of the Saptamātrkā (seven mother goddesses), depicted in her terrifying emaciated form dancing on a corpse. Her presence at Mainamati reflects the Tantric traditions of early medieval southeast Bengal.

A Navagraha panel depicting the nine planetary deities: Sūrya, Candra, Maṅgala, Budha, Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Śani, Rāhu and Ketu. Such panels were placed above temple doorways as protective devices in the Hindu/Brahmanical tradition of medieval Bengal.

A collection of weighing instruments and standardised weights (bāṭkhārā) recovered from Mainamati excavations. These attest to active trade and commerce at Mainamati-Devaparvata. The presence of standardised weights confirms the town's role as a major riverine trade port on the banks of the Kṣirodā river.

The most striking discovery of Itakhola Mura Vihāra — a stucco figure of Buddha Akṣobhya preserved in situ. Stucco figures were common in Gandhāra art but rare in Bengal, making this exceptional. Akṣobhya is the 'Unshakeable' Dhyāni Buddha of the eastern direction.

A life-size standing sandstone image of the Buddha discovered from a chamber of the temple at Rupban Mura Vihāra. Standing 2.15 m high, it is one of the most impressive stone sculptures from Mainamati. Rupban Mura Vihāra is considered the earliest of the excavated monasteries at Mainamati.

A colossal seated bronze Buddha displayed to the left of the museum entrance — the first major piece visitors encounter. A key highlight of the museum's collection representing the early Tantric Buddhist artistic tradition of southeast Bengal. Dated to the 7th century CE.

Mahāpratisarā — 'the great amulet' — a multi-armed Buddhist protective goddess. This metal image from Rupban Mura is one of the important protective deity images from Mainamati. She is worshipped for warding off misfortune and danger.

Credit_Donor: Excavation — Ānanda Vihāra (Deva Dynasty, Śrī Ānanda Deva)
Description: A colossal bronze Avalokiteśvara recovered from Ānanda Vihāra — the largest Buddhist monastery in Mainamati (195 m a side), built by Śrī Ānanda Deva, third ruler of the Deva dynasty. One of the most important bronze sculptures from the entire Mainamati corpus.

A large life-size bronze head of Avalokiteśvara collected near Kutila Mura. Its identification is based on the miniature figure of Amitābha on its exquisitely ornamented crown. Dated to around the 10th century CE — one of the most impressive bronzes from Mainamati.

Artifact_Name: Bronze Votive Stupa (with Four Female Deities)
Description: A remarkable bronze votive stupa found during excavations at Salban Vihāra, with four female deities on four sides each seated under a shrine placed against the drum of the stupa. A unique example of votive Buddhist metalwork from medieval southeast Bengal.

Credit_Donor: Excavation — Salban Vihāra (Deva Dynasty, Śrī Bhavadeva)
Description: Terracotta sealings bearing the inscription: 'Śrī-Bhavadeva Mahā Vihāra-Ārya-Bhikṣu-Saṃghasya' — 'of the order of the noble monks of the monastic establishment of Śrī Bhavadeva.' These confirm King Bhavadeva of the Deva dynasty as patron of Salban Vihāra.

Credit_Donor: Excavation — Salban Vihāra (Khadga, Rata, Deva, Candra Dynasties)
Description: Seven copper plate inscriptions from Salban Vihāra representing multiple dynasties. Key plates: Kailan copper plate of Śrīdhāranarāta (c. 665–675 CE); copper plate of Rajputra Balabhaṭṭa (c. 715–730 CE); Asiatic Society copper plate of Bhavadeva (c. 815–840 CE); Pascimbhāgh copper plate of Śrīcandra (c. 925–975 CE). Primary sources for the history of southeast Bengal.

Credit_Donor: Excavation — Multiple Sites (Khadga, Harikela-Paṭṭikera, Candra Dynasties)
Description: Approximately 350 gold and silver coins recovered from Mainamati sites, primarily from Salban Vihāra. Includes Gupta imitation gold coins, Harikela-Paṭṭikera type silver coins from Rupban Mura, and Pāṭṭikera style silver coins from Itakhola Mura. Provide crucial evidence for dating the sites and the prosperity of Mainamati as a trade centre.

Finding_Place: Salban Vihāra / Bhoja Vihāra, Mainamati, Comilla
Description: Hundreds of terracotta plaques recovered from Salban Vihāra and Bhoja Vihāra depicting Buddhist, Hindu and secular subjects. Bhoja Vihāra's central temple was 'profusely decorated' with such plaques. They represent one of the richest terracotta collections from medieval Bengal.

Innumerable tiny terracotta and clay votive stupas, seals and sealings enshrined within the eight box-chambers of the Dharmacakra-shaped foundation of the central stupa at Kutila Mura. Together with fine Buddhist sculptures in soft grey shale, these represent a unique and rare ritual deposit.

Artifact_Name: Buddhist Sculptures in Soft Grey Shale (Kutila Mura)
Description: A class of fine Buddhist sculptures in soft grey shale found within the stupa chambers of Kutila Mura. Distinguished by the use of softer grey shale rather than the black basalt typical of the Pāla period, suggesting an earlier regional tradition. Includes an Avalokiteśvara seated on a principal lotus with attendants.

A copper plate inscription recovered from Itakhola Mura Vihāra — one of the two earliest monasteries at Mainamati, built by Khadga King Balabhaṭṭa. An important epigraphic record for the early history of southeast Bengal.

Artifact_Name: Bronze Votive Images — Amitābha, Akṣobhya & Gaṇeśa
Description: Six bronze votive images recovered from Itakhola Mura Vihāra: images of Amitābha, Akṣobhya and Gaṇeśa. The Buddhist images bear a stamped Buddhist creed on their back — a distinctive feature. Gaṇeśa's presence alongside Buddhist deities reflects religious syncretism at Mainamati.

A medium-size soft-shell image of Amitābha, the 'Infinite Light' Dhyāni Buddha of the western direction, found at Bhoja Vihāra. Amitābha was among the most popular Dhyāni Buddhas in medieval Bangladesh, depicted in dhyāna mudrā (meditation posture).

A medium-size soft-shell image of Akṣobhya ('the Imperturbable'), the blue Dhyāni Buddha of the eastern direction, found at Bhoja Vihāra. Along with Amitābha, Akṣobhya was one of the most popular Dhyāni Buddhas at Mainamati.

Finding_Place: Bhoja Vihāra / Rupban Mura, Mainamati, Comilla
Description: Harikela-Paṭṭikera type silver coins found at multiple Mainamati sites including Bhoja Vihāra and Rupban Mura. Pāṭṭikera (modern Paitkara, Comilla) was an important administrative seat that eventually formed a separate kingdom with ties to Pagan (Bagan) and Arakan of Myanmar.

A massive bronze bell weighing 370 kg — one of the museum's most dramatic exhibits. Bronze bells were used in Buddhist religious ceremonies. The museum also holds a separate giant bronze object weighing approximately 500 kg. These bells attest to the sophisticated metal-casting technology of medieval Mainamati.

A black stone sculpture of Nandī, the sacred bull and vehicle (vāhana) of Lord Śiva. This Brahmanical sculpture is one of several Hindu pieces in the Mainamati collection, reflecting the multi-religious nature of medieval southeast Bengal where Charpatra Mura was the only purely Brahmanical site.

An ancient manuscript written on palm leaves in the Burmese script, attesting to the cultural and religious connections between Mainamati-Pāṭṭikera and Myanmar (Pagan and Arakan). Reflects the wider cultural network through which the art idiom of Mainamati spread to Myanmar and Java.

A collection of iron objects — tools and implements — recovered from Mainamati excavations, demonstrating the iron-working technology of medieval inhabitants. Iron objects include agricultural and craft tools that sustained the economic activities supporting the monasteries.

A variety of clay toys — animals, figurines and objects — recovered from Mainamati excavations. These secular objects provide evidence of daily life and material culture of the lay population that supported the Buddhist monastic complex at Mainamati-Devaparvata.

A large pottery collection including Common Light Gray Ware recovered from the Mainamati excavations. Changes in pottery type help archaeologists distinguish the two major historic phases of Mainamati (6th–13th century CE). Increase in Common Light Gray Ware marks the second historic phase associated with the Candra dynasty.

Over 150 miniature bronze Buddha images recovered mostly from the monastic cells and votive deposits at Mainamati — the largest such collection from medieval Bengal. These were used for personal devotion and as votive offerings. They represent the Tantric Buddhist pantheon: Dhyāni Buddhas, Bodhisattvas and Tārās.

A collection of semi-precious stone beads including carnelian and agate recovered from Ānanda Vihāra and other Mainamati sites. These beads attest to trade contacts and the material wealth of the monastery patrons, reflecting long-distance trade networks linking Mainamati to wider South and Southeast Asia.

A standing bronze Bodhisattva Padmapāṇi ('lotus-bearer'), a form of Avalokiteśvara holding a lotus. One of the many bronzes recovered from Salban Vihāra's 115 monastic cells and surrounding excavations. It is identified in the museum as 'Bodhisattva Padmapāṇi, Salban Vihāra.'

Various types of standing Lokottara ('supramundane') Buddha statues in stone. Lokottara Buddha images represent the transcendent aspect of the Buddha beyond his human manifestation — a key concept in Mahāyāna and Vajrayāna Buddhism. Multiple examples are on display in the museum.

A stone image of Viṣṇu in his Trivikrama form — the three-strides dwarf avatāra (Vāmana) — depicting his cosmic stride that covered earth, sky and heaven. This Vaiṣṇava sculptural subject reflects the Hindu traditions coexisting with Buddhism at Mainamati during the Candra period.

A stone image of Durgā slaying the buffalo demon Mahiṣāsura — the most iconic form of the goddess Durgā in Hindu iconography. Reflects the multi-religious character of Mainamati where Buddhist and Hindu (Śākta) traditions coexisted during the Candra period.

A stone image of Mārīcī, the Buddhist goddess of dawn and light, depicted with multiple arms. Mārīcī was a popular goddess in Tantric Buddhism of medieval Bengal. Images of this goddess are found at both Mainamati and other major Buddhist sites of Bangladesh.

A stone image of Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva of wisdom, holding his characteristic sword (to cut through ignorance) and the Prajñāpāramitā text. The seated form of this deity is also known as Mañjuvara. Mañjuśrī was one of the key Bodhisattvas worshipped at Mainamati.

Preserved woodwork patterns and wooden artifacts recovered from Mainamati excavations. Given the humid delta climate of Bengal, wooden objects rarely survive in the archaeological record, making these fragments particularly rare and valuable.

Five Gupta imitation gold coins recovered from Rupban Mura Vihāra — among the earliest datable objects from Mainamati. These coins suggest the site's origins in the late Gupta or immediately post-Gupta period (6th–7th century CE) and confirm the first historic phase of Mainamati.

A Pāṭṭikera style silver coin salvaged from Itakhola Mura Vihāra. The name Pāṭṭikera appears in coin legends from the 8th century CE levels of Salban Vihāra and also in the Cambridge University Manuscript of Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā (copied in 1015 CE). Pāṭṭikera eventually formed a separate kingdom.

Finding_Place: Nārāyanpur, Barurā Police Station, Comilla District
Credit_Donor: Collection — Nārāyanpur, Barurā, Comilla (Dept. of Archaeology, Bangladesh)
Description: Nārāyanpur, Barurā Police Station, Comilla District

A terracotta relief plaque from Salban Vihāra depicting a snake and mongoose in combat — a motif of profound symbolic significance in South Asian iconography. The snake–mongoose combat symbolises the eternal conflict between earth and the underworld, life and death, and is a common auspicious subject on Buddhist and Hindu decorative plaques. This piece is part of the rich terracotta assemblage recovered from Salban Vihāra's central temple, which was 'profusely decorated' with such plaques. The terracotta modelling is characteristically bold and vigorous, typical of 8th century CE Samatata workmanship. Source: ResearchGate, Double-bodied lion and related Salban Vihāra terracotta series (fig. 307670905); Dept. of Archaeology, Bangladesh.

A remarkable architectural sculpture of a double-bodied lion (dvimukha vyāla or śārdūla) — a single leonine head with two bodies extending in opposite directions — carved from buff sandstone at Salban Vihāra. Such double-bodied mythical creatures served as decorative and apotropaic (protective) elements on Buddhist temple architecture, typically placed at corners of temple bases or friezes. The image demonstrates the sophisticated stone-carving tradition at Mainamati alongside its more celebrated bronze corpus. The motif of the vyāla — a rearing composite leonine beast — is widespread in South Asian temple architecture from the Gupta period onwards. Source: ResearchGate fig. 307670905; 'Double-bodied lion, 8th Century CE, Salabana Vihara, Mainamati Museum, Bangladesh.'

A display group of four important stone deity sculptures mounted in the main gallery against a magenta-red velvet backing (image: mainamati3.webp). From left to right: (1) a multi-armed standing deity with attendants — possibly Viṣṇu or a Bodhisattva, found likely at Mainamati-Lalmai; (2) a standing deity with globe and serpent attributes, from Gujrābar, Artisha, Comilla (per museum label, 8th–10th century CE); (3) a multi-armed standing deity with rich jewellery and attendant figures, also from Gujrābar, Artisha, Comilla; (4) a dancing deity figure — possibly Naṭarāja or Heruka. The museum label for the second figure reads 'Gujrābar, Artisha, Comilla' and dates it to the Pāla period. This display showcases the full range of Buddhist and Brahmanical sculptural production from the greater Comilla-Samatata region. Source: Museum display photograph; Dept. of Archaeology, Bangladesh.
A stencil duplicating machine used by Bangabandhu after 7 March 1971 to send messages to party leaders, newspapers, and the people of Bangladesh during the non-cooperation movement.

The telephone set located on the south side of the personal library, near the door. Bangabandhu used this phone to announce the freedom of the Bengali nation; the declaration was transmitted via wireless, telephone and telegram across Bangladesh.

A collection of books of famous writers and novelists kept by Bangabandhu in his personal library. The books bear visible bullet holes from the attack on the house during the night of 25 March 1971, serving as physical evidence of the violence.

Artifact_Name: Portrait Gallery of Assassinated Family Members
Description: Framed portraits displayed on the eastern and western walls of the ground-floor corridor depicting the deceased family members of Bangabandhu along with guests who were killed in the house on 15 August 1975.
The original dressing table from Bangabandhu and Begum Mujib's bedroom on the second floor. The furniture still displays blood-spots and bullet marks from the assassination of 15 August 1975.
Original desk table from Bangabandhu's bedroom on the second floor, bearing bullet marks and blood-spots from the assassination of 15 August 1975.
Original reading table from Bangabandhu's bedroom, displaying physical evidence of the 15 August 1975 assassination through bullet marks and blood-spots.
A betel (paan) vase that was part of the personal effects in Bangabandhu's bedroom. Preserved as a personal relic bearing blood-spots and bullet damage from the 1975 assassination.
A preserved letter addressed to Bangamata (Sheikh Fazilatunnesa Mujib), kept in Bangabandhu's bedroom on the second floor. One of the personal documents recovered after the family regained the house.

The original dining table placed near the entrance of the family dining room on the first floor. Bangabandhu and his family members used it for meals. Bangamata served food to Bangabandhu and guests at this table.
Original dining jugs used by Bangabandhu and family members at the dining table in the family meeting room. Part of the preserved dining accessories.
Original drinking glasses from Bangabandhu's family dining set, displayed in the family meeting room on the second floor.
Original dining plates from Bangabandhu's household used at family meals, now displayed on the dining table in the family meeting room.
Original teacups from Bangabandhu's household, part of the preserved dining accessories displayed in the family meeting and dining room on the second floor.
Original spoons from Bangabandhu's family dining set, displayed among the regular dining accessories in the family meeting room.
Original cutlery knives from Bangabandhu's family dining set, displayed alongside other regular dining accessories in the family meeting room.
A handmade pickle jar belonging to Bangamata Sheikh Fazilatunnesa Mujib, displayed in the family dining and meeting room on the second floor as a personal relic of Bangabandhu's wife.
One of Sheikh Russell's two favourite bicycles (youngest son of Bangabandhu, born 18 October 1964, killed 15 August 1975), displayed in the family dining and meeting room.
The second of Sheikh Russell's two favourite bicycles displayed in the family dining and meeting room, a personal relic of Bangabandhu's youngest son.
An original Coca-Cola bottle displayed in the family dining and meeting room, one of the personal items preserved from Bangabandhu's household.
A tin container with raw rice, preserved as a household item from Bangabandhu's family kitchen and dining area, displayed in the family meeting room.

An old Citizen brand television with a dark body, standing in the southeast corner of the family meeting room on the second floor. Bangabandhu used to sit here and watch TV with family members. Bullet marks are visible in the room.
A ball belonging to Sheikh Russell (youngest son of Bangabandhu), one of his childhood playing items preserved and displayed in the museum.

Artifact_Type: Personal Effect / Sports Equipment / Children's Item
Description: A hockey stick used by Sheikh Russell, preserved as a childhood relic of Bangabandhu's youngest son, displayed in the museum.

Artifact_Type: Personal Effect / Sports Equipment / Children's Item
Description: A cricket bat belonging to Sheikh Russell, one of his sporting items preserved and displayed in the museum.
A helmet belonging to Sheikh Russell, preserved and displayed in the museum as part of his personal belongings.
An aquarium belonging to Sheikh Russell, one of the possessions of Bangabandhu's youngest son preserved and displayed in the museum.
Various childhood toys belonging to Sheikh Russell, preserved and displayed in the museum along with his other possessions.
Watches belonging to Sheikh Russell, preserved and displayed in the museum as part of his personal effects.

Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's iconic tobacco pipe, one of his most recognized personal accessories. Originally displayed in the museum; later handed over to the Bangladesh National Museum by the Bangabandhu Memorial Trust in August 2022 with PM Sheikh Hasina's approval.

The iconic black sleeveless jacket (Mujib coat) worn by Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, which became a symbol of his identity and the Bangladeshi independence movement. Transferred to the Bangladesh National Museum by the Bangabandhu Memorial Trust in August 2022.
Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's white punjabi (long shirt), part of his signature attire. Transferred to the Bangladesh National Museum by the Bangabandhu Memorial Trust in August 2022.
Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's pajama (lower garment), part of his traditional attire. Transferred to the Bangladesh National Museum by the Bangabandhu Memorial Trust in August 2022.
Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's personal eyeglasses, one of his recognizable accessories, preserved and displayed in the museum along with other personal effects.
Various personal accessories and items used by Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, displayed alongside his eyeglasses and pipe as personal relics in the museum.

Personal diaries found by Sheikh Hasina after the house was returned to the family in June 1981. The diaries were later edited and published as memoirs (Unfinished Memoirs / Karagarer Rojnamcha). The original manuscripts were preserved at the museum.
Clothing items bearing bloodstains from the assassination of 15 August 1975, exhibited as evidence of the tragic event. The museum maintained these as part of its exhibits on the assassination.

Finding_Place: Various archives, government records, personal family collection
Description: A large and rare photographic collection documenting the entire life of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, from his early political days through his role as founding president of Bangladesh. Displayed throughout the museum including the corridor gallery and ground floor.
Photographs documenting the aftermath of the 15 August 1975 assassination, showing the violence and destruction in the house. Displayed to remind visitors of the brutal killing.

Artifact_Name: Bullet Holes in Walls and Staircase
Description: Physical marks of bullet holes preserved in the walls of the office room, the main staircase, the bedroom, and the library of the Bangabandhu Bhaban. These serve as primary physical evidence of the 1975 assassination and cannot be separated from the building structure.

Artifact_Name: Sheikh Kamal's Room Contents / Office Room Display
Description: The ground floor office room (reception hall) where Sheikh Kamal (Bangabandhu's eldest son) was killed on 15 August 1975. The room was closed to visitors but preserves the physical evidence of the assassination including bullet marks on walls.
The northeast ground-floor room where Sheikh Russel was born on 18 October 1964, and originally resided by Sheikh Hasina and Sheikh Rehana. Preserved as a memorial space.

Artifact_Name: Drawing Room / Salon Furniture and Décor
Description: The furniture and interior décor of the ground-floor meeting room (salon) used by Bangabandhu for political discussions, meeting party leaders, professionals, and the public. The room was the nerve center of major political decisions from 1962 to 1971.
A curated gallery of portraits and images documenting the golden history of Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, displayed in the drawing room on the ground floor as visitors first enter the museum.

The northeast first-floor room where Sheikh Hasina (eldest daughter of Bangabandhu) lived from 1966. The room was damaged by bullets during the 15 August 1975 assassination and was kept locked and not opened to visitors.

The main staircase of the Bangabandhu Bhaban where Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman was killed on 15 August 1975. He descended the stairs to confront the intruding assassins and was shot on the staircase. The staircase is preserved as the primary site of the assassination.

Artifact_Name: Documents Chronicling Political Life of Bangabandhu
Description: A collection of documents, official papers, and historical records related to Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's political life, his role in the liberation war, and post-independence governance, displayed in the museum.
