The station is equipped with 5 specialized laboratories and indoor and outdoor cistern complexes for marine fish research. It has conducted research on marine fish stock assessment, aquaculture of marine species, seaweed cultivation, and shrimp post-larvae collection. The display includes photographs of laboratory activities, maps of research survey areas in the Bay of Bengal, and information on key research outputs that have informed government fisheries policy. The MFTS Cox's Bazar is the primary marine fisheries research institution in Bangladesh.

Finding_Place: Bay of Bengal and coastal waters, Cox's Bazar
Credit_Donor: BFRI Marine Fisheries and Technology Station
Description: A display of preserved shrimp and prawn specimens representing the major commercially important crustacean species of the Cox's Bazar coastal region and the Bay of Bengal. Bangladesh is one of the world's largest shrimp exporters, and the coastal fisheries of Cox's Bazar contribute significantly to this industry. Species displayed include the Black Tiger Prawn (Penaeus monodon), Banana Shrimp (Penaeus merguiensis), White Shrimp (Litopenaeus vannamei), and several smaller wild-caught shrimp species. The display provides information on shrimp biology, the shrimp aquaculture industry of the Chittagong region, export economics, and the environmental concerns associated with shrimp farming — particularly the impact of shrimp ponds on mangrove and coastal wetland habitats.

Artifact_Name: Coral and Reef Specimens — Saint Martin's Island
Description: A display of coral specimens from Saint Martin's Island — Bangladesh's only coral island, located 9 km south of the Cox's Bazar mainland in the Bay of Bengal. Saint Martin's is the only place in Bangladesh where a coral reef ecosystem exists, supporting a unique diversity of tropical marine life. The coral specimens displayed include brain coral, table coral, and finger coral skeletons, shown alongside photographs of the living reef ecosystem. The display emphasizes the conservation significance of Saint Martin's coral reef, which is under severe threat from tourist pressure, boat anchoring, coral collection, and climate-change-induced bleaching. The museum positions coral conservation as one of the most urgent marine environmental issues in Bangladesh.

Artifact_Name: Traditional Fishing Gear — Coastal and Marine Methods
Credit_Donor: Donated by fishing communities of Cox's Bazar
Description: A display of traditional fishing gear used by Cox's Bazar's coastal fishing communities, including a cast net (jhaki jal) for reef fishing, a long-line set for offshore bottom fishing, crab traps of bamboo and wire, and a traditional hand line for shore fishing. Cox's Bazar has a centuries-old tradition of sea fishing by communities of the Rakhaine (Arakanese) and Bengali Muslim fishermen. Their fishing methods are adapted to the specific conditions of the Bay of Bengal — the monsoon currents, the sea bed topography, and the seasonal movements of target species. The display documents this traditional ecological knowledge alongside information on how industrial fishing methods are displacing traditional practices.

Artifact_Name: Dried Squid and Dry Fish Processing Display
Description: A display documenting the traditional dried fish (shutki) processing industry of Cox's Bazar — one of the most important and distinctive economic activities of the region. Cox's Bazar is Bangladesh's largest producer of dried fish, which is produced by the Rakhaine (Arakanese Buddhist) community and Bengali fishermen by drying fresh fish and squid in the sun on beach racks. The display includes dried fish and squid specimens, photographs of the traditional drying racks on the beaches near Cox's Bazar, and information on the major species processed (small fish, Bombay duck, squid, dried shrimp). Dried fish is an important protein source for poor households across Bangladesh and a major export product. The display celebrates this traditional food preservation technology and the communities that practice it.

A magnificent four-headed Brahma image in black basalt — one of the finest examples of Pala-Sena period sculpture in northern Bangladesh. The deity is shown with four heads (three visible in front) and four arms, with beard and moustache, seated on a lotus pedestal, holding a water jar (kamandalu) and a rosary. The sculpture exemplifies the fully developed Brahma iconography described in the Puranas and represents the high-point of sculptural achievement in the Dinajpur region, which was one of the most artistically productive areas of medieval Bengal. The Dinajpur Museum holds one of Bangladesh's most important regional collections of Hindu and Buddhist sculpture.

A beautiful standing image of Parshvanatha — the 23rd Tirthankara (ford-maker / spiritual teacher) of the Jain tradition — in black basalt. The deity stands in the kayotsarga (arms-at-sides, non-touching posture of deep meditation) on a lotus base, beneath a seven-hooded serpent canopy. Dikpalas (directional guardians) are shown riding animals around the figure, and the goddess Chakreshvari sits below on the pedestal. This image is significant evidence for the presence of Jainism in medieval northern Bengal — a religion less commonly associated with Bangladesh than Hinduism or Buddhism. The Dinajpur Museum holds two Jain sculptures in its collection, making them rare survivors of this tradition in the region.

Six punch-marked silver coins from the ancient period, among the oldest monetary artifacts in the Dinajpur museum's collection. These pre-Mauryan and Mauryan-period coins are blank silver pieces stamped with multiple symbols representing different minting authorities. They provide evidence that northern Bangladesh was integrated into the wider monetary economy of the Mauryan Empire and earlier. The Dinajpur region — ancient Pundravardhana / Varendra — was one of the most prosperous agricultural and trading zones of ancient Bengal, and coins are the primary evidence of its commercial activity. The museum's coin collection of over 800 items spans from these ancient punch-marked coins through colonial period currency.

The largest single category in the Dinajpur Museum's collection: 674 colonial-period coins spanning the East India Company (1757–1858) and British India (1858–1947) eras. The collection includes sicca rupees, company rupees, Victoria rupees, and the full range of colonial subsidiary coinage from the Anna down to the Pie. The Dinajpur region was intensively administered by the British colonial government as a major agricultural district of Bengal, and coins are abundant from this period. The collection documents the gradual standardization and decimalization of the monetary system in Bengal under colonial rule and the replacement of the traditional rupee-Anna-Pice system.

Artifact_Name: Decorated Bricks — 102 Items from Medieval Structures
Description: A collection of 102 decorated fired bricks from medieval archaeological sites in the Dinajpur district — the largest sub-category of the museum's small objects collection. The bricks bear a variety of surface treatments: incised geometric patterns, molded floral designs, stamped inscriptions, and relief-cut decorative bands. They derive from the remains of temples, mosques, and elite residential structures of the medieval period. The Dinajpur region is particularly rich in medieval brick architecture: the famous Kantanagar Temple (18th century) nearby is covered with thousands of terracotta plaques. The museum's brick collection provides evidence for the earlier medieval building traditions that preceded the Kantanagar tradition.

A collection of 14 stone inscriptions in various scripts and languages — Sanskrit in Siddhamatrika and Bengali scripts, Arabic, and Persian — representing the multilingual epigraphic heritage of the Dinajpur region across nearly a millennium. The Sanskrit inscriptions relate to Hindu religious endowments and the recording of land grants; the Arabic and Persian inscriptions are from mosque foundation slabs and tomb markers. Together they document the successive cultural and political regimes that shaped northern Bangladesh: Hindu-Buddhist Pala period, the independent Bengal Sultanate, and the Mughal administration. Several of the inscriptions were recovered from the rubble of destroyed structures and would otherwise have been lost.

Credit_Donor: Sitakot excavation (1968 joint dig with Archaeology Dept.)
Description: Artifacts recovered from the Dinajpur Museum's own excavation at Sitakot Vihara in Nawabganj, Dinajpur District — a Buddhist monastery site jointly excavated with the Directorate of Archaeology of East Pakistan in mid-July 1968. The excavation was one of the museum's most significant early activities and yielded terracotta plaques with Buddhist imagery, fragments of bronze figurines, pottery, and architectural brick. Sitakot Vihara was a Buddhist monastic establishment dating to the early medieval period. The excavation finds are among the few primary archaeological materials in the museum collected through systematic excavation rather than chance finds or donations, giving them particular scientific importance.

The core of the Dinajpur Museum's archaeological collection: 99 Hindu sculptures in black basalt and grey stone from the Pala and Sena periods (8th–13th centuries CE). The collection includes images of Vishnu, Shiva, Durga, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Ganesh, Surya, and Brahma, as well as attendant figures and narrative relief panels. These sculptures were recovered from fields, river banks, and demolished structures throughout Dinajpur district. Northern Bangladesh (Varendra) was one of the most productive centers of stone sculpture in the entire Bengal region during the Pala period, and the Dinajpur collection — though damaged during the 1971 Liberation War when many pieces were broken and looted — remains one of the most significant regional sculpture collections in Bangladesh.

Artifacts and documents from the Liberation War of 1971 and the post-war recovery, including photographs of the war's impact on Dinajpur, documents relating to the liberation struggle in northern Bangladesh, and objects representing the district's contribution to independence. The Dinajpur Museum was nearly completely destroyed during the 1971 Liberation War: stone sculptures were broken, metallic articles looted, and the collections severely damaged. The post-war recovery of the museum — with international support (a NORAD donation funded a new building in 1983–85) — is itself part of the museum's history. These artifacts document both the destruction and the resilience that characterizes the museum's story.

Artifact_Name: Pottery Collection — Medieval and Early Period
Description: A collection of pottery from the ancient to medieval periods recovered from archaeological sites in the Dinajpur District, including grey ware, red-slipped ware, black ware, and decorated earthenware. The pottery spans from the pre-Mauryan period through the Sultanate era and provides evidence for the continuous settlement of the Dinajpur region over two millennia. Different pottery traditions are associated with different cultural periods: the grey ware with the ancient period, the red-slipped ware with the Gupta era, and later wares with the Pala and Sultanate periods. The Dinajpur region's rich alluvial soil made it one of the most densely settled areas of ancient Bengal, and pottery is the most abundant and consistent evidence of that settlement.

Finding_Place: Central hall, Ethnological Museum, Agrabad, Chittagong
Description: A full-scale reconstructed model of a typical Chakma homestead, displayed beside the large wall map of ethnic group locations in the museum's central hall. The Chakma are the largest indigenous community of the Chittagong Hill Tracts, traditionally living in raised bamboo houses (machang) built on stilts above the ground for protection from flooding, wild animals, and dampness. The model shows the characteristic bamboo-platform construction, woven wall panels, and thatched roof of a traditional Chakma dwelling. This reconstruction is one of the most popular exhibits for visitors, providing an immersive, three-dimensional introduction to indigenous architecture that complements the museum's flat photographic and object displays.

Credit_Donor: Donated by Mro community / Dept. of Archaeology field collection
Description: A traditional dugout boat of the type used by the Murong (Mro) people of the Chittagong Hill Tracts, carved from a single large log. The Mro are one of the indigenous groups of the hill tracts, traditionally inhabiting the more remote hill areas and maintaining distinctive cultural practices including their own script (Mro script, invented in the 1980s) and animist-influenced religious traditions. This boat exhibit is highlighted among the museum's notable artifacts as a striking example of indigenous craftsmanship and the riverine and stream-based transportation systems essential to hill tract communities living in a landscape of steep terrain and numerous waterways.

Finding_Place: Chittagong Hill Tracts (Marma and Mro communities)
Credit_Donor: Donated by community members / field collection
Description: A showcase of silver ornaments worn by Marma and Murang (Mro) women of the Chittagong Hill Tracts, including necklaces, bangles, and headpieces. The Marma are the second-largest indigenous community of the hill tracts, with strong cultural and religious connections to Buddhist Myanmar (Burma), reflected in their ornament styles and Buddhist ritual objects. Silver jewelry is an important marker of social status and ethnic identity among hill tract communities, often passed down through generations and worn during festivals such as the Marma Sangrai (water festival) celebrating the Buddhist new year. The collection is one of the museum's notable exhibits, illustrating the metalworking and decorative traditions of the region's indigenous peoples.

Artifact_Name: Tipra (Tripura) Weapons and Daily Use Articles
Description: A display of weapons, tools, and articles of daily use belonging to the Tipra (Tripura) people, alongside specimens of their traditional writing, axes, scissors, baskets, and bamboo pipes. The Tripura are an indigenous community found in both the Chittagong Hill Tracts of Bangladesh and the neighboring Indian state of Tripura, with a Tibeto-Burman linguistic heritage and distinctive traditions of jhum (shifting) cultivation. The display documents the full range of material objects used in everyday Tripura life — from agricultural and craft tools to weapons used historically for hunting and defense — providing visitors with a comprehensive view of the community's traditional self-sufficient way of life in the hill terrain.

Artifact_Name: Manipuri Traditional Dress and Weaving Loom
Dimensions: Loom: various dimensions; dress: standard size
Description: A display of traditional Manipuri dresses alongside a working model of a Manipuri hand loom, representing the textile heritage of the Manipuri community concentrated in the Sylhet region of Bangladesh. The Manipuri people, who migrated to the Sylhet area from the historic kingdom of Manipur, are renowned for their weaving skills and distinctive dance traditions (Manipuri dance, particularly Ras Lila). The hand loom on display demonstrates the traditional weaving technology used to produce the intricately patterned Manipuri textiles, an important economic and cultural activity for the community. The exhibit reflects the museum's broader mission to represent ethnic groups from across Bangladesh, not only the Chittagong Hill Tracts.

Artifact_Name: Garo, Hajong, Dalu and Mandai Material Culture Display
Finding_Place: Mymensingh region (Garo, Hajong, Dalu, Mandai communities)
Description: A combined display representing the material culture of the Garo, Hajong, Dalu, and Mandai ethnic communities of the Mymensingh region of northern Bangladesh, including textiles, tools, and household items. The Garo are the largest of these communities and maintain a distinctive matrilineal social structure; the Hajong, Dalu, and Mandai are smaller groups with their own languages and cultural practices, often living in close proximity to the Garo in the hill and foothill zone bordering Meghalaya, India. This gallery section complements the larger collections devoted to the Chittagong Hill Tracts communities, ensuring the museum's stated goal of representing all 29 ethnic groups of Bangladesh, including those in regions far from Chittagong itself.

Artifact_Name: Santal, Oraon, Rajbangshi and Polia Artifacts — Rajshahi-Dinajpur Region
Finding_Place: Rajshahi-Dinajpur region (Santal, Oraon, Rajbangshi, Polia communities)
Description: Artifacts representing the Santal, Oraon, Rajbangshi, and Polia ethnic communities of the Rajshahi-Dinajpur region of northwestern Bangladesh. The Santal are one of the largest indigenous communities in South Asia, with a significant population in this border region; the Oraon are a Dravidian-speaking community originally from the Chota Nagpur plateau who migrated to work on tea estates and agricultural land in Bengal. The display includes agricultural tools, traditional dress items, and craft objects reflecting the agrarian lifestyle and distinct cultural traditions of these communities, who maintain identities separate from the majority Bengali population in this border region.

Artifact_Name: International Tribal Collection — Swat, Sindh, Punjab, Kafiristan
Finding_Place: Pakistan (Swat, Sindh, Punjab regions) and Kafiristan (Afghanistan)
Description: An international ethnographic collection acquired during the museum's early development, representing tribal communities of Swat, Sindh, and Punjab in present-day Pakistan, and the Kafiristan (Nuristan) region of Afghanistan. The collection includes silver ornaments of Swat, Sindh, and Punjab tribes, a model of a typical Punjabi woman, materials of daily use and photographs of Punjab and Kafiristan tribes, weapons of Swati tribes, and models depicting a Sindhi bride, mother, and child. This international dimension reflects the museum's origins in the pre-1971 period when Bangladesh (then East Pakistan) was part of a single Pakistani state, and the collection has been preserved as historically significant ethnographic material documenting cultures connected to the subcontinent's shared past.

Artifact_Name: Folk Articles of Bengali-Speaking Communities (1996 Gallery)
Description: Folk articles of the majority Bengali-speaking population of Bangladesh, displayed in a gallery added to the Ethnological Museum in 1996 to complement its primary focus on the country's smaller ethnic minority communities. The gallery includes everyday craft objects, textiles, and household items representative of mainstream Bengali rural folk culture. This addition reflects an evolution in the museum's mission: originally focused exclusively on tribal and minority ethnic groups, the institution expanded to provide a more complete ethnographic picture of Bangladesh's population by including the cultural practices of the Bengali-speaking majority alongside the indigenous and tribal communities that form the museum's core collection.

Period_Dating: Established with museum opening (1974), updated periodically
Finding_Place: Central hall, Ethnological Museum, Agrabad, Chittagong
Description: A large wall map of Bangladesh displayed in the central hall of the Ethnological Museum, showing the geographic distribution of all the country's ethnic groups across its various regions: the Chittagong Hill Tracts groups (Chakma, Marma, Tripura, Mrung, Bawm, Khyang, Khumi, Chak, Rakhine, Pankhoa), the Sylhet region groups (Khasia, Manipuri, Pangan, Patra), the Mymensingh region groups (Garo, Hajong, Dalu, Mandai, Cooch), the Rajshahi-Dinajpur region groups (Santal, Oraon, Rajbangshi, Polia), and the Jashore-Jhenaidah region groups (Buno, Bagdi). This orientation map is the conceptual centerpiece of the museum, helping visitors understand Bangladesh's ethnic diversity as a coherent geographic and cultural system before exploring the detailed regional galleries.

A collection of ancient and medieval coins from the Faridpur region, spanning the Bengal Sultanate through the Mughal and British colonial periods. Faridpur District is located on the fertile Padma river plain and has been inhabited and commercially active for many centuries. The coin collection documents the monetary history of the region through the successive political regimes that controlled it. Sultanate and Mughal coins reflect the area's integration into the Bengal provincial economy; British colonial coins document the transformations of the colonial era. The Faridpur region was also noted in the colonial period as the native area of several prominent Bengali political and cultural figures.

Archaeological finds from excavations and chance discoveries along the Padma River banks in Faridpur District, including terracotta pottery, fragments of terracotta figurines, and bronze objects. The Faridpur region's fertile delta landscape has been settled for millennia, and river erosion frequently exposes buried archaeological layers. The finds document the region's ancient and medieval settlement history and its participation in the wider cultural traditions of the Bengal delta. The Padma (upper course of the Ganges in Bangladesh) was one of the most important riverine trade routes in pre-modern Bengal, and Faridpur's location on its banks made it a significant settlement site.

Artifact_Name: Portrait and Documents — A.K. Fazlul Huq (Sher-e-Bangla)
Credit_Donor: Faridpur Museum collection / donated by family
Description: A portrait and documentation display of A.K. Fazlul Huq (1873–1962) — Sher-e-Bangla ('Tiger of Bengal'), the most celebrated political leader from the Faridpur region. Fazlul Huq was a barrister, politician, and statesman who served as Chief Minister of Bengal (1937–43) and Prime Minister of East Bengal / East Pakistan (1954). He introduced the Lahore Resolution (1940) that called for independent Muslim states in the Indian subcontinent, and as Chief Minister introduced the Debt Settlement Act that relieved indebted farmers — a transformative measure for the rural poor. The Faridpur Museum celebrates him as the region's greatest son and the broader Faridpur district's contribution to Bengal's political history.

Credit_Donor: Donated by local families and craft organizations
Description: A collection of traditional textile and craft objects from the Faridpur region, including examples of hand-woven cotton fabrics, bamboo and cane basketry, and clay pottery. The Faridpur division has a rich craft heritage rooted in its agricultural economy — cotton weaving, bamboo work, and pottery have been the primary craft traditions of its villages for centuries. The objects document the material culture of rural life in the Padma River delta and the skills of the artisan communities (weavers, potters, basket-makers) who have sustained these traditions. The collection serves as a record of craft traditions that are being rapidly displaced by factory-made goods.

Credit_Donor: Donated by freedom fighters and families
Description: A collection of Liberation War artifacts from Faridpur district, including photographs of local freedom fighters (muktijoddha), documents relating to the liberation struggle in the Faridpur region, and personal effects of local martyrs. Faridpur was part of Sector 8 of the 1971 Liberation War and saw significant guerrilla activity and Pakistani Army operations. The museum's Liberation War collection documents the local dimension of the independence struggle — the specific battles, resistance activities, and sacrifices of Faridpur's freedom fighters — and integrates them into the national narrative of the war. Personal testimonies from surviving freedom fighters have been collected and displayed alongside the artifacts.

Credit_Donor: Donated by folk musicians and cultural organizations
Description: Traditional musical instruments from the Faridpur region, including instruments associated with the region's rich folk music traditions. Faridpur is noted for its connection to Pallikabi (rural poet) Jasim Uddin (1903–1976) — one of the greatest folk poets of Bengal — and to the baul and devotional music traditions of the central Bengal delta. The collection includes a khamak (plucked drone instrument favored by baul singers), a dhol (double-headed drum), a harmonium, and a bamboo flute. A separate Pallikabi Jasim Uddin Museum (branch of Bangladesh National Museum) is also located in Faridpur and focuses specifically on the poet's legacy; the Faridpur Museum complements this with a broader regional cultural collection.

Artifact_Name: Agricultural Tools — Padma River Delta Farming
Description: Traditional agricultural tools from the Faridpur region's rice and jute farming tradition, including a wooden plough (hal), an iron sickle (kaste), a bamboo winnowing tray (kula), and a hand-woven paddy-carrying basket. The Faridpur delta plain is one of Bangladesh's most productive agricultural areas, and the region's farmers have developed specialized tools adapted to its alluvial soil, seasonal flooding, and crop varieties. These tools represent centuries of agricultural knowledge and adaptation. The collection is displayed alongside photographs of the farming cycle — land preparation, planting, harvesting, and threshing — and information panels on the cropping patterns of the Faridpur region.

Artifact_Name: Historical Photographs — Faridpur Town and District
Description: Historical photographs of Faridpur town and district from the late 19th century to the post-independence period, documenting the town's development, its notable buildings and institutions, and the changes in the landscape over more than a century. The photographs include images of the colonial-era Faridpur Collectorate, the historic riverfront, early educational institutions (Government Rajendra College was established in 1918), and scenes of rural life in the district. The photographic collection provides a visual history of Faridpur that complements the museum's artifact-based displays and serves as an irreplaceable documentary record of the district's built and natural heritage.

A Gazi pata — a traditional painted narrative scroll depicting the deeds of Gazi Pir, the Islamic folk saint worshipped by both Hindu and Muslim communities in Bengal. The scroll is painted in the folk style on a long strip of cloth, with sequential panels showing scenes from the Gazi legend: the saint's battles with crocodiles, his miraculous feats, and his veneration by devotees. The Gazi tradition blends Islamic sainthood (the pir concept) with indigenous Bengali nature worship and the crocodile cult of the Sundarbans region. The scroll is displayed as one of the most remarkable examples of Bengal's syncretic folk religion expressed through visual art. It is one of approximately 500 items in the Folk Heritage Museum's collection.

A nakshi kantha — a traditional embroidered quilt made from layers of old sari cloth stitched together with colored thread — from the Bangla Academy's folk art collection. The surface of this kantha is covered with a central lotus motif surrounded by concentric bands of stylized flora, birds, peacocks, and folk narrative scenes. Nakshi kantha-making is one of the most celebrated of Bengali folk arts, traditionally practiced by women in rural homes as a form of artistic expression and domestic craft. The Bangla Academy's Folk Heritage Museum has preserved outstanding examples of this tradition as part of its collection of approximately 500 folk art items.

A shataranji — a traditional hand-woven flat-weave cotton floor mat with bold geometric patterns in red, black, green, and white — from the Rangpur region, the center of Bangladesh's shataranji-weaving tradition. Shataranji is woven on a traditional floor loom using a discontinuous supplementary weft technique that creates the geometric surface patterns. The Rangpur shataranji industry dates back centuries and produces floor coverings, prayer mats, and decorative textiles. It is one of the crafts highlighted in the Folk Heritage Museum as a living tradition under pressure from cheaper machine-made alternatives. The museum displays both historic and contemporary examples to show the continuity and evolution of the craft.

A hand-painted rickshaw panel in the distinctive Dhaka style — the brightly colored, folk-painted back panel that is the most iconic form of urban folk art in Bangladesh. This example depicts a Bengali rural landscape: a river with sailing boats, coconut palms, birds in flight, and a village at dusk. The panel is painted in vivid enamel colors — red, green, blue, yellow — with confident, rapid brushwork. Rickshaw painting emerged as a distinct art form in Dhaka from the 1940s and developed its own visual vocabulary of nature scenes, film imagery, and Bengali cultural symbols. The Folk Heritage Museum's collection of rickshaw panels documents this unique intersection of folk tradition and modern urban culture.

A collection of traditional folk musical instruments from different regions of Bangladesh, including a dotara (two-string lute from the north), an ektara (single-string drone lute of the baul tradition), a dhol (barrel drum), a sarinda (bowed lute), a khamak (plucked drum), and a bamboo bashi (flute). Each instrument is associated with specific folk music traditions and communities: the ektara with baul singers, the dhol with festival percussion, the sarinda with the Bede (boat-dwelling) community. The collection represents the extraordinary diversity of folk musical traditions in Bangladesh — from the mystic songs of the bauls to the devotional music of the kirtan tradition and the boatmen's bhatiyali songs.

A collection of traditional Bengali folk ornaments including necklaces (hansuli — crescent collar necklace), bangles (shakha-pola — conch shell and red lacquer bangle set), anklets (nupur), nose rings (nath), and ear ornaments from different regions of Bangladesh. Traditional Bengali jewelry reflects regional variations in style and material — the distinctive nath and hansuli of the Rajshahi region, the glass bangles of Dhaka, and the silver work of the Chittagong Hill Tracts. The collection documents the material culture of adornment across social classes and communities in Bengali society, from everyday glass bangles worn by rural women to the elaborate silver jewelry of wealthier households.

Materials from the Language Movement Museum established within the Bangla Academy's Burdwan House — inaugurated by Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina on 1 February 2010. The collection includes book covers, photographs, and documents relating to the history and events of the 1952 Language Movement: the movement to establish Bengali as an official language of Pakistan. Exhibits include the cover of the booklet Pakistaner Rashtra Bhasha, photographs of the protests of 21 February 1952, and materials relating to the language martyrs who died when police fired on demonstrators. The Bangla Academy's location at Burdwan House — where literary and language movement activities were centered from the 1940s — makes it an appropriate home for this collection.

Artifact_Name: National Literature and Writers' Museum Display
Description: Exhibits from the National Literature and Writers' Museum established within Bangla Academy's Burdwan House, dedicated to the history of Bengali literature and its major figures. The display includes panels on the Muslim Sahitya-Samaj — a progressive literary group established in Dhaka in the 1920s — featuring portraits of its founders: Kazi Abdul Wadud, Abul Hussain, Qazi Motahar Hossain, Abul Fazal, and Abdul Quadir. The museum is open every day except government holidays from 11:00 am to 4:00 pm. It celebrates the institutional role of Bangla Academy in the development of Bengali language and literature and provides context for understanding Bangladesh's literary heritage.

Material: Fired earthenware, natural and commercial pigments
Finding_Place: Various regions of Bangladesh (Rajshahi, Comilla, Khulna)
Description: A collection of traditional folk pottery from different regions of Bangladesh, including the black clay pots (kalo mati shilpa) of Rajshahi, the decorative red-painted pots of Comilla, and the simple utilitarian pots of the Khulna region. Bengali folk pottery has a continuous tradition stretching back to the Neolithic period, and modern folk potters (kumors) maintain forms and techniques with ancient roots. The collection includes storage pots, water vessels, oil lamps, piggy banks (children's hundi), and molded animal figures. The Bangla Academy's folk pottery collection represents the diversity of Bangladesh's regional pottery traditions before the introduction of factory-made plastic and aluminium vessels displaced much of the traditional market.

Artifact_Name: Jamdani Fabric Sample — UNESCO Intangible Heritage
Description: A sample of authentic Dhakai Jamdani fabric — the hand-woven muslin textile decorated with discontinuous supplementary weft floral motifs, inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2013. The sample shows the characteristic gossamer-fine cotton ground with a white-on-white pattern of stylized flowers (buta motifs) distributed across the field. Jamdani weaving is centered in the Rupganj and Sonargaon areas of Narayanganj District near Dhaka and is one of the finest textile traditions in the world. The Bangla Academy's collection of Jamdani samples documents the tradition's evolution across the 20th century and celebrates it as a central element of Bangladesh's intangible cultural heritage.

Land deeds and estate records from the Jamalpur zamindari estate in Thakurgaon District — documents recording land tenure, tenant registers, and revenue records from the colonial-era zamindari system. The Jamalpur Estate was one of the zamindari estates of northern Bangladesh under the Permanent Settlement system (from 1793), collecting land revenues from cultivating tenants (raiyats). These documents are primary sources for the agrarian history of Thakurgaon District and for understanding the zamindari system that shaped rural Bengal's social structure until its abolition under the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act of 1950.

A teak wood dining table from the Jamalpur zamindari estate house — a solid, utilitarian piece with a plain top and turned legs, representing the domestic furniture of a provincial northern Bengal zamindari household. Unlike the marble-top tables of the grander Dhaka zamindars, this table is of simpler construction, reflecting the more modest means of a district-level estate. The table would have been used by the zamindar family for their daily meals and for official dinners with district administrators and notable guests. The furniture collection of the Jamalpur Estate Museum documents the domestic material culture of a provincial zamindari household in northern Bangladesh during the colonial period.

Artifact_Name: Iron Safe / Cash Box — Zamindari Estate
Description: A cast iron safe (tijori) from the Jamalpur zamindari estate, used to store cash, revenue receipts, and important documents. The safe has a hinged lid secured by a heavy steel lock mechanism with a key. Such iron safes were standard equipment in zamindari estate offices across Bengal, where the nayeb (estate manager) kept the daily revenue collections secure. The Jamalpur estate collected revenue from cultivating tenants across Thakurgaon District. This safe is a tangible artifact of that revenue collection system and of the physical security infrastructure that zamindari administration required.

Artifact_Name: Terracotta and Pottery — Thakurgaon Archaeological Finds
Description: Terracotta and pottery artifacts from the Thakurgaon region, recovered from agricultural fields and local excavations. The northern Bangladesh region of Thakurgaon (ancient Varendra area) has been settled since ancient times and archaeological finds including terracotta figurines, decorated bricks, and pottery fragments are regularly discovered during agricultural activities. The museum collects and displays these chance finds alongside systematic excavation materials, providing evidence for the ancient settlement history of the Thakurgaon area. The terracotta tradition of northern Bangladesh, centered in the Rajshahi-Dinajpur-Thakurgaon belt, is one of the oldest and most significant in the subcontinent.

Historical photographs documenting the heritage sites, notable buildings, and historical events of Thakurgaon District, including images of colonial-era buildings, estate houses, and local cultural events. Thakurgaon is the northernmost district of Bangladesh, bordering India on three sides, and has a distinctive heritage shaped by its geographic position and its history as a colonial-era district in the Bengal Presidency. The photographs document both the physical landscape of the district — its tea gardens, agricultural fields, and rivers — and its human heritage of communities and institutions.

Credit_Donor: Donated by local artisans and families
Description: Traditional folk craft objects from the northern Bangladesh region, including bamboo and cane basketry, hand-woven cotton textiles, and clay pottery. Northern Bangladesh has a distinctive craft tradition shaped by its proximity to the Bengal-Assam hill zones and its contact with tribal communities such as the Santal, Oraon, and other groups who inhabit the Barind region. The craft collection documents both the mainstream Bengali craft traditions and the influence of these neighboring communities on the material culture of the Thakurgaon area. The objects include everyday utilitarian items — baskets, cooking pots, storage containers — and more decorative pieces produced for festivals and ceremonies.

Artifact_Name: Liberation War Artifacts — Northern Bangladesh Sector
Credit_Donor: Donated by freedom fighters and families
Description: Liberation War artifacts and documentation from the northern Bangladesh sector of the 1971 war, including photographs of local freedom fighters, weapons and equipment used during guerrilla operations, and documents relating to the liberation of Thakurgaon District. The northernmost districts of Bangladesh — Thakurgaon, Panchagarh, Dinajpur — were part of Sector 7 of the Liberation War and were liberated in December 1971 during the final military offensive. The museum documents the local experience of the war and the specific contributions of Thakurgaon's freedom fighters to national independence.

Credit_Donor: Museum curatorial team / Thakurgaon District administration
Description: A display documenting the architecture of the Jamalpur estate house — the physical building that houses (or is associated with) the museum. The display includes measured drawings of the estate house's floor plan and elevation, historical photographs showing the building's condition at different periods, and architectural analysis of its style and construction. Estate houses (zamindar baris) of northern Bangladesh have a distinctive architectural character, combining colonial Neoclassical elements (columned verandas, arched windows) with traditional Bengali domestic spatial organization (courtyard plan, separate men's and women's sections). The Jamalpur Estate house is documented as a heritage building representing the zamindari architectural tradition of the Thakurgaon region.

Credit_Donor: Bangladesh National Museum / Kushtia cultural institutions
Description: A formal portrait of Kangal Harinath Majumdar (1833–1896) — poet, journalist, social reformer, and the founder of Gram Barta Prokashika (Rural News), the first Bengali-language newspaper published from rural Bengal (from 1863, Kumarkhali). Harinath was known as 'Kangal' (the destitute) reflecting his identification with the rural poor. He was a close associate and spiritual disciple of Lalon Shah (the great mystic poet) and also a mentor of the literary figures Akshay Kumar Maitreya and Jagadish Chandra Bose (the scientist). The portrait is the central exhibit of the memorial museum, which is a branch museum under Bangladesh National Museum established in 2013 in Harinath's home town.

Artifact_Name: Original Issues of Gram Barta Prokashika (Rural News)
Description: Reproductions and surviving original issues of Gram Barta Prokashika — the pioneering Bengali rural newspaper founded and edited by Kangal Harinath Majumdar, published from Kumarkhali from 1863. The newspaper was remarkable for its time: it was the first major newspaper published outside Calcutta in Bengali, and it focused on the grievances of rural farmers against the indigo planter system and the colonial administration. Harinath's courageous journalism exposed the exploitation of peasants by British indigo planters, a campaign that continued even when he faced personal threats. The newspaper is a landmark in the history of Bengali journalism and rural social reform.

Material: Cast iron, steel type (replica or period press)
Description: A hand-operated printing press of the type used at the Mathuranath Press — the printing establishment in Kumarkhali through which Harinath Majumdar published Gram Barta Prokashika and other works. The press represents the material infrastructure of 19th-century Bengali journalism in rural Bengal — the physical technology that enabled Harinath to disseminate his reformist message to rural readers. The Mathuranath Press was one of the earliest printing establishments outside Calcutta to publish a regular Bengali newspaper and played a significant role in the development of Bengali print culture beyond the urban center. The press display is accompanied by information on the history of Bengali printing and journalism.

Artifact_Name: Kangal Harinath's Published Works — First Editions
Description: First or early editions of the literary works of Kangal Harinath Majumdar, including his collections of baul-influenced devotional poems, his essays on social reform, and the publications of Gram Barta Prokashika. Harinath was not only a journalist but a poet in the baul tradition — he wrote devotional songs influenced by his spiritual relationship with Lalon Shah. His works represent the intersection of journalism, social reform, folk spirituality, and Bengali literary culture in 19th-century Kushtia. The book collection documents his output as a writer and thinker and contextualizes his journalism within a broader vision of social and spiritual transformation.

Artifact_Name: Connection to Lalon Shah — Display and Documents
Description: A display documenting the relationship between Kangal Harinath Majumdar and Lalon Shah (1774–1890) — the great mystic poet and baul philosopher who is one of the most celebrated figures in Bengali culture. Harinath was both a disciple of Lalon and his contemporary in the Kushtia region; he documented Lalon's life and songs at a time when Lalon's work was little known outside the immediate community. The Kushtia region — home to both Lalon Shah and Kangal Harinath — is one of the most culturally significant areas of Bangladesh, and this display explores the spiritual and intellectual relationships that made Kushtia a center of Bengali folk philosophy and reformist thought in the 19th century.

Artifact_Name: Connection to Jagadish Chandra Bose — Documents
Description: A display documenting Kangal Harinath's mentorship of Jagadish Chandra Bose (1858–1937) — the pioneering scientist who made fundamental contributions to physics and plant biology and is considered the father of Bengali science. Bose spent part of his childhood in Kumarkhali and was influenced by Harinath's intellectual example. The display includes photographs of Bose, facsimiles of correspondence, and text panels tracing the relationship between the village journalist and the future world-class scientist. This connection makes the Kangal Harinath Memorial Museum relevant not only to Bengali journalism and literature but to the history of science in South Asia.

Credit_Donor: Museum research / Bangladesh National Museum archives
Description: Documents and displays relating to Kangal Harinath Majumdar's journalistic campaign against the indigo planter system — the forced cultivation of indigo (neel) by Bengali peasants under British planters, which was one of the most brutal forms of economic exploitation in colonial Bengal. Harinath's Gram Barta Prokashika was one of the few newspapers to consistently champion the cause of the peasants against the planters and the colonial administration. The display includes facsimiles of newspaper articles exposing planter abuses, documents relating to the Indigo Revolt of 1859–60 (which occurred shortly before the newspaper's founding), and information on the social context of rural exploitation in the Kushtia-Nadia region.

Credit_Donor: Donated by Majumdar family descendants / Bangladesh National Museum
Description: Personal effects and household objects associated with Kangal Harinath Majumdar's life in Kumarkhali, donated by family descendants and the Bangladesh National Museum. The objects include writing implements, a personal seal, and household items from the period. These simple personal objects complement the intellectual and journalistic legacy displayed elsewhere in the museum, providing a human dimension to the reformist journalist's life. They are displayed alongside family photographs and biographical text panels in the main memorial gallery, which is designed as a personal memorial to Harinath rather than a purely historical display.

Artifact_Name: Princely Bust — Bharat Bhayana Excavation (5th–6th century CE)
Finding_Place: Bharat Rajar Deul (Bharat Bhayana), Jessore District
Description: A sandstone bust of a princely male figure recovered from the excavations at Bharat Rajar Deul (Bharat Bhayana) in Jessore District — one of the most significant archaeological sites in the Khulna Division. The site, associated with the legendary kingdom of King Bharat, yielded the substantial ruins of a brick-built structure and several stone sculptures including Hindu deity figures and busts of princely male figures, dated to approximately the 5th–6th century CE on stylistic grounds (Gupta period). The bust shows a young male with elaborate headdress and jewelry in the Gupta sculptural tradition. This Bharat Bhayana material forms one of the core collections of the Khulna Divisional Museum.

Artifact_Name: Hindu Deity Figures — Black Basalt Gallery
Description: A collection of black basalt Hindu deity sculptures from the Khulna Division, primarily recovered from the Jhenaidah District area (Barobazar site) and other excavations in the division. The deities represented include Shiva (lingam and anthropomorphic forms), Vishnu, Durga, and attendant figures in the Pala-Sena artistic tradition. The Khulna Division, though geographically distant from the primary Pala sculpture centers of northern Bangladesh, received the influence of this tradition through trade and religious patronage networks. The museum's sculpture gallery is one of its most visited sections, displaying what a local student described as 'hundreds of years old Shiva statues and mythological characters of Hinduism made by black basalt.'

Artifacts from the Barobazar archaeological site in Jhenaidah District — one of the most important Sultanate-period mosque complexes in southern Bangladesh. Barobazar contains the ruins of over a dozen mosques from the Bengal Sultanate period (15th–16th centuries), making it the largest concentration of Sultanate mosque ruins in southern Bengal. Artifacts include terracotta decorative panels, carved stone inscriptions, decorated bricks, and architectural fragments from the mosque walls and mihrabs. These materials are among the most significant Sultanate-period archaeological finds in the Khulna Division and form a major part of the museum's historical collection.

Artifact_Name: Gold and Silver Coins — Mughal Emperor Jahangir Period
Dimensions: Gold mohur ~22 mm; Silver rupee ~20 mm
Description: Gold and silver coins from the reign of Mughal Emperor Jahangir (1605–1627) — among the most prized numismatic items in the Khulna Divisional Museum. Jahangir's coins are famous for their fine portraiture and calligraphy; his gold mohurs sometimes bore unusual features including his own portrait (in violation of Islamic artistic conventions, reflecting his eclectic personality) or zodiac sign imagery. The coins recovered from the Khulna region document the area's integration into the Mughal monetary economy during the 17th century, when Dhaka was the Mughal provincial capital and the Bengal economy was at its most prosperous.

A dedicated gallery documenting the ecology and heritage of the Sundarbans — the world's largest mangrove forest, shared between Bangladesh (Khulna Division) and India (West Bengal), inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997. The display includes photographs of the Sundarbans ecosystem, specimens of mangrove plant species, maps of the forest, information on the Bengal Tiger (the Sundarbans Royal Bengal Tiger population is one of the world's largest), and displays on the traditional fishing and honey-collecting communities (bawalis and mawalis) who have lived in the Sundarbans for centuries. The Sundarbans Gallery is one of the museum's most distinctive features, celebrating the ecological heritage that defines the Khulna Division's global significance.

A collection of ancient and historical household utensils recovered from excavations and chance finds across the Khulna Division, as described by local visitors: old-time household materials including utensils, ornaments, and tools used by ancient landlords and ordinary communities. The collection spans from the early medieval period (iron tools, clay pots) through the Mughal era (brass and copper vessels) to the colonial period (enamel-ware and early industrial goods). These everyday objects complement the spectacular sculptural and numismatic collections and provide evidence for ordinary domestic life across the division's long history. Several items show the influence of trade with the Sundarbans communities — fishing weights, boat fittings, and forest-harvesting tools.

Credit_Donor: Bangladesh Liberation War archives / donated by freedom fighters
Description: A gallery of Liberation War photographs displayed at the entrance stairwell of the museum, showing historically important liberation sites and events from Khulna Division and broader Bangladesh. Khulna was a major theater of the 1971 Liberation War: the Khulna-Bagerhat-Satkhira region saw significant guerrilla operations and Pakistani Army actions. The photographs include images of liberation sites, freedom fighter groups, the liberation of Khulna, and the post-war reconstruction. The museum positions these photographs at the main entrance to ensure every visitor encounters the liberation narrative as the foundational context for understanding Bangladesh's present.

Artifact_Name: Terracotta Objects — Gupta and Medieval Period
Description: Terracotta objects from Gupta and medieval period excavations in the Khulna Division, including decorated plaques, figurine fragments, and architectural terracotta pieces. The Khulna Division's terracotta heritage is concentrated in the Jhenaidah and Jessore districts, where pre-Sultanate Hindu and Buddhist communities produced terracotta objects in the Bengal tradition. The Bharat Bhayana site in particular yielded significant terracotta material alongside the stone sculptures. These objects document the artistic traditions of southern Bengal in the pre-Islamic period and provide the cultural context for the later Sultanate mosque-building that transformed the region's religious landscape.

Artifact_Name: Copper, Iron and Glass Objects — Historical Collection
Finding_Place: Khulna Division (Bharat Bhayana, Barobazar, other sites)
Description: A mixed collection of copper, iron, brass, clay, and glass objects from archaeological excavations and finds across the Khulna Division, spanning from the Gupta period to the British colonial era. The collection includes copper plates, iron tools and weapons, brass vessels, clay figurines and pots, and glass bangles and beads. As a divisional museum, Khulna displays material from the full geographic range of the division — from the Sundarbans coastal zone to the inland agricultural districts of Jhenaidah, Narail, and Bagerhat. The diversity of the collection reflects the varied ecological and historical contexts of these different areas within the single administrative division.

Artifact_Name: Khan Jahan Ali Heritage Display — Bagerhat Connection
Description: A display documenting the heritage of Khan Jahan Ali and the historic Mosque City of Bagerhat — a UNESCO World Heritage Site in Khulna Division. Khan Jahan Ali (d. 1459) was the Muslim saint-administrator who established the city of Khalifatabad (modern Bagerhat) in the 15th century and built the famous Sixty-Domed Mosque (Shat Gambuj Masjid) — the largest mosque in Bangladesh. Artifacts from excavations at Bagerhat are displayed alongside photographs and architectural documentation. The display connects the Khulna museum to the broader Islamic heritage of the division, from the Sultanate period mosque-building at Barobazar to the magnificent monument complex of Bagerhat.

Archaeological finds recovered from the Kishoreganj district, a region characterized by its extensive haor (seasonal wetland) basins in the Mymensingh-Sylhet borderland. The finds include terracotta pottery fragments, ancient coins, and bronze object fragments, recovered from elevated settlement mounds that rise above the flood-prone haor landscape. Kishoreganj's distinctive geography — vast wetlands that flood for half the year and become agricultural land in the dry season — has shaped a unique pattern of ancient and medieval settlement on raised ground, and the artifacts document the continuous habitation of these settlement islands across many centuries.

Artifact_Name: Portrait and Memorabilia — Begum Sufia Kamal Connection
Description: A display honoring the connections between Kishoreganj district and notable Bengali literary and cultural figures associated with the region, including documentation of literary and educational contributions from the district. Kishoreganj has produced several important figures in Bengali cultural and political life, and the museum's Notable Personalities Gallery situates the district's contribution to the broader currents of Bengali intellectual and political history within the specific context of its haor-region geography and agrarian society.

Artifact_Name: Traditional Boat Models — Haor Region Watercraft
Credit_Donor: Constructed by museum craftspeople / local boatbuilders
Description: A collection of scale models of traditional boats used in the Kishoreganj haor region, including the distinctive narrow, swift boats used for racing during the monsoon season and the broader cargo boats used to transport goods and people across the flooded wetlands. Kishoreganj's haor basins — including the renowned Nikli, Mithamoin, and Itna haors — transform the district into a vast inland sea for several months each year, making boats the essential and often only means of transportation for entire communities. The museum's boat collection documents this distinctive water-based way of life that defines much of Kishoreganj's regional identity.

Credit_Donor: Donated by freedom fighters and families
Description: Liberation War artifacts and documentation from Kishoreganj district, including photographs of local freedom fighters, documents relating to resistance activities, and personal effects of local martyrs of the 1971 war. Kishoreganj, part of the greater Mymensingh region during the war, saw significant guerrilla resistance activity, with the haor landscape providing both challenges and strategic advantages for resistance fighters operating in difficult-to-access wetland terrain. The museum's Liberation War collection documents the specific local contribution of Kishoreganj's freedom fighters to the national independence struggle.

Artifact_Name: Folk Musical Instruments — Haor Region Traditions
Credit_Donor: Donated by folk musicians and cultural organizations
Description: Traditional musical instruments associated with the folk culture of the Kishoreganj haor region, including instruments used in bhatiyali (boatmen's songs) and other water-based musical traditions specific to communities whose lives are organized around the seasonal flooding cycle. The haor region's musical culture reflects its unique relationship to water: songs traditionally sung by fishermen, boatmen, and farmers navigating the transition between dry-season agriculture and wet-season boat travel. The collection includes a dotara, a dhol, and bamboo flutes used by haor-region folk performers.

Agricultural tools specifically adapted to the haor farming cycle of Kishoreganj district, including a single-crop rice cultivation toolkit suited to the brief dry-season window when haor land is exposed for farming before the monsoon floods return. The tools include a specialized plough, harvesting implements designed for rapid use before flooding, and storage equipment for protecting the harvest from water damage. Haor agriculture is one of the most distinctive farming systems in Bangladesh, requiring precise timing and specialized knowledge to successfully grow a single annual boro rice crop in the brief window between flood seasons.

Artifact_Name: Historical Photographs — Kishoreganj Town and Haor Landscape
Description: Historical photographs documenting Kishoreganj town and the surrounding haor landscape across different seasons, showing the dramatic transformation of the district from a dry agricultural plain to a vast inland sea each monsoon. The photographs include images of the famous Nikli, Mithamoin, and Itna haor areas, traditional haor village architecture (homes built on elevated earthen platforms to survive flooding), and scenes of community life adapted to this unique hydrological cycle. The photographic collection documents one of Bangladesh's most visually striking and ecologically distinctive regional landscapes.

Traditional fishing equipment used by Kishoreganj's haor-region fishing communities, including large seine nets for communal fishing during the flood season, bamboo fish traps, and specialized equipment for the rich seasonal fish harvest that the haors produce when they flood. Fishing in the haor region is both a subsistence activity for local communities and a significant commercial industry, with the flooded wetlands supporting large populations of native fish species. The collection documents the traditional ecological knowledge developed by generations of haor-region fishing communities to harvest this seasonal aquatic resource sustainably.

Material: Gourd, bamboo, metal string, animal skin
Credit_Donor: Donated by baul community and Lalon Academy
Description: A collection of traditional baul musical instruments from the Kushtia region — the heartland of the baul tradition associated with the mystic poet Lalon Shah (1774–1890). The collection includes an ektara (one-string gourd lute), a dotara (two-string melody lute), a khamak (plucked drum), and a dugdugi (small hourglass drum). Kushtia is the center of Bangladesh's baul tradition, and its instruments are UNESCO-recognized Intangible Cultural Heritage. Lalon Shah's shrine at Chheuriya, Kumarkhali draws thousands of devotees annually. The museum's baul instrument collection celebrates Kushtia's identity as the spiritual capital of baul music and philosophy.

Material: Photographic print / painted portrait; personal effects
Credit_Donor: Donated by Lalon Akademy and Kushtia cultural institutions
Description: A portrait and display of memorabilia associated with Lalon Shah (1774–1890) — Bangladesh's most celebrated mystic poet and baul philosopher, born and buried in Chheuriya, Kumarkhali, Kushtia District. Lalon's songs (Lalon geeti) are among the most profound expressions of Bengali spiritual philosophy, drawing on Hindu, Islamic, and Buddhist traditions while transcending all sectarian boundaries. He wrote over 2,000 songs exploring the relationship between the individual soul and the divine, challenging caste, religious prejudice, and social hierarchy. The museum's Lalon display complements the larger Lalon Academy (Lalon Akademy) in Chheuriya and serves as an introduction to the philosopher-poet for visitors to Kushtia town.

Credit_Donor: Donated by Kushtia cultural institutions / Tagore family archives
Description: Documents and photographs relating to Rabindranath Tagore's long association with Kushtia District — where his family owned the Shilaidaha Kuthibari estate (now a protected museum). Tagore spent extended periods at Shilaidaha between 1891 and 1901, managing his family's zamindari estate on the Padma River, and wrote some of his greatest poetry here, including most of Gitanjali (the collection that won him the 1913 Nobel Prize for Literature). The Kushtia Museum's Tagore collection complements the Shilaidaha Kuthibari Museum and situates Tagore's Kushtia years within the broader cultural history of the district. Photographs show the Shilaidaha house, the Padma River, and scenes of village life that inspired Tagore's work.

Archaeological finds from the Kushtia region, including terracotta pottery, figurine fragments, ancient coins, and stone artifacts recovered from fields and river banks. The Kushtia District encompasses part of the ancient Gangetic Bengal delta where settlement has been continuous for millennia. The Mathabanga and Gorai rivers that flow through Kushtia were important ancient trade routes, and archaeological finds from their banks document the area's participation in the broader cultural traditions of Bengal from the ancient period through the Mughal era.

Credit_Donor: Donated by weaving community and cultural organizations
Description: Examples of traditional woven textiles from the Kushtia region, representing the district's craft heritage. The Kushtia-Rajshahi zone has a significant tradition of silk weaving, and the Jamdani tradition of fine cotton weaving has practitioners in the region. The textile samples displayed include both everyday cotton fabrics and more elaborate woven pieces, showing the range of the district's weaving tradition. The collection is displayed alongside information on the social organization of weaving communities and the impact of industrial textile production on traditional handloom weavers.

Credit_Donor: Donated by freedom fighters and families
Description: A collection of Liberation War artifacts and documents from Kushtia District. Kushtia has a notable place in the history of the Liberation War: it was one of the first places where Bangladesh Radio broadcast the independence declaration (from Kalurghat, though also relayed from Kushtia area), and the freedom fighters of the Kushtia-Jhenaidah area fought significant early actions against the Pakistani Army. The collection includes photographs of local freedom fighters, documents relating to liberation activities in the district, and personal effects of martyrs. The display is presented as a tribute to the freedom fighters of Kushtia and contextualizes the district's contribution to national independence.

Artifact_Name: Traditional Household Objects — Kushtia Rural Life
Description: Traditional household objects from the rural villages of Kushtia District, including brass cooking vessels (handi, karahi), clay water pots (kalshi), bamboo grain storage containers (dhamer bhar), and wooden kitchen implements. These everyday objects represent the material culture of Bengali village life in the Kushtia region — the tools and vessels used for cooking, water storage, and food preparation in a typical rural household. The collection serves as a material history of domestic life in Kushtia, complementing the more famous cultural legacy of Lalon Shah and Kangal Harinath with a record of ordinary everyday life in the district.

A collection of Mughal miniature paintings displayed in the Lalbagh Fort — the museum housed in the Hammam (bathhouse / bathing palace) attached to the Diwan-i-Aam of the fort. The paintings include court scenes, hunting scenes, and portrait studies in the Mughal painting tradition. Mughal miniature painting reached Bengal during the reign of Aurangzeb and his governors in Dhaka; the paintings displayed at Lalbagh represent the artistic culture of the court that built and occupied the fort. The Lalbagh Fort is described as housing Mughal-era artifacts including miniature paintings alongside coins, carpets, calligraphy, swords, and firearms.

Material: Ink on paper / cloth, gold highlights
Description: Calligraphy panels in the Mughal tradition displayed in the Lalbagh Fort. The panels feature Arabic and Persian text in various calligraphic styles — naskh, nasta'liq, and thuluth — including Quranic verses, religious phrases, and possibly poetic verses. Calligraphy was the highest art form in the Islamic tradition, and Mughal governors and nobles patronized master calligraphers whose work decorated court buildings and movable artworks alike. The calligraphy panels at Lalbagh provide evidence of the artistic and literary culture of the 17th-century Mughal court in Bengal and complement the architectural calligraphy found on the Pari Bibi tomb within the fort complex.

Artifact_Name: Mughal Swords and Firearms — Arms Collection
Description: A collection of Mughal-period swords and firearms displayed in the Lalbagh Fort. The swords include straight double-edged swords and curved single-edged swords (shamshir) of the Mughal cavalry type, with steel blades and hilts of iron or brass. The firearms include a flintlock musket and a matchlock pistol of the type carried by Mughal infantry and cavalry in the 17th–18th centuries. These weapons represent the military power of the Mughal governors of Bengal who built and occupied Lalbagh Fort. The fort was constructed by Prince Muhammad Azam (later Emperor) from 1678 during his governorship of Bengal, as a royal residence and administrative complex; military equipment was an essential element of such a compound.

Dimensions: Silver rupee ~20 mm; Gold mohur ~22 mm
Description: Mughal coins from the Dhaka (Jahangirnagar) mint, displayed as numismatic evidence of Dhaka's importance as the Mughal provincial capital of Bengal. The coins bear the mint name 'Dar-ul-zarb Jahangirnagar' — confirming Dhaka's role as a major coin-producing center. Silver rupees, gold mohurs, and copper falus from the Aurangzeb period (1658–1707 CE) are the most relevant to the fort's construction period. These coins were the currency of the city that surrounded Lalbagh Fort and of the fort's own garrison and administration. The numismatic collection provides a direct material link to the economic life of 17th-century Dhaka.

Artifact_Name: Pari Bibi Tomb Documentation — Architectural Survey
Description: Documentation and material samples relating to the Tomb of Pari Bibi (Bibi Pari) — the most architecturally significant structure within the Lalbagh Fort complex and one of the finest examples of Mughal architecture in Bangladesh. Pari Bibi was the daughter of Shaista Khan (the Mughal Subahdar of Bengal after Prince Azam's departure) and the fiancée of Prince Azam; she died during construction of the fort, and her death caused Shaista Khan to consider the fort inauspicious and abandon its completion. The tomb is a square structure with white marble cladding, black basalt detailing, and glazed tile mosaic floors. Material samples from the tomb — including marble and tile fragments — are displayed alongside photographs and architectural drawings.

Pottery and ceramic artifacts recovered from excavations within the Lalbagh Fort compound, including glazed earthenware bowls and Chinese-import celadon-type pieces that reflect the cosmopolitan material culture of the Mughal court in 17th-century Dhaka. The fort's occupation period (from 1678 onward) is well-documented by pottery, which provides evidence for the use of the different spaces within the fort complex. Chinese porcelain was imported to the Mughal court of Bengal in large quantities; fragments of these prestigious wares found in fort excavations confirm the elevated social status of the compound's inhabitants. The pottery collection complements the architectural and artifact displays in the museum.

Artifact_Name: Mughal Textile Fragments — Carpet and Fabric
Description: Textile fragments including a carpet fragment and silk fabric samples from the Mughal period, displayed as evidence of the luxurious material culture of the Mughal court in Bengal. Mughal carpets — woven in Persia, Central Asia, and later in imperial Indian workshops — were essential furnishings of Mughal royal and administrative buildings. The Diwan-i-Aam (Hall of Public Audience) at Lalbagh Fort, where the governor held public court, would have been furnished with carpets and fine textiles. The fragments displayed provide evidence of the textile culture of the 17th-century Mughal court in Dhaka and complement the miniature paintings and calligraphy in presenting a picture of the court's artistic life.

Documentation of the Hammam (Turkish-style bathhouse) that houses the Lalbagh Fort — described as 'the only structure within Lalbagh Fort that is fully accessible to visitors.' The Hammam is a single-storied structure attached to the west of the Diwan-i-Aam, built in the Mughal period as a private bathing facility for the governor and court. It features the characteristic Mughal hammam layout with heated floors (through a hypocaust system), a dressing room, and bathing chambers. Documentation includes measured drawings of the floor plan, photographs of the interior before and after conservation, and samples of the original tile and plaster finishes. The Hammam is a rare surviving example of Mughal domestic architecture in Bangladesh.

Artifact_Name: Fort Construction History Display — Prince Muhammad Azam
Description: An educational display documenting the construction history of Lalbagh Fort — begun in 1678 CE by Prince Muhammad Azam, son of Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb, during his governorship of Bengal. The fort (also known as Fort Aurangabad) was intended to be a royal residence and administrative complex but was left unfinished when Azam was recalled to the Deccan by his father. His successor Shaista Khan abandoned the project after the death of his daughter Pari Bibi, considering the fort inauspicious. The display includes maps of the fort's layout, architectural plans, photographs of all major structures (Diwan-i-Aam, Pari Bibi's Tomb, the Three-Domed Mosque), and a timeline of the fort's construction and subsequent history as a protected monument.

Replica documents from the governorship of Shaista Khan (1664–1688) — the most celebrated of the Mughal Subahdars of Bengal and the administrator who continued work at Lalbagh Fort after Prince Azam's departure. Shaista Khan's governorship is remembered as a golden age for Dhaka: he reportedly reduced the price of rice to such a low level that it became a proverb ('Shaista Khaner amol' — the age of Shaista Khan — means a time of prosperity). He also built the Choto Katra caravanserai, the Sat Gambuj Mosque, and extended Dhaka's defenses. The documents include facsimiles of imperial farmans (orders), revenue records, and correspondence that illuminate the administration of Mughal Bengal from Dhaka.

Material: Metal, gas flame mechanism, stone inscription
Period_Dating: Established 1996 CE (original site); relocated to new building
Finding_Place: Liberation War Museum entrance, Agargaon, Dhaka
Description: The Eternal Flame (Shikha Chirantan) burns continuously at the entrance of the Liberation War Museum, accompanied by a stone inscription bearing the museum's founding vow: 'In the name of the moon and sun on the sky, in the name of the blood-stained soil of Bengal, we vow not to forget any of our martyrs, any event of our history.' The flame is the symbolic threshold of the museum, marking the transition from ordinary city life into the solemn commemorative space dedicated to the approximately three million people who died and the untold numbers who suffered during the nine-month Liberation War of 1971. It has burned continuously since the museum's original 1996 inauguration at Segunbagicha.

Artifact_Name: Gallery of Heroes — Martyred Intellectuals Exhibit
Finding_Place: Various locations, Dhaka and across Bangladesh
Credit_Donor: Donated by families of martyred intellectuals
Description: An exhibit dedicated to the Martyred Intellectuals of 1971 — the systematic killing of Bengali doctors, professors, writers, journalists, and other intellectuals carried out by the Pakistani Army and local collaborators (Al-Badr militia) in the final days of the war, most notoriously on 14 December 1971, just two days before the surrender. The exhibit displays photographs, personal belongings, and biographical documents of murdered intellectuals, presenting this targeted intellectual genocide as a calculated attempt to cripple the new nation's leadership capacity. The 'Gallery of Heroes' is among the most emotionally powerful and frequently cited sections of the museum by visitors.

Credit_Donor: Liberation War Museum Trust / government archives
Description: Documents and materials relating to the Declaration of Independence of Bangladesh, proclaimed on 26 March 1971 following the Pakistani Army's crackdown (Operation Searchlight) launched the previous night. The collection includes materials relating to Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's declaration and Major Ziaur Rahman's radio broadcast of the declaration from the Kalurghat radio transmission center near Chittagong. These documents mark the formal beginning of Bangladesh's nine-month armed struggle for independence and are among the most historically significant items in the museum's collection of over 21,000 artifacts.

Material: Photographic prints, newspaper clippings, eyewitness accounts
Finding_Place: Dhaka (University of Dhaka, Old Dhaka, Rajarbagh)
Credit_Donor: Liberation War Museum Trust / journalist and survivor donations
Description: Photographic and documentary evidence of the genocide launched by the Pakistani Army on the night of 25 March 1971 under the codename Operation Searchlight, which targeted the University of Dhaka (killing students and faculty including at Jagannath Hall and Iqbal Hall), the Rajarbagh Police Line, and predominantly Hindu neighborhoods of Old Dhaka. The exhibit presents photographs taken by journalists who managed to document the attacks, newspaper reports from the period, and survivor testimonies. This material forms the evidentiary foundation for understanding the scale and systematic nature of the violence that triggered the full Liberation War.

Artifact_Name: Refugee Crisis Photographs — 1971 Exodus to India
Finding_Place: Border regions, India-Bangladesh frontier and refugee camps
Description: Photographs documenting the massive refugee crisis of 1971, in which an estimated 10 million Bengalis fled across the border into India to escape the violence of the war, creating one of the largest refugee movements in modern history. The images show refugee columns on roads, makeshift camps in West Bengal, Tripura, and Assam, and the humanitarian response from international organizations and the Indian government. This refugee crisis became a major factor in galvanizing international attention and eventually Indian military intervention in December 1971, contributing directly to Bangladesh's liberation.

Artifact_Name: Weapons of the Liberation War — Mukti Bahini Arms
Credit_Donor: Donated by veteran freedom fighters and their families
Description: A collection of weapons used by the Mukti Bahini (the Bangladeshi guerrilla and regular forces) during the Liberation War, including rifles, grenades, and improvised weapons used by the resistance forces who fought a combination of guerrilla and conventional warfare against the Pakistani Army across the nine sectors of the war. The weapons are displayed alongside maps of the sector organization of the resistance and information on the formation and command structure of the Mukti Bahini, which grew from scattered initial resistance by EPR and Bengal Regiment defectors into an organized force that, with Indian military support, achieved victory in December 1971.

Artifact_Name: Personal Belongings of Freedom Fighters and Victims
Credit_Donor: Donated by families of freedom fighters and war victims
Description: Personal belongings of freedom fighters and victims of the 1971 war, including clothing, identification cards, letters, and personal effects, collected through the museum's crowd-funded, citizen-led collection effort since its founding. As 'the outcome of a citizens' effort,' the museum has relied on the general public coming forward with artifacts, including personal belongings and even human remains, to build its collection of more than 21,000 items. These deeply personal objects humanize the statistical scale of the war's casualties (estimated at up to three million deaths) by connecting visitors to specific individuals and families affected by the conflict.

Material: Facsimile of original instrument of surrender
Finding_Place: Race Course Ground (now Suhrawardy Udyan), Dhaka
Credit_Donor: Liberation War Museum Trust / government archives
Description: A facsimile of the Instrument of Surrender signed on 16 December 1971 at the Race Course Ground in Dhaka, by which Lieutenant General A. A. K. Niazi of the Pakistani Eastern Command surrendered to the Joint Command of Bangladesh and Indian forces under Lieutenant General Jagjit Singh Aurora. This document marks the formal end of the nine-month Liberation War and the birth of independent Bangladesh. The surrender is commemorated annually as Victory Day (Bijoy Dibosh) on 16 December, and its documentation forms the climactic conclusion to the museum's chronological gallery sequence, which begins with Bengali heritage and colonial-era resistance and ends with this moment of national triumph.

Artifact_Name: Pre-1971 Heritage Gallery — Bengali Resistance to British Rule
Description: Materials from the museum's first gallery, which exhibits the heritage of the Bengali people and their historical struggle against British colonial rule, providing essential historical context for the 1971 war. This gallery situates the Liberation War within a longer narrative of Bengali political resistance, beginning with opposition to British rule and continuing through the partition of 1947 and the subsequent grievances under Pakistani rule (1947–1971) documented in Gallery 2. By beginning the museum's narrative arc more than two centuries before 1971, the curators position the Liberation War as the culmination of a long historical process of Bengali political self-assertion.

Artifact_Name: Library and Study Center Archive — War Documentation
Credit_Donor: Liberation War Museum Trust research program
Description: The Liberation War Museum's library and study center, containing books, magazines, periodicals, and other research materials about the Bangladesh Liberation War and the broader history of Bangladesh.
