The library supports the museum's educational mission and serves researchers, students, and the general public seeking deeper engagement with the war's history beyond the exhibition galleries. The museum also operates a mobile mini-museum that travels to schools across different regions of Bangladesh, extending its educational reach to communities and young people who may not be able to visit the Dhaka facility, fulfilling the institution's mission to ensure that the memory of the Liberation War is transmitted to future generations.

A nakshi kantha from the Lokayon Museum collection — one of the museum's examples of Bangladesh's most celebrated folk textile art. The word 'lokayon' itself means 'folk world' or 'folk culture' in Bengali, and the museum's mission is the systematic collection and preservation of objects from the material culture of ordinary Bengali life. This kantha exemplifies that mission: a quilt made from old sari cloth by a rural woman, transformed through embroidery into a work of art. The patterns include a central sun motif surrounded by floral and animal borders. Lokayon Museum collects folk objects that would otherwise be discarded or lost, preserving the creative heritage of ordinary people alongside the monumental heritage of elite culture.

Credit_Donor: Donated by kumor (potter) communities / museum field collection
Description: A collection of folk pottery from the kumor (potter) communities of Bangladesh, including ritual objects (mangal ghat — auspicious water pots, Lakshmi and Shiva figurines), household vessels (kalshi, handi, patil), and decorative pieces (painted clay horses and elephants). The kumor caste has been producing pottery in Bengal for thousands of years, maintaining techniques and forms with ancient continuity while adapting to changing markets and tastes. Lokayon Museum's pottery collection represents multiple regional traditions: the red-washed pottery of Comilla, the black pottery of Rajshahi, and the white-painted pieces of Sylhet. The collection documents a craft tradition under severe economic pressure from factory-made alternatives.

Material: Enamel paint on metal; wood carvings
Finding_Place: Dhaka and other cities of Bangladesh
Description: A collection of decorated transport objects representing Bangladesh's unique tradition of painted and decorated public vehicles, including rickshaw back panels, hand-pulled cart decorations, and cycle van adornments. Rickshaw art is Bangladesh's most distinctive urban folk art form, transforming functional vehicles into mobile artworks through bright enamel painting, tinsel decorations, and narrative imagery. The collection includes panels depicting landscapes, animals, film stars, historical events, and religious imagery. Lokayon Museum collects rickshaw art as a legitimate and important folk art tradition that captures the intersection of urban culture, folk imagery, and popular aesthetics in Bangladesh's cities.

Artifact_Name: Agricultural and Domestic Tools — Rural Life Collection
Credit_Donor: Museum field collection from rural Bangladesh
Description: A comprehensive collection of agricultural and domestic tools representing the material culture of rural life in Bangladesh, including wooden ploughs (hal), iron sickles (kaste), bamboo winnowing trays (kula), paddy-husking mortars (dheki), spinning wheels (chakra), and weaving implements. These are the tools of everyday life and labor in the Bengali village — the instruments with which rice was grown and processed, cloth was woven, and households were maintained. The Lokayon Museum collects these 'ordinary' objects with the same care as more prestigious art objects, recognizing that the history of ordinary people is as important as the history of kings and aristocrats.

Artifact_Name: Traditional Games and Toys — Children's Folk Culture
Description: A collection of traditional children's games and toys from rural and urban Bangladesh, including clay dolls (mati putul), wooden spinning tops (lattu), bamboo kites (ghuri), marbles (golok), a bamboo hobby horse, and cloth rag dolls. Traditional Bengali children's toys are a significant but often overlooked category of folk craft, made by parents and toy-makers using locally available materials. The collection documents the play culture of Bengali children before the dominance of plastic factory toys and preserves evidence of the skills and imagination involved in handmade toy production. Several of the toys are associated with specific festivals — kites with Sakrain, marbles with the monsoon season.

Artifact_Name: Fishing Equipment — Inland Water Folk Culture
Credit_Donor: Donated by fishing communities / museum field collection
Description: Traditional fishing equipment from the inland water fishing communities of Bangladesh, including a polo (conical bamboo trap), a chaluni (cylindrical wicker trap), a bana (bamboo basket trap), a jhaki jal (cast net), and a traditional baited line. Bangladesh's extensive network of rivers, haors, beels, and floodplains supports a vast inland fishing tradition, and the tools used are adapted to the specific conditions of each water body. The Lokayon Museum collects fishing equipment as evidence of the traditional ecological knowledge of Bangladesh's fishing communities — knowledge that is increasingly under threat from overfishing and habitat loss.

Credit_Donor: Donated by folk artists / museum field collection
Description: Traditional folk musical instruments and performance artifacts from Bangladesh's diverse folk music traditions, including instruments associated with jatra (folk theater), kirtan (devotional music), baul (mystic song), and bhatiyali (boatmen's songs). The collection includes a khol (barrel drum for kirtan), a jhanjh (finger cymbals), a sarod-type bowed lute (sarangi), and a bamboo pungi (snake-charmer's instrument). Folk performance is central to the cultural life of rural Bangladesh, marking festivals, life events, and seasonal celebrations. The Lokayon Museum documents these performance traditions as living heritage and collects their material artifacts to preserve evidence of their practice.

Credit_Donor: Donated by communities / museum field collection
Description: A collection of traditional ornaments and body decoration items from different communities across Bangladesh, including the distinctive conch-shell bangles (shakha) and red lacquer bangles (pola) of Bengali Hindu married women, the glass bangle sets of Muslim women, silver anklets, nose rings of different regional styles, and the shell and bead ornaments of tribal communities. The collection represents the diversity of body adornment traditions across Bangladesh's social and religious communities and documents the craft skills of the specialist artisans — shankhari (conch-shell craftsmen), mali (garland makers), and silver-smiths — who produce these objects. The shakha-pola bangle set is among the most culturally loaded objects in Bengali folk culture, inseparable from the identity of a married Hindu woman.

Artifact_Name: Photograph Album — Mohammad Ali with World Leaders
Material: Silver gelatin photographic prints, bound album
Description: A bound photograph album documenting Mohammad Ali of Bogra (Mohammad Ali Bogra, 1909–1963) — Prime Minister of Pakistan from 1953 to 1955 — in meetings with world leaders including Queen Elizabeth II, U.S. President John F. Kennedy, and Indian Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru. Mohammad Ali Bogra was the grandson of Nawab Altaf Ali and a member of the prominent Nawab family of Bogra. His premiership came during a critical early period of Pakistani statehood, and his international diplomatic engagements placed Bogra's Nawab family at the center of South Asian and global politics in the 1950s. The album is one of the centerpiece exhibits of the museum, illustrating the family's national and international significance.

A collection of coins dating to the East India Company period (1757–1858), preserved as part of the Nawab family's historical collection at the Palace Museum. The coins include Company-issued sicca rupees and subsidiary copper coinage that circulated in Bengal during the era when the Bogra Nawab family's predecessors were establishing their position as a prominent zamindari and administrative family in northern Bengal. The coin collection reflects the family's nearly two-century continuous presence in Bogra and their participation in the colonial-era economy as substantial landholders and, later, government officials.

A collection of antique guns from the Nawab family's historical armory, including flintlock and percussion-cap firearms typical of 19th-century Bengal zamindari households. As a prominent landowning family with administrative responsibilities, the Bogra Nawabs maintained arms for personal security, hunting, and ceremonial display. The firearms collection is displayed in the historic Nawab Palace alongside other artifacts of the family's elite domestic life, illustrating the material culture of a northern Bengal nawabi household across multiple generations leading up to Mohammad Ali Bogra's 20th-century political prominence.

Material: Printed paper, leather and cloth binding
Description: A collection of rare books, approximately 100 years old, preserved from the personal library of the Bogra Nawab family. The collection includes works of Bengali and English literature, religious texts, and reference works that reflect the educated, cosmopolitan character of the Nawab household. The family's commitment to education and literary culture is reflected in this collection, which provided the intellectual environment in which Mohammad Ali Bogra and other family members were raised before later generations pursued careers in national and international politics, administration, and diplomacy.

A collection of traditional and formal costumes and clothing belonging to members of the Bogra Nawab family, spanning from the late 19th century through Mohammad Ali Bogra's diplomatic career in the mid-20th century. The costumes include formal sherwanis, ceremonial robes, and items of Western-style formal dress worn for state occasions and diplomatic functions. The clothing collection documents the sartorial evolution of an elite Bengali Muslim family across the transition from colonial-era zamindari status to post-independence national political leadership, reflecting both Islamic cultural traditions and the cosmopolitan, internationally engaged identity of the later generations.

Well-decorated terracotta panels from the architectural fabric of the Nawab Palace, the historic two-storied building constructed on the western bank of the Karatoya River that now houses the Mohammad Ali Palace Museum. The palace building, over 180 years old, has eight rooms and nine doors on its upper floor and sixteen rooms and thirteen doors on the ground floor. The terracotta decoration reflects the architectural ambitions of the Nawab family in establishing their residence as a landmark of Bogra city. The palace was officially declared a Preserved Antiquity by the Department of Archaeology in May 2016, recognizing its historical and architectural significance.

Sculptures created by the prominent Bangladeshi artist Aminul Karim Dulal, who designed several statues and structures now on display at the Palace Museum, including paper-made eye-catching statues described as among the museum's notable attractions. One room of the museum has been specially decorated with paintings of Nawab family members alongside Dulal's sculptural works. This combination of family portraiture and contemporary sculptural art reflects the museum's dual mission: preserving the specific history of the Nawab family of Bogra while also serving as a venue for Bangladeshi artistic expression and a cultural attraction for the wider public, especially young visitors learning about regional history.

A series of portrait paintings depicting members of the Nawab family of Bogra across multiple generations, displayed in a dedicated room of the Palace Museum. The portraits trace the family lineage from Nawab Altaf Ali through to Mohammad Ali Bogra, documenting the family's evolution from regional zamindari aristocracy to national political leadership. The 180-year-old Nawab Palace itself is dedicated to the memory of both Mohammad Ali and the broader Nawab family, who are remembered for contributions to improving local living conditions in the Bogra region. The portrait gallery provides visual continuity to the family's multi-generational story alongside the documentary photographs and personal artifacts displayed elsewhere in the museum.

Furniture preserved from the original interiors of the Nawab Palace, including pieces from the family's reception rooms and private quarters. The furniture reflects the domestic material culture of a wealthy northern Bengal Muslim aristocratic household across the late colonial and early independence periods. As the largest family museum in northern Bangladesh, the Palace Museum places particular emphasis on these domestic artifacts to give visitors — especially the young students who form a large part of the museum's visitorship — a tangible sense of how the Nawab family lived, distinct from the more abstract political history represented by the photographs and documents elsewhere in the collection.

Artifact_Name: Nawab Family Graves and Memorial Site Documentation
Credit_Donor: Department of Archaeology / Bogra District administration
Description: Documentation of the graves of Nawab family members located within the Palace Museum grounds, which include the palace, an amusement park, a market, and the family burial site. Photographs and site plans document the location and inscriptions of the family graves, providing genealogical and historical information that complements the indoor exhibits. The park surrounding the palace, with its seventy-one trees and three ornamental gateways (including one with a clock and searchlight), forms an integrated heritage landscape with the museum buildings, all situated on the eastern bank of the Karatoya River near Satmatha — the historic commercial center of Bogra city.

Museum_Name: Birshreshtha Munshi Abdur Rouf Library and Museum
Credit_Donor: Bangladesh National Museum / Liberation War archives
Description: A formal portrait of Lance Nayek Munshi Abdur Rouf (8 May 1943 – 20 April 1971), recipient of Bangladesh's highest military honor, Bir Sreshtho, for his extraordinary bravery during the Liberation War of 1971. Abdur Rouf served in the 11th Wing of the East Pakistan Rifles and died on 20 April 1971 at Burighat in the Chittagong Hill Tracts, holding back Pakistani Army forces with his machine gun until he was killed, enabling his comrades to retreat to safety. Born in Salamatpur (now Roufnagar) in Faridpur, he is one of only seven freedom fighters awarded the Bir Sreshtho — the nation's highest gallantry award. The portrait is the central exhibit of the museum, placed at the entrance where all visitors pass.

Museum_Name: Birshreshtha Munshi Abdur Rouf Library and Museum
Credit_Donor: Bangladesh Border Guard / Liberation War archives
Description: A replica of the East Pakistan Rifles (EPR) uniform and insignia of the type worn by Lance Nayek Munshi Abdur Rouf during the 1971 Liberation War. The uniform consists of the standard khaki EPR field dress with the rank insignia of Lance Nayek (one stripe) on the sleeve. The EPR (now the Border Guard Bangladesh / BGB) was the paramilitary force in which Rouf served. On 25–26 March 1971, when the Pakistani Army launched Operation Searchlight, EPR soldiers like Rouf joined the resistance immediately, forming the backbone of the early guerrilla forces of Sector 1. The uniform is displayed alongside a map showing the Chittagong Hill Tracts theater of operations where Rouf fought and died.

Artifact_Name: Machine Gun (LMG) — Type Used by Abdur Rouf (Replica)
Museum_Name: Birshreshtha Munshi Abdur Rouf Library and Museum
Finding_Place: Liberation War theater, Chittagong Hill Tracts
Credit_Donor: Bangladesh Army / Liberation War Museum archives
Description: A deactivated replica of the Light Machine Gun (LMG) of the type used by Lance Nayek Munshi Abdur Rouf in his final battle at Burighat on 20 April 1971. According to Liberation War records, Rouf single-handedly manned his LMG post against a Pakistani Army assault, continuing to fire even after he was wounded, enabling his sector to hold and his comrades to reach safety. He died at his post. The LMG display is accompanied by a detailed narrative of the Burighat battle and the tactical context of Sector 1 operations in the Chittagong Hill Tracts during April 1971. This exhibit is the most emotionally charged in the museum.

Artifact_Name: Bir Sreshtho Award Citation and Medal (Replica)
Museum_Name: Birshreshtha Munshi Abdur Rouf Library and Museum
Dimensions: Citation: A3 framed; Medal: diameter ~5 cm
Description: A replica of the Bir Sreshtho citation and gallantry medal — Bangladesh's highest military honor — awarded posthumously to Munshi Abdur Rouf by the Government of Bangladesh. The Bir Sreshtho (Supreme Hero) is the highest of Bangladesh's six valour awards, given for the most conspicuous bravery. Only seven freedom fighters received it during the 1971 Liberation War; all seven are now celebrated as national heroes. The citation documents Rouf's specific act of bravery at Burighat. The original medal and citation are held by the family; the museum displays a high-quality replica alongside the official gazette notification of the award. A panel explains the Bir Sreshtho award system and profiles all seven recipients.

Museum_Name: Birshreshtha Munshi Abdur Rouf Library and Museum
Credit_Donor: Liberation War archives / donated by sector veterans
Description: A collection of photographs documenting the operations of Sector 1 of the 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War — the sector in which Munshi Abdur Rouf served and died. The photographs include images of EPR guerrilla fighters, the landscape of the Chittagong Hill Tracts theater, and Liberation War memorial sites. Sector 1 covered the Chittagong and Hill Tracts region and was commanded by Major Ziaur Rahman (later President of Bangladesh) in the early weeks of the war. The photographs are displayed with detailed captions tracing the military history of the sector and contextualizing Rouf's sacrifice within the broader liberation struggle.

Museum_Name: Birshreshtha Munshi Abdur Rouf Library and Museum
Description: A printed record and digitized audio recording of the testimony of Mokidunnesa — the mother of Munshi Abdur Rouf — given at the museum's inauguration ceremony on 28 May 2008. Mokidunnesa attended the inauguration as a special guest and spoke about her son's childhood, his service in the EPR, and the news of his death. Her account is one of the most direct personal testimonies relating to any of the seven Bir Sreshtho recipients and provides a human dimension to the heroic narrative. The document is displayed alongside a photograph of the inauguration ceremony showing Mokidunnesa with government officials. Her presence at the opening was one of the most moving moments in the museum's history.

Museum_Name: Birshreshtha Munshi Abdur Rouf Library and Museum
Credit_Donor: Faridpur District administration / museum research team
Description: An educational display documenting the history of Roufnagar village (formerly Salamatpur) — the birthplace of Munshi Abdur Rouf — including historical photographs, a map of the area, and text panels on the village's geography, demography, and economy. The display traces the village's history from its colonial-era name Salamatpur through its renaming as Roufnagar in honor of the Bir Sreshtho hero. The village is located in Modhukhali Upazila of Faridpur District on the banks of the Padma River, and the display includes information on the river's influence on the local economy and culture. The museum is positioned very close to the river bank, and river erosion has been a documented threat to the museum building.

Museum_Name: Birshreshtha Munshi Abdur Rouf Library and Museum
Credit_Donor: Government of Bangladesh; donated by public
Description: The museum's integrated library collection, comprising books on the Bangladesh Liberation War, the seven Bir Sreshtho heroes, military history, the history of Faridpur district, and Bengali literature. The library was established alongside the museum in 2008 as part of the government's initiative to open ten memorial museums in honor of the Bir Sreshtho recipients and language martyrs. The collection includes published memoirs of Liberation War sector commanders, official government publications on the war, biographies of Munshi Abdur Rouf, and a selection of Bengali literature. The library is open to local students and researchers and serves an educational function complementary to the museum's memorial role.

Artifact_Name: Map of Bangladesh Liberation War (1971) — All Sectors
Museum_Name: Birshreshtha Munshi Abdur Rouf Library and Museum
Description: A large wall map of Bangladesh showing the eleven sectors of the 1971 Liberation War, with Sector 1 (Munshi Abdur Rouf's sector, covering Chittagong and Hill Tracts) highlighted. The map shows the major battle sites, guerrilla bases, Pakistani Army positions, and refugee routes. It provides essential geographical context for visitors to understand the strategic situation of the liberation struggle and the specific location of the Burighat battle where Rouf died. The map is accompanied by a timeline of the key events of the war from 25 March to 16 December 1971 and photographs of major liberation war sites across all eleven sectors.

Artifact_Name: Personal Effects — Childhood Artifacts from Roufnagar
Museum_Name: Birshreshtha Munshi Abdur Rouf Library and Museum
Credit_Donor: Donated by Munshi Abdur Rouf family
Description: A small collection of personal effects and childhood artifacts associated with Munshi Abdur Rouf's early life in Roufnagar, donated by his family for the museum collection. The items include a childhood photograph, a school exercise book, and simple household objects from the family home. These personal items humanize the heroic narrative of the museum, showing Abdur Rouf not only as a military hero but as a son, student, and village boy who grew up in ordinary rural circumstances in Faridpur. The display is accompanied by a brief biography tracing Rouf's life from his birth on 8 May 1943 through his enlistment in the EPR on 8 May 1963 (his 20th birthday) to his death at age 27 in 1971.
